div.head: for the year ending April 30th, 1888:
div.p: for the year ending April 30th, 1888:

Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a , balance exceeding £15,000.

Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consepted to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Powke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,928 its 9d. The total amount of payments was £163,018 14s ld, leaving a balance upon the year's accounts of £15,292 45 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Od. 11 The amount paid in Claims daring the year was £77,479, inoluding £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid lup to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 is 10d. The number of Assuran.ts upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10,1, showing a net increase of 39,07 a Assurants, and £27,820 us 9d in Premium Income. SILVER AND GOLD. Farewell, my little sweetheart, Now fare you well and free; I claim from you no promise, YOq claim no vows from me. The reason why ?—the reason Right well we can -uphold— I have too much of silver, And you've too much of gold! A puzzle, this, to worldlings, Whose love to lucre flies. Who think that gold to silver Should count as mutual prize! But I'm not avaricious, And you're not sordid-souled; I have too much of silver, And you've too much of gold. Upon -our heads the reason Too plainly can be seen: I am the Winter's bond-slave, You are the Summer's queen; Too few the years you number, Too many have I told; I have too much of silver, And you've too much of gold. You have the rose for token, I have dry leaf and rim'; I have the .obbing vesper You, morning bells at chime. I would that I were younger, (And you grew never old)— Would f had less of silver. But you no less of gold! —Scribner's .Magazine. BY EDITTI M. THOMAS.

Small comfort—A baby. Surplice Population—The clergy. "Down in the mouth "—The root of the tongue. We are in the stream of life not to soak, but to swim.. The wasp has one strong point, but it is not in his favour. Pride is like a shoe with hied' heels, good for mud but bad for corns. Learn the past, and to a large extent you will know much of the future. The Napoleonic test of character is success, and the final test of success is permanence. A character is formed midst storm and strife; talent Is developed in calm and quietude. "Brown, what did you clear by that speculation ? Perhaps you worry over that bill you've owed ; me for the past two years." "John," responded his wife, "I would meke it hot for you." As her words admitted of more than one inter- pretation, John said nothing more about the coffee. In Limerick an hotel-keeper said to a customer who was complaining about the bad times, "You're a land- lord, sir, and must put up with the times, and make a reduction to your tenants of 50 per cent." This was be- fore dinner. After it came the bill, amounting to eighteen shillings. "Hers, waiter," said the diner. "is half a sovereign. Give your master nine shillings, and keep the change. Ile is an honest fellow, and must put up with the bad times!" It was on a long East India voyaee on a a pleasant evening some sailors were spinning yarns as a pastime. One of them had been wrecked. The ship went down under the crew, and sent them suddenly afloat. He said—" After swimming ten hours, I felt myself about going down, when I saw a cask rolling about in the heavy sea. I mounted it astride, and waited to see what would turn up. At the end of three days I saw a sail: it was a French ship. I sang out, Ahoy, ship ahoy !' 'Who are von?' the helmsman sang out. Where are you bound?' I cried. 'To Calcutta.' 'That's a pity. I am bound to Batavia—and I will not wait !' " Pcyzmiso SoLossots.—The Rev. Dr. Ritchie, of Edin- burgh, though a very clever man, once met his match. When examining a student as to the classes he attended, he said, "I understand you attend the class for mathematics? "Yes." "How many sides 11a8 a circle ?" "Two," said the student. " Indeed ! What are they ?" ••• An inside and an outside." A laugh among the students followed this answer. The doctor next enquired, "And you attend the moral philosophy class also ?' "Yes." "Well, you doubtless heard lectures on various subjects. Did you ever hear one on cause and effect?" "Yes." " Does an effect ever go before a cause?" "Yes. Give me an instance." "A barrow wheeled by a man r The doctor hastily sat down, and proposed no more questions. On the occasion of an entertainment being given by his employer, in Duns, Watt Stobie, a herd, was sent for to lend a helping hand. Tea was being handed round just after the arrival ot the guests, and the part assigned to the worthy shepherd was to carry round a plate of very thinly-cut slices of bread and butter. Walter, on his native heath, had been accustomed to pass good sub- stantial scones to his neighbours when they shared his hospitality, and he viewed with considerable disgust the apologies for substantial food that he had the honour to offer the ladies present. At last, he could stand dt no longer, and seizing an opportunity when no one was looking, lie " dunched " a lady on the elbow, saving, in a low but audible voice, "Clap twa bits Uiegither, ens am, and then ye'll get a guid bite! Were Bs:oases' GUILD.—Perhaps the most curious of a guilds in an Oriental town, and one which flourishes exceedingly in Cavalla, is the beggars' guild. Like other gailds they have their own laws, their president, and their council; this council gives a deploma to those who wish to beg, and without permission no one durst seek alms at the churches, mosques, or street-doors; all the legitimate beggars would rise up in arms against him, and his life would not be worth Much. Friday is the recognised beggars' day, on which they go round from door to door and get their wallets filled with .breed and ; beans; these are divided by the community, nothing is private property; it is against their creed. The beggars' brotherhood ie rich; they possess house property, the income of which is spent for the benefit of the commu- n!ty and ince a year, on the day of St. John the Charit- able, they have a feast. They all go to church on this day; it would be difficult to recognise the tidily-dressed members of this honourable community in their best clothes; rags and tatters are only de rieueur for them when they are on their rounds. Beggary pays very well; if a beggar's daughter marries she is endowed by the community, the president sees to the bethrothal, and his consent is essential to the union. At Salonica, Blind Demetrius is the president; he is easily recognised as he parades the streets, singing his everlasting wail:— Day and night, day and night I live in the dark. Wretch that lam I hear the world, but I cannot see It. And though you know him to be a rich men, that his wife is well dressed and that his daughter will receive a handsome dower, his plea for alms is almost irresistible.— Cornhill Magazine. THE DISAPPEARANCE OF "BLIND JOE."

Joseph Finch, or, as he is more commonly called, "Blind Joe is a newsboy who has for some years been well known in Warrington, where his usual occupation has been selling the evening prints in the streets, varied by an occasional spell at reading the " blind " bible in the Market on a Wednesday or Saturday. Although blind, Finch has always seemed able to pass about the streets in perfect safety, and he is credited with having done aby no means des- picable business from a commercial point of view. When, about a fortnight ago, he was missed from the town, his absence caused some comment, and towards the end of last. week various ugly rumours were bandied about as to what bad become of him. One report was to the effect that he had been found drowned in the canal near Sankey, and it was even asserted that his dead body was lying at the Black Horse Hotel in that township to await an inquest. On inquiry, there was found to be not the slightest foundation/for the rumour, and other reports of his having come to an untimely end, were afterwards received with extreme caution. All doubt as to his wh(reabouts, however, was set at rest on Wednes- day, when a letter from him was received at the local office of an evening paper where "Joe" had recently been employed. The letter, which is unique in its way, read as follows: " Workingmen's Home, 'Higher Hillgate, Stoakpoart, Sept. 18, 1888. Dear —, I write these fewlines to you hopping to find you itt good health, has it leaves me at present remember ma to all the boys they have been spreading false reports about me in Warrington that I was drowned at Widnes. It is not right for them to set them tailes out, and tell the if he does not mind what he is about I will have him don, and if you like to pay fair I will coom and show my fase once more, but I shall never coom to stay at Warrington anny more. I have no more to say at present, from your affectionate friend. JOSEPH FINCH." "Blind Joe," although suffering from the infirmity that. his name implies. displays a marvellous apti- tude in finding his way about, arid when living in Warrington he frequently journeyed to other towns, either to sell papers, or to make his affliction a means of gaining money.
NEWTON PARLIiMENTARY REVISION

div.head: COURTS.
div.p: COURTS.

Mr. James Thomas Foard, barrister-at-law, who has been appointed to revise the lists of the voters for the Newton Division of South- West Lancashire, commenced the work on Saturday. It may be here " mentioned that the number of objections made by the Liberals to voters in the Newton Division is 120, and that the number made by the Conservatives is 180. The Liberals made = ownership claims and the Con- servatives 84. -

div.head: P&WETH. '
div.p: P&WETH. '

The first court was held at the Crown Hotel, Penketh, on Saturday, business commencing at half-past ten o'clock in the morning.—Mr. P. M. Campbell, registra- tion agent, Newton, appeared for the Liberals, and the Conservatives were represented by Mr. Wallhead, solici- tor, Warrington, witty whom was Mr. W. Holbrook, registration agent, Newton.—When the list ot voters for Sankey was under consideration objection was taken by -the Liberals to the name being on the list of the Rev. H. A. Macnaughten,the late Vicar of Preston. The gro.:nd of objection was that the reverend gentleman had left the district. The Conservatives did not oppose the objec- tion.—The Liberals put in an objection to the name of John Hampson remaining on the list as an occupier in Oreat Sankey, on the ground of insufficiency of occupa- tion. Mr. Wallhead put in a letter from Mr, Hampson, in which the writer stated that he had not reckived notice of ebjection.—Thereupon Mr. Campbell called a witness, who stated that he served a notice at the late residence of Mr. Hainpson on the 20th of August, and who also said that the presenttenant of the house informed him that Mr. Hampson finished his occupation of it three months before that date. The Revis- ing Barrister expressed the opinion that the Act had been complied with by reason of the fact that the notice had been delivered at the house. At the same time he thought that it was rather curious that in the ordinary way the notice had not been forwarded on to Mr. Ilannwm by the present tenant, if it were left at his house.—The objection was sustained. —James Woodward, Heath-road, Penketh, claimed as a lodger. The Liberals objected to the claim on the ground that the claimant did not occupy rooms of sufficient value.—Mr. Wallhead then took exception to the notice of objection that had been 'served, contending that it was misleading and altogether bad. The description at the head of the notice was—" Parliamentary and County Government (Division 3)." Then the paper read—" I hereby give you notice that I nbject to your name being on the Penketh, No 3, Old Lodgerk' List (Division 3)." There was no such list.—The Revising Barrister: Sup- posing you strike out the words "Division 3." Then the information is complete, is it not ?—Mr. Wallhead: But it is headed Parliamentary and County Government as well, and the notice in the body is—" as a parliamen- tary voter for the Newton Parliamentary Division." I maintain that the notice is bad altogether.—The Revi- sing Barrister: Well it does not seem the best way to put it.—Mr. Wallhead said that the same objection ap- plied to three other claims.—The Revising Barrister held that the notices were bad, and allowed the votes.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

..... _ Mr. Foard resumed the revision on Monday, when he held two sittings, one in the morning and the other in the evening, in the Parade Room at Warrington Police Station. On this occasion he revised the lists for the townships of Rixton-with-Glazobrook, roulton-with- Fe.arnhead,Warrington (extra municipal), and Woolston- with-111artinscroft. The representation of the political parties was the same as at renketh. The business was mainly of .a routine character, and the evening sitting only Lasted for about half an hour. At the morning sitting the Conservatives made an objection tothe vote of John Ilankinson Gm-nail. J.P., medical officer of the borough of Warrington, on the ground of his removal from Penketh Lodge, l'enketh. to Latchford. In the list Dr. Gornall was described as being of the former address.—The Revising Barrister asked why Dr. Gornall had not made a declaration ? Br. Gornall said that he had received an unstamped notice of objection from the Tory party.—The Revising Barrister: But you saw the list of objections, I suppose, put upon the Church doors ?—Dr. Gornall: No, sir; I do not go to church.—The Revising Barrister said that he might have seen the list at some public place.—Dr. Gor- nail : I have never taken the trouble to look.—The Re- vising Barrister: It is an objection to your residence. You do not live at Penketh Lodge now /—Dr. Gornall: I have lived at Ribblesdale, Latchford, for more than a year.—The Revising Barrister: You could have saved trouble by a. declaration. I wonder why you did not do it to save trouble.—Dr. Gornall: It was no trouble to come down.—The vote was allowed, the description be- ing altered from " Penketh Lodge, Penketh," to " Rib- blesdale Llouse, Latchford."

div.head: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.

• The Revising Barrister, Mr. J. T. Foard, attended at the Assembly-room, Lion Hotel, Warrington, on Monday afternoon, for the purpose of calling over and stamping the recently revised lists of voters. The two political parties were represented by their respective agents, Mr. Clayton (Liberal) and Mr. Hampson (Conservative). At the conclusion of the ‘formal business, Mr. Hampson said he wished to compliment the assistant overseers on the good lists they hadprepared this year, and he ttiaiiked them and those they represented for the care they had taken. He also congratulated the Liberal party on their choice of agent. Mr. Clayton looked thor- oughly after the interests of his party, but they had got on much more pleasantly together at that revi- mon than they did the year before. He likewise, thanked the Revising Barrister for the kindness he had shown to him (Mr. Hampson) and his party.— Mr. Clayton endorsed all that had been said by Mr. Hampson as to the manner in which the overseers had presented the lists. He was pleased such a good feeling existed between the two parties, and he trusted that it would continue to exist in the future. He was also obliged to Mr. Foard for the care he had shown if going through the lists.— The Revising Barrister thanked them for their kind expressions. He quite agreed with them that the lists had been carefully and creditably pre- pared, and he didn't think they had any reason to complain. Agreat deal of care had been shown by the agents of the political parties nnd by the assistant overseers, and he was glad of an opportunity of say- ing so in public, because sometimes there was neglect in that respect. He quite agreed with Mr. Hampson that the revision had gone on very much easier than it often did, and perhaps with much less friction.

div.head: GREAT JEWELLERY SWINDLE AT
div.p: A GREAT JEWELLERY SWINDLE AT
RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Curt, on Tuesday, before Mr. James Handley, a middle-aged man, named George Cleverley, who had been employed on the Ship Canal Works, was charged that he, being the bailee of certain goods belonging to William Leach, general manager,of the quarries and other works of the Bridgewater Trustees, did on the 27th August unlawfully appropriate the same to his own use. It appeared that the two men became acquainted to- wards the end of July, when the prisoner told Leach that Mr. Kirkham had contracted to build him a wooden house in Dukes Fields for £6O, but the Bridgewater Trustees would not allow him to have the land. He asked Leach if he could have the use of the Old Baths at the Ferry or the sailroom, but Leach said he had no power to give such permission. The prisoner then wrote to Mr Berry, the agent to the trustees at Walkden, on the matter, but that gentleman replied that they could let the buildings for living purposes. These transactions brought the prisoner and prosecutor very much together, and on one ' occasion the prisoner stated that he had at one period of his career travelled with jewellery for a farm of Man- chester Jews, and Leach remarked that he "did a bit in that trade" himself. The prisoner pointed out that he was very well acquainted witlr the men on the Ship Canal, and that if Leach would let him have a watch or two he could easily dispose of them, and pay tho. money in a day or two. Believing that the man was in good circumstartces, Leach entrusted him with a silver lever watch and a lady's gold guard, worth £5 , 13s. Od. In a few days the prisoner paid 5s ' on account of these articles, and subsequently Leach entrusted him at different times with three gold watches, nine silver, watches, three gold chains, eightsilverchains, and eight gold finger rings, valued altogether at about £45. On the 24th August the ?risoner asked to be sup- plied with two valuable gold watches, but Leach was not able to comply with his demand. As the instalments were not paid regularly, only £2 15s being received, Leach began to suspect that all was not right, and on the 27th August he went to the address in Brindley-st., ' given by the prisoner, and found the place quite empty, prisonerhavingabsconded and conveyed by rail furniture which had been hired from Messrs. Lea, of High-st. A warrant was issued for his apprehension, and on Mon- , day he was captured in Salford by Sergeant Gosling. It ' was discovered that the prisoner had pawned several watches and chains with Mr. Marsh, pawnbroker, Church-st., Mr. Davies, pawnbroker, High-st., and at several places in Manchester. At the place where the prisoner was living a large bundle of cards, setting forth that the prisoner *as a furniture broker, was found. The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Knutsford Quarter Sessions.

div.head: MR. URAILBERLA.IN AT BRADFORD.
div.p: MR. URAILBERLA.IN AT BRADFORD.

At a conference of Liberal Unionists of Yorkshire and the North of England, held at Bradford, on Wednesday, Lord Hartington sent a letter of apology, in which he de- clared that the policy of the Home Rulers had shown iti self to be based on principles a lawlessness, which seemed to be meeting with increased acquiescence on the part of their English allies. Lord Derby wrote expres- sing the opinion that the question seemed to be whether those who encouraged resistance to law should be al- lowed to do so with impunity, and should be regarded as martyrs if their offence brought its legal punish- ment.—On the motion of Mr. W. S. Allen, secqpded by Mr. Richards, a resolution was adopted, acknowledging the patriotic and unselfish action of Liberal Unionists in the House of Commons, which enabled the Government to maintain the integrity of the empire and the supremacy of Parliament, to make satisfactory progress in the restoration of law and order in Ireland, and to pass important and valuable laws for the good of the kingdom. On the motion of Mr. Caine, M.P., a resolution affirming the desirability of better organisation amongst Liberal Unionists and cordial co- operation with the Conservative party was carried unani- mously, and the proceedings terminated. In the even- ing Mr. Chamberlain, addressing a great Liberal Unionist meeting said the Gladstonian Liberals had no policy. They had only a leader, and they did not care into what ditch he was going to lead them. The Liberal Unionists were denounced because they had taken the right view of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill, and they would not now consent to follow a man tsvho made this proposal into a second proposal, the details of which he refused absolutely to disclose. He (Mr. Chamberlain) found an analogy to the shortsightedness of the Glad- stonians in the history of the French revolution. The Girondins allowed their talents to be placed at the ser- vice of the revolution, and they were used to cover its excesses. They thought they were guiding the storm when they were really being swept away by it. In the same manner the Gladstoniaas would be swept away by the persons with whom they were now allied after the legislation which had been effected on behalf of the Irish tenants. He ridiculed the idea that evictions now going on could be unjust, and he defended the Govern- ment in their administrationvf the Crimes Act.

--- On Thursday morning, he said he was very much en- couraged by his visit to Bradford, and by what he had heard as to the progress of their principles. No one had desired more than he that with further time for con- sideration the differences between the two sections of the Liberal party should be removed, and at an earlier stage he saw no difficulty in the way of their removal. Under these circumstances it was unnecessary to decide upon anything in the nature of a final arrangement or alliance with the Conservative party, but his hopes had been entirely disappointed, and so far from getting neater to the Gladstoniana, the distance was becoming greater. All hope of reconciliation with the Glad- stonian party being at an end, Liberal Unionists in the various localities should take steps to establish the alli- ance with the Conservative party. He was ready to share the responsibility with the Government for their policy. Their opponents might abandon the hope of a division taking place in the Unionist rank. Herbert James Lcadbeater, formerly in the service of the London arid North-Western Railway Company, was arrested at Morley, near Leeds, on Thursday, on the charge of stealing a mail bag containing securities valued at £5,000 from Batley station. div.p: HBLPIIiG A "BOBBY" OUT OF A FIX. By A. BOOBY. -
(From the " Blackburn Times.")

. One Friday night, some years ago, I was going home late from my work up that narrow, tortuota, and at that time badly-lighted street (I cannot call it la thoroughfare), named Northgate. I had safely passed the mouths of those ancient relics of old Blackburn slums called Upper and Lower Cockcroft, the throttle- valve leading on to Blakey Moor and Engine-street, ewhere the used-up betting men, lazy bricklayers, slink butchers, and bloated bum-bailiffs most do congregate; when, on approaching Cannon-street, I heard certain ,sounds, not at all unusual, which convinced me that a street row was in a state of fermentation, and that there was no policeman to look after it. Now, at this particular corner, having passed it late and early for twenty-five years, I have seen brawny policemen quail and hesitate to interfere when big- bellied bullies, who did nothing but eat, drink, fight, and dissipate, have struck cowardly blows in their pre- sence; blows calculated to knock the very life out of a weakly-frame; and in this district lived two brothers, one of whom used to boast that he had killed a man with one blow, and the other pounded a man's head on the flags with such force that he perished in a day or twe ; the man who was•,killed being at least 501bs. lighter than the other. The screaming of a woman was the first sound that attracted my attention, mingled with the brutal jeers of drunken men, and on looking over the heads of the crowd I saw a woman laid on the rough stones in the centre of the ring formed round her, mad drunk. She was young and fair, had long black hair, was plump as a partridge and had had a baby in her arms which a kind-hearted female had pityingly taken from her lest it should be killed with its mother's mad antics.

Several neople who appeared to know her tried in vain to get her on her feet, but she kicked and.cursed them until at last a foolish young policeman hove in eight, and the crowd, which was now increased by the rakings of the tripe shops and beerhouses opened out to admit him. He was very tall and stout, barefaced, and had a weak voice; but he was no match for this fearful example of frail womankind. He said she was worse to handle than a man, and be shaped very badly from the start. Ile had evidently only just got into the force from some rural district ' where the clergyman had recommended him as a solid and stolid young man, fresh from the cart-tail. So he hauled this virago up Northgate clinging to one wrist, whilst she with the other hand loose tore his cape off his back, damaged his helmet by pelting him on the head with it, and left the marks of five of her command- ments On his brow. All the while he whistled vigorously for help, but none was forthcoming. • When he had got her as far as opposite the Mason's Arms, on that portion of the street which the Corpora- tion of Blackburn cannot *claim, but must keep clean, he appealed to me, as I looked at him rather sympatheticcally, for help, and, in an evil moment, I consented. I felt sure we should have her at the Town Hall in quicksticks, and told him so, but I reckoned without the host, or rather hostess. _ .

• We each seized her wider the armpits, lifted her off her feet, and turned the., corner of Thunder Alley smartly, and were going at a good pace past the Charity School, the mob following gaily up to see the fun, which they evidently knew was in store for them, the woman with the child begging of the officer not to ill-use the poor little thing's mother. At this point the wily creature we were carrying sud- denly arrested our progress in a manner we little sus- pected, for she, suddenly twined each of her legs round one of mine and the officer's—in fact, "leg-locked" us, which had the immediate effect of bringing us all three down to the ground with a crash; and as bad luck would have it I was it the bottom, a twelve-score police- man on me, and the delicate but abandoned female on the top of the pile. The crowd of tag-rag and bobtail fairly enjoyed them- selves now, two or three of the spiteful ones kicking us in the ribs whilst we were engaged in the process of dis- entanglement on the floor; and the woman who was carrying the child said it was a shame for two great hulking men like U 9 to abuse a woman the way we were doing. On hearing this, the woman we were abusing, noticing that I had a decent pair of whiskers, entwined her taper fingers in the roots thereof, and as it was dark, and the policeman could not see to entwine them, I had to do it myself, but it was only with great pain and the loss of two handfuls of good black hair that I succeeded In loosening her tenacious grip. I now felt very much inclined to desert my post as amateur peace officer, and the paid constable, noticing that I was none too eager in resuming my task, cheered me up by remarking that it would be made all right at the station: and as I thought there might be more pains and penalties attached to the job if I shirked it than those I had already suffered, I unwillingly awaited further instructions, and anxiously looked over the heads of the crowd in the direction of the Town Hall for the help which would not come. ' His instructions were couched in the following terms :—"Yo' see, mestur, if we carry her like we dud afooar hoo'l leg us deawn ageeon, so we mun ayther on us gad howd ov a arm an' lap it reawnd eawr necks, an' then we mun whip her up off her feet and seeaze a leg apiece sooa as hoo cornd leg us deawn. We's happen sum on us be hort itiwe keep foin', an' my clooas ull nod be fit to be sin ageeon, for to mek things wos aw've split my treasurs across t' knees, an' them- new uns." I implicitly obeyed the bobby's injunctions as to the leg and arm arrangement, and we quickly had her hoisted shoulder high, amid the groans of the scum of Northgate ; but still she was not powerless for mis- chief, for, although her limbs were fast, it did not pre- vent her from spitting first in his face, and then in mine in sheer drunken spite. When the procession had passed down the side of the Town Hall and reached the weighing machine, where Old Lolly used to dispense tickets to the just and the unjust, we found no less than four policemen awaiting our arrival, and one of them rudely dispossessed us of our burden, and said he would show us how to convey drunken women to the lock-ups. Upon this he took her long black hair and wound it tight round his great brown hand until it touched the back of her head, and thus he dragged her Into the police-station, I and the woman with the infant meekly bringing up the rear. The charge was duly entered against her in the police books, and the child also was taken Into custody, but still there was no sign of any recognition of my conduct in the affair, and as the stolid young man who had been my partner In the hugging business said nothing, I was duly cleared out of the building, along with two or three of the loafers who had followed us in to see the result, without even being thanked. From that night my somewhat high-falutin' notions of the majesty of the law, and the necessity of law- abiding subjects responding to the call of duty when a fellow-creature is in danger or distress received a rude shock, and I am now more than ever inclined to take the other side of the street, in case I see a row when I am plodding quietly home, as my personal appearance might be considerably altered if I again attempted the part of a (bad Samaritan.

RHYMES 111-THE DIALECT. TH' OWD HAGMON. Ther's nooan better known than th' owd ragmon, For nobrv's mooar kindly at heart He's weel liked hi th' wimmin an' childer As flock, when he comes, reawnd his cart. It. drawn bi a payehunt owd jackass, A quote un' weel used an' weel fed ; tin childer like stroking poor Neddy, An' givin' it bits o' ther bread. ills voice seawnds so hearty an' cheerful, As on he gooas sheawtin' thro' t' Street; Tho' th' owd wossinin' wi' wear fast, An' slaakey a bit ov his feet. He's nowt to complain o'er for custom, What's t' cause on't aw herdly con tell, It's happen his clooas as folk pities— He's an owd wawkin' ragshop hisser / A while sin, when th' owd fella sterted, He'd a truck as he pood up an' drawn; Wi' colors an' o sooarts o' oddments,- 0 th' lot happen wo'th hawf a creawn ; But he managed to scrat up a livin' Wi' rags an' booans, owd shoon an' spoons, An' he oft riled a tidy bit eawt on't, When he coom reawnd at fleet wi' balloons! Id wur then as he blew an' owd bugle, Wi' a "Ra.ta-ta " dismal enuff, An' for rags he'd swap matches an' toffy, fleaw childer wur 'Geed wi' his stuff! An' then, for a while, he'd a peep show, For a hawp'ny, or rags, yo' could look At o th' wonders he hed Chad sooap box, But he never stopt long i' one nook. Wed pictures he hed! They wur stunners, Cut eawt o' t' waste papers he'd bowt, An' he'd stop when he met poorly childer, An' show 'em his treasures for nowt, An' faythers an' mothers took kindly To t' chap, good an' thowtful as that!. An' checked o t' ruff lads fro' ther antics, For some on 'em hed used t' fella bad. After thad, he begun sellin' whitestooanes, Wi' yollo' stooanes, brickdust, an' sand; An' as trade week hi week kept on mendin', Lie soon geet some brass weel i' hand. 'Twur then as he bowt yon ow'd donkey, An' a nice tidy cart, too, beside; But his oboes dudn'd mend wi' his trappin's-- It's a sign as th' owd mon's little pride. He'll buy owt at o at's wo'th buying, An' gi e yo' full value for 't, too, It's mony a year neaw he started, But nobry's yet cod him a Jew. Yon's him! Aw con hear his voice ringin'! " Nea,w, fooak, do yo' want brass or sawt? Brine yo'r rags an' booans eawt !" Stur up, wimmin, Go an' trade. If yo' dorn'd it's yo'r fawt ! 'JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.head: FIER BROTHER'S *KEEPER.'
div.p: FIER BROTHER'S *KEEPER.'
BY Mts. J. K. SPENDER,
Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives,* "Both In the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.,
CHAPTER XL ADBEYFORD IS ASTONISHED.

"Oh, to spend one's life there," Ursula had said more than once to herself, when she had been over- worked and struggling with poverty in Paris, as a vision of her grandmother's home had risen • before her tired eyes. But after a few weeks of the coveted bliss her tone had altered.
"I used to think it an ideal thing," she said fo Dr. Havard, to whom she chattered freely about her affairs, but now, though I wouldn't admit it to Ray, I confess it seems sometimes a trifle triste."

The contrast between the lazy quietness of St. Agatha's and the excitement and brilliancy of Paris would have jarred on many girls. Ursula had not known till now how that foreign life to which she had been accustomed from a child, suited her far better than the present social respectability. The life had not only been more enjoyable and natural than the dull regularity of an ordinary English home to one who saw and felt so keenly; but the foreign climate seemed to have gifted her with a vivacity, and independence which were irrepressible, though there was not the least taint of coquetry about her.

Even to the most liberal-minded person there was something very startling in the bold opinions ad- vanced by one BO young. "It could not go on. No," as Miss Havard said, after a short experience of the girl's free and inde- pendent talk, "it could not possibly go on," Sooner or later she would have to tell Ursula how "all. Abbeyford " were talking of her. To be "talked about" was, in' Miss Havard's eyes, to be guilty of the most heinous offence. Meanwhile, fortunately for everyone there was the usual -egress. for July and August. People were excursibnizing everywhere, rrom the New Forest or. Malvern, as samples of inland ' places easily . accessible, to Llandudno, Bude' or Scarborough, for those who aimed at more distant seaside resorts than Weston or, Dawlish. A few 'of the more adventurous were planning excursions to the Highlands, to the Black Forest, to Switzer- land, or to Norway, whilst the meet daring of all let their houses for six months, intending to winter in Italy, and one or two were even intending to see the Sphinx, which was just then attracting attention owing to a talk of digging it out of the desert. So far had the mania for modern travel infected even the quiet Abbeyford folk. It was a little hard for Ursula, who had given out, in her imperative way, "I shall not go anywhere. I shall stay at home and enjoy St Agatha's when everyone has gone." She WAS not a girl to break her resolution, but as she acknowledged to her brother she was already beginning to long after the "jolly outside world.' She was already beginning to find life at St. Agatha's a somewhat unliveable life. But -a "sense of duty," as she solemnlyannouneed, "came before travelling," and as she added with a pretty air of importance, "There was so much to see to connected with the estate." "Get your brother out as much as you can. The place is pretty enough, no doubt, but at this time of the year it is a confounded hole," grunted the doctor, in disapproval of Raymond's languid ways. "A; soon as the grouse shooting begins we'll make him. work in some way or another—some stiffish walking an a Highland moor would do him more good than all the foreign watering places." For a little while both of them delighted in the country, especially that part of it said to belong to Ursula. Even then the walks and rideswere rather wild ones. Ursula and Raymond did odd, unconven- tional things. "You need not shock people's prejudices," pleaded Margaret Havard, when she visited them one day. "I want you to be particular before the Abbeytord season begins. You have only met a few people, and have been to no large assemblies as yet; young girls should not be talked about, and Mrs. Wilson. is so lax."

_ "Oh ! Mrs. Wilson is a dear old thing ;'she never annoys us in the least," rejoined Ursula, with a saucy smile and a tender look, in spite of it, which seemed to smite a chord in Margaret Havard's heart. "She lets us do just as we like, and you know we have always been used to it." "Mrs. Wilson- ought to have too much-sense," muttered Miss Havard, loud enough to be heard. "No, indeed, you would do just the same in her place. They want to iron me down to one pattern —send me to the wash and stiff-starch me," said the girl, fondling the hands encased in the old creased kid gloves which Miss Havard was given to wear- ing, • You don't think so badly of me as all that?" Margaret Havard was on the verge of tears. She was not a woman of narrower prejudices than the majority of her sex; but her instincts were properly insular, and she did not know what to do with a girl who defied all her previously conceived theories. She was intending to give recondite directions to Ursula'as to the right method of dealing with all the different "sets " of Abbeyfordian society, whom she would have to meet, conciliate, and keep separate when the winter began. The girl annoyed her by tossing her head and saying it was like the riddle of " the fox, the goose, and the bag of corn." How in the world was Margaret to teach her the "ins and outs of things" when she was so refractory? And yet it was necessary for Ursula's manners to be lacquered with a little more tact and rourtz,sy, if she meant to be at all popular in the neighbour- hood, and to avoid treading on the corns of others. Margaret had herself been trained adeording to English methods to have endless patience with other ladles, even when they were fatiguing, and was fairly taken aback, when Ursula exclaimed breathlessly— " Well, for my part, 1 always lude to receive visitors We were so shut up—Ray and I—with our comrades in Paris (she positively said ' cona- rades ' when speaking of young men • and appalled Miss Havard) that our first impulse is to get away from too many new faces. We have so little in common with them. They Want to hold back in everything, and we—we want to go forwards. En avant! varwarte," she almost shouted to Migs Havard's consternation, spreading out her pretty, well-shaped arms, as if she were a sort of bird in- tending to take flight, and leaving that lady open- mouthed anti staring. "You underrate our good friends here," said Mar- garet, who in her own quiet way was given to study- ing character, and fancied she had a distinct gift for classifying the men and women whom she met. "The) aro so reFigions, 60 charitable, so particular--you' i rarely hear of anything wronggoing on n Abbey-ford." " Indeed !" said the girl, shrugging her shoulders; "I really cannot judge. I don't care to make friends I with people who pretend to be se much better than their neighbeurs."- . She could not have put it into words, and yet she thought to herself that they were many ef them very earth-hound souls indeed whom Miss Havard was so fond of calling religious. Neither could she explain to the lady, whose Protetitant feelings were strong, that her sole idea of a religious servicewasof a certain mystic dreaming. in which she had a luxurious sense of losing herself. In such dreams she had occasion- ally been accustomed to indulge during the gorgeous services of the cathedrals in Paris.

" I have a great horror of these light-headed, specu- lative, talkative sort of young wouien,with their Will- o'-the-wisyish theories • they are choke full of irrever- ence," said XiP+3 Hamill, impatiently. "She is different from other girls," answered her brother,;in another tone ; "she has been a good deal alone, and ho.s had time to nurse all sorts of idealisms."

"Idealisms ! You cannit tell vetat she believes." "Only stroug faith can give us a real firm grasp of what we beliove, and charity for those who do not see as We do," answered the doctor, gravely. Ittwas amusing to notice how he always saw the faults of the bey, arid how unwilling his sister was ts• admit the good points of the girl. :If Dr. Ilavard's stricture was correct, that Raymond was so linnikin that he would always need to be under his Sister's wing—that it would never do for him to beeeme a husband or a father lest he should:tormdnt laimself to flddlestrings in these new relationships—if it was true that the lad was weak and could invent all sorts of ways of suffering for himself and for other people, it was equally true that Ursula could scarcely open her lips without shocking Miss Havarch prejudices. That lady's imagination rarely extended beyond Abbeyford and its local pre- judices. Paris was a wicked place, Germany the alxxle of Socialists, Italy that of cut throats. In her conversation with Ursula, sharp discussion was to be avoided, the two were perpetually jarring on one another. - _ -

The doctor's advice that the Campions should be perpetually in the open air increased the complica- tionsassoon a.v, the Al-01031°rd people began to return froin their seaside visits. Miss Ilavard was almost juvenile in her desire to chaperon Ursula. "What are you going to do to-morrow, or the next day or what did you do yesterday ?" was her eon-

stant refrain,asshedrove over frorqAbbeyford,having suspicions that Mrs. Wilson was scarcely up to her duty. If there was an excursion on foot, )n the carriage, or to an afternoon party Miss Havard was always ready with her code of instructions. She nervously inquired how the visitors bad been received—knowing that the Abbeyford people were on the look out for oddities ; while she considered that Mrs. Wilson was almost as bad as Ursula in her ignorance of what was wing on in the sensible world around her. Even her brother did not deny that Margaret had a good deal to 'pa up withosonsidering her invincible repugnance to anything unconventional and her horror of hearing her best friends at Abbeyford spoken of as if they were unreasoning "Philistines.' She could not, as she said, endure the girl's " taking-for-granted " way. To see two young folks .go trampling with iron heels over everyone's prejudices was as bad as turning out a couple of 'donkeys into a flower garden. To hear Ursula descant on the decrepit prejudices of some of the good ladies who came again to call upon her was enough to try the patience of a saint. Neither he nor his more particular sister could at all understand the expression of surprise and contempt on the girlish face, when Margaret once referred to.the possibility of Ursula's marnage. "As if that were a subject which could possibly cor earn me r she exclaimed, with an indifference which could not be assumed.

Neither of her friends guessed that anything was kept back, and, indeed, in Urania's sense there was milling to be told. • She had only heard once or twice from Louis Grandet, and then he had scarcely dared to address her as a lover. To be "engaged " in her sense had never meant more than what people of a lower social grade in England call "keeping company." i To be married was n the young man's ca,seutterly out of the question. He had been terrified rather than en- couraged by Ursula's sr,clden change of fortune. To do him justice, he had not the courage to urge him- self and his claims just at a time when Ursula was rich and important, and having never told the story of his love affair to .his father and mother, did not think it wise to enlighten them at that crisis. She had been strenuous in the promise she exacted from Louis in her days of poverty not to tell his parents till he reached the age which would release him from the necessity of asking dutifully for the consent of his relations.

"It will give us plenty of time," she had said, in the prctty authoritative manner which had marked all her dealings with men. " but you can write to me, mon ami, now and then." The letters were to be addressed to Raymond as well as to herself: Indeed, on Ursula's side, the com- pact had never meant anything more than rather a stronger dose than usual of the platonic friendship which she was ready to accord to many of the more industyious students with whom she, as well as Ray- mond, had been "

- There were quite enough difficulties just then be- tweet) herself and Miss Havard, without her thinking it necessary to increase them by explaining all this. I "What Radical ideas the girl has picked up, to be sate !" lamented her chaperon, with a sigh, and what courage it required to be always unmercifully correct- ing her foreign accent. The poor lady's brain reek% when- Ursula tried to make her understand that wifehood and mother- hood were but• incidental facts of womanhood, and that celibacy in the present day meant something else than mere conventual life for women. Ursula Cam- pion was by no means inclined to, take any active part in the new movement for the emancipation of her sex. She had no desire for public usefulness, but the, distant echoes of the contest had perhaps affected her; the whole question of domestic duty was altered for her as it is for many girls in the present day, who no longer see why they should stand behind the battle and be content with quietly beating the ordinary ills of a passive life. The struggle for better things, for making her own little corner in the world greener and better seemed to her bracing and stimulating. Why should women be relegated to one narrow held of domestic duty? She gave Miss Havard to understand that momentous revolutions were taking place in this as well as in other questions which were being revised in this nineteenth century—that the assumption that every happy woman should be a wifewas passing away with the old-fashioned tyranny,which allowed women no real career but that of married life, and restricted them by artificial and unwholesome barriers. "I never saw such idiots as most people are when they think themselves in love," continued the irre- pressible Ursula, who dearly liked to tease Miss Havard. "There is such a ridiculous inability to think of anyone else but themselves--such a quintessence of selfishness—only it is a selfishness ci deux. I don't see the difference. I' "My dear!" expostulated the old lady, with tears in heK- eyes, remembering her own little romance. Between the two kind ladies,who were inclined just then to despair of her, Ursula sometimes felt the positive necessity for escaping to the refreshment of solitary walks excursions , or of excuions with her brother. But there were drawbacks connected with these ex- cursions. Even the doctor was bound to admit that the two were not yet used to English ways, and were too fond of pottering about in a little cockle- shell of a boat on a river, the currents of which were sometimes strong as well as dangerous. "Do you mean to say they have gone on the water to-niyitt / " cried Mrs. Wilson, in abine alarm, one evening in August, when the weather had cleared, after an interval of heavy raih. She had already told Ursula that the river would be turbid and swollen, and determined, as she usually was, to say nothing disparaging of the two in- experienced 'young people,. she could not help losing her patience, and exclaiming— " She is really the most headstrong girt I over came in contact with." _ _

Yet Ursula had been far from intending to be headstrong when she ooaxed Raymond into the fresh air for a row on the tempting-looking river with its water deep grey and black in the shadows after the heat of the day, and glittering here and there as if with diamonds. Fartlibr. on it widened into a broad expanse of water, which during the rainy weather had been often lashed by squalls. There was a strong and dangerous eddy round the point setting in for the weirs which any Abbeyford people would have left on that special evening at a respect- ful distance. It needed a cunning hand to steer the little boat carefully. Raymond, whose nerveless arms had never been strengthened by football or cricket, was content, as usual,to lean back on the cushions' whilst his stronger sister took the skulls, nothing abashed at her own inexperience in rowing. So long as the tiny craft could be propelled in one fashion or another the two were content. - "I suppose this is what all women will do when they get their rights ?" said the boy, well pleased. And the girl answered him with a smile, scarcely conscious that they were floating with the current. Her eyes were fixed on the changing aspect of the evening sky .with bright clouds relieving its gloom, like those bright-coloured hopes and wishes surround- ing her own young life with a sort of nebulous atmosphere of unreal delight. To be out was to escape from worry. She oould net long be troubled about anything, her horizor: was for ever expanding, in accordance with lier sanguine disposition and her elastic character. She had confidence in herself, and confidence in Ray, who would develop into a fine type of the country gentleman; and what ideal could- be higher than that of 's. country gentleman? It was•like being shaken down from the seventh heaven into very com- monplace reality when she heard an exclamation from her brother, who was alarmed at the sight of biggish waves running up against the boat. "Take care! What are you about? That is just like a woman," he cried out in sudden terror.. . _ _

, ...___ ~ ... No more time to think of the roseate purple of the sky. She caught her breath as she saw that Ray- mond, in his agitation, had lost all command of the rudder. . "Keep still," she said quietly; "I will bring her head round."
But the eurrent wa-s too strong •, the little boat wee drifting towards the weirs, and Ursula remembered that the doctor had warned her to avoid them: _ _ _

_ "They should put up a danger post. It will be their fault if we are drowned," she said, with her innate tendency to be constantly redressing grievances. At another moment she would ,have laughed loud and merrily at the strange figure her brother cut,half on his knee.: and appealing to her with an involun- tary groan. To an Englishman the sight would have been more contemptible then to a Frenchman. It might have suggested that there were cowardly depths in the sensitive nature as well as those raw surfaces, against which it was so easy to brush. But Ursula was ever indulgent to the delicate lad's bodily weakness, though it was not in her own nature to cry out at any crisis. The boat was darting forward,but with the quick- ness already intelligence she rowed hard for the shal- lower water near the bank with a hope of arresting its motion and stranding it on the sand. "Steady, steady, backwater," someone cried slid. denly, in a voice which rang out cheerily from the slwre. • _ _ .
The unexpected directions given in a man's deep tones, somehow helped to give extra strength to her arm. She made another vigorous, effort which +ha &bat, in nontact with a shelf of rock. It

seemed likely to go to pieces, but at any rate it 19111, successfully stranded for a time. "Take your nat and bale out the water,. Itke palled to Raymond, who was anxious to is his boll and to contend with the sick feeling which hinderel him—the perspiration breaking from every pore el , his skin. .And then she felt that her skirts vt„ete already getting wet, and that the water was rapiolY rushing in with a rich gurgle into the boat. And she next instant the figure of a young man only a few years older than Raymond—half swinr ming, half wading, was seen striking out with d„r termination from the bank. Before she had time tl` realise what the stranger intended to do, he had take!, her coolly round the waist and set her down on slippery stones, where she found it difficult to UT her footing. Then he went back instantly tO her brother. he P as' Her skirts were soaked through. and her 1026. sodden with wet. The hairpins had come out of'!',l hair, and she was conscious of a shivery feeling, ice applied to the spine. But there was no time remember thesorry figure which she cut, for it Vitw Raymond who demanded immediate attention; throwing himself down from sheer inability to sttur as soon as they reached a dry place on the bort';', "Is he liable to these attacks of faintness-% asked the stranger, a little scornfully, surveYil him as if he were a natural curiosity. "It is Y. who ought to be upset. You righted .the b° pluckily enough." et He did not mean to be rude. He was '6l enough himself, minus coat and waistcoat, dropping water all round him like a big Newfoal land dog—he evidently did not know lie wa.a addt69' sing the young chatelaine of St. Agatha's. ce " Oh, I—" answered Ursula, laughing, "I 'hi' never been known to break down. But my brothet Is not strong." Ah, I understand, the sort of weakness which *° man can't always help." 1,4 Then their eyes met. He was not handsome,-,,-, she thought him all the stronger, manlier, for t' zet sinewy hands and rough-cut, expressive facciei What was there in the face which gave her an °. sensation, difficult to define or analyse—a sen..4att°otil of which she had been conscious once or twice in life before—of having a sort of involuntmy recognitl".o of this stranger, as if there was a synipatbeti relatedness between them which would make it WI. possible for him long to remain a stranger. Yet hs did not even tell her his name. He &Pre; cated het thanks with the brightest assurance that 1.1. was quite used to that sort of thing and had ogl done it before, as if he were an übiquitious aø of the Humane Society; declared that he was 00 a in the neighbourhood of Abbeyford for the nay, ttcl3l4 should have just time to join his friends and 013 his clothes at a neighbouring inn, and that it w°,. be impossible for him to accept her courteous inviw' tion. "How ridiculous of me to have felt as if voehr met in some other sphere:before, when in all pr°,4 ability I shall never set eyes on him again," thoug'a Ursula with a touch of self-contempt as they rent% the manor house at a late hour to find Mrs. Wl' reduced to the last extremity of terror. (To be continued.)
THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON'S 131- PRESSIONS OF GERMANY. ..,,„
The Rector of Warrington, the Rev. F. W. W 1 after travelling on the continent for some time.

turned to Waii:ington last week CO. take ebarge4 the affairs Of the parish. During the course a 1114, sermon at the Parish Churck, on Sunday evening, told his hearers some of the impressions that P.., had received during his temporary sojourn in Gel-4i many. Wherever he was, he said, he had made.; a point to carefully notice ,the manners and ea', toms of the people, and to ti.y to learn soniethial,' from them that might be of use to the peon &amongst whom he was now to live and labow There were many things with respect to the Of man nation that were worthy of imitation and ar, miration. He did not mean to say that the mans were a perfect nation, but certainly 00 were a great nation, Indeed, some of the Ger!fll_. thbught that Germau was the nation of the futu, They had their faults, but they had also their tues. One great virtue they had was order discipline. They were a great military' nation, " though it might be that the militarymovementlil carried to an extreme. Wherever one went, allj, where least expected, he sav men being drilltled The Germans said they were afraid of the count's:re on either side of them. It was a fact that t"„"fo. was a good strong Government in the countrY, 0 that law and order were respected. The Pe°-F,, obeyed like children, believing that what they. w'iee. told to do was for their good. There was a tit°, when the German nation looked upon the Engl,9 with envy and jealousy, but it had passed awl". and he could not help thinking that to iv great e tent they now looked upon its with a kind of at, temptuous feeling. Another thing he noticed 1, that, from the highest to the very lowest and blest, there was perfect cleanliness with regar,d dress, food, and household arrangements. T 4aein was a time when ties English nation was looked to as a model of cleanliness, but he doubted whetao it was so now. Another virtue of the Gerrnaue,rhe their sobriety. Wherever he had travelled had gone over the greater part of the German e'it pire—he had never seen anyone the worse for driato although it was the habit of the men and woraeP .• drink beer. These seemed to him to be point! Is, which we, as an English nation, needed reformat,L°4 He also noticed that in many places the Lord's was observed as man's day—a day of pleasurelll3,6 work—and he saw the effect of this both on and beast. He urged the importance of revereilo the Lord's Day, which should be to all of them s of rest from unnecessary work, and a day of instr" tion and worship.

FURTHER FlUiff i..NG AT SITAKIM. %atm, Mompor.—At daybreak this morning the ..,telels appeared in force, coming from the direction of igt andoub. Her Majesty's ship Gannet opened fire, and tticceeded in dispersing them. They then occupied a 'Poeition in the vicinity of the water fort, and, taking advantage of cover, remained there during the day, 'keeping up a desultory fire, whiCh the forts returned. ,O_Ce Egyptian was wounded in the water forts. The mber casualties taiong the rebels is not known. A PEROCIOU€ DUEL: SHOCKING SPEC- TACLE. Mun, MONDAY NIONT.—A duel of the most fero- ,ek n) may bloodthirsty character has just taken place in `uergal, a small town in the province of Elusive. Two Yming men, who were engaged to two sisters, quarrelled 'Over some trifling matter, and agreed to settle their die- 'Pate by a duel, in which both should be wounded and One at least should be killed. The conditions agreed t2Pon were that the right foot of the one should be tied tithe left foot of the other, and then each being armed With a dagger they were to stab one another by turns 'Until one shank( die. These barbarous conditions were ,e4trtied out to the letter, and with the most coldblooded rerocity, and in the presence of seconds. Each of the °r3robatants received seven wounds before one of them Pired while still tied to his antagonist. The other was woo removed in a dying state. ALARM-LNG FLOODS ON THE CONTINENT. IMMENSE DAMAGE. ...Serious floods are reported from the Trentino and the 1-Yrol. and the Vorarlberg has been the scene of fright- hi calamity. On Monflay evening the Rhine burst _rough the dykes at Koblach and Maeder, completely aeoding the villages of Maeder, Altach. and Bauern, and taaVering the whole country as tar as Hohenembs. A few 'molars later the dykes at flohenembs and Lustenau were 'wept away, and the last-named village became cote Dletely inundated. The whole valley of the Rhine be- tween Mseder and Jwpsac has now the aspect of a lake. znailway communications are interrupted, many persons cave been killed, and whole herds of cattle have been de- It-Toyed. The damage to property is immense. Such floods lave not been seen in the Vorarlberg since 1817. Serious inundations are reported from St. Gall and the Austrian Irontiers. The Rhine is overflowing, and fifteen thousand 44eYe5,,... of land are covered by water two metres deep The frightened people are abandoning the villages pro- tected by the dykes, the stability of which is threatened, between Lustenau and Hobenembs. The crops are en- tirely destroyed. The river Adige is now slowly sub- siding, but the country extending from below Callian, 10 the Italian frontier is all flooded. The damage done by the inundations in the valley of the Adige is enor- rnous, and the Campo di Trentino is covered with water three feet in depth. BREAD RIOTS IN PARTS. Nam, SUNDAY.—In consequence of a municipal de- cree lowering the price of bread, the bakers in St. Denis, Yesterday, closed their shops. This greatly incensed the workmen, who in the evening broke into and plundered the bakers' shops. The police had to interfere, and ,teveral arrests were made. Some of the bakers at St uetais, fearing fresh hostile demonstrations, re-opened their shops this morning. The situation is, however, Still somewhat serious, and the Prefect of Police has left for the dist urbed distriot. VOLUNTARY SELF-SACRIFICE OF A WIDOW. CAtcrorrA, SITNDAY.—A remarkable ease of suttee has Occurred near Cawnpore. The widow of a Brahmin '4llager, after the funeral party had left the pyre, still burning, got there unperceived, and was found dead beside her husband's remains. The police report that the relatives did not connive at or assist in the sacrifice

div.head: ANOTHER SHIP CANAL
div.p: ANOTHER SHIP CANAL

The latest project in canal communication is a Scheme to connect Bridgewater Bay Harbour in the Zristol Channel with Exeter, where there exists good communication with the English Channel by tho estuary of the Exe. As an idea the proposal is old enough, hut, remarks a contemporary, now that canals are • gaining in estimation among commercial Then, the Bridgewater and Exeter Canal may actually be constructed. There are no insuperable obstacles. °TIP hill over 500 feet in height need not even be tun- nelled ;it may be circumvented by engineers. The watercourse would be level from end to end, with anly sea locks to. suit the tides. This would there- fore make the canal available to large sea-going vessels. It is proposed by Mr. Owen, the projector, to have a depth of 21 feet, with 36 feet width at bottom and 125 let width.at surface. The total length would be 62 miles. Vessels of from 1,000 to 1,500 tons, drawing 18 feet of water, would be able to use the canal. On the face of it the scheme is feasible, and apparently the traffic would be remunerative. A long and often tempestuous voyage would be spared many a craft round the Land's End. and the sea-going route to London and Plvitionth from Cardiff would be con- siderably shortened. To fact, the collieries of South Wales would be on equal terms with .those of the north- ,. 4,, east coast in reaching the London market.

A.TTEMPf ED THI PLE MURDER. THREE BROTHERS FIBED AT. Shortly after noon on Sunday, the town of Worksop was thrown into a state of great excitement by the report that a triple murder had been attempted in the public Itreets. It appears that Messrs. Mark, John. and Thomae nollety, three brothers who carry on business at the %ton Works, Canal-road, Worksop, as timber mer- chants and wood turners, were returding from the tnorning serviee at the Westeyan Chapel, and had reached a street known as Church-walk, *hen they heard a pistol shut fired behind therm Turning round they saw an old man named 'John Caudwell with revolver in his hand from which smoke was issuing shot fired had passed through Mark finitely's' left coat sleeve, just above the elbow, and also through the body ,of his coat, on the same side, without, however, 'doing nirn any serious injury. immediately Mark finitely turned round Caudwelt.fired a second shot, which struck hitn on the right shoulder. • The injured man fell to the ground, and John Hollely seized Candwell by the arms. AA Soon as he got hold of him Caudwell fired a third Shot, which struck :Rho flolleiv in the centre of the fore- head. Owing to the man's axiom being pinned, however, the hall glanced upwards, and merely grazed the skin 011 the forehead in its upward course. John Hollely then succeeded in tal,ing the pistol away from Can& Well. police-constable Reeves arrived on the scene and took Gaud well into custody. Mark Uollely was con- l'eyed to the house of his brother John, and placed under medical care. Dr. Casson, who was called in, • found a bullet embedded in the right shoultler. He endeavoured to extract it, hut failed to do so, as the ball had penetrated into the shoulder bone, tracturing it Severely. The injured man now lies in a most dangerous Condition. inn. Caudwol I was for many years in business 11.8 a timber merchant and wood turner at the works now „oecupied by Hollely liras. About five years ago he lailed, and the Doliely Bros. bought the business from the trustees of the estate. They, however, retained Audwell as manager until about two years ago, when he recommenced Int.iness on his own Recount. The Works were under a Mr. Parkin, who absconded, where- Upon the mortgagees lacked the works up, and Caud- welt was thrown out of employment. Latterly he has been working as a labourer. He is about 70 years of age, and resides within a few yards of the attempted mur (lets, Caudwell leis been in a depressed state for a long tirne, the lot,e ,‘' his business having, it is believed. l'erion9ly pre- d :rein his mind.
