OPENING OF THE INQUIRY.

Justices Hannen, Day and S. L. Smith, in the High Courts of Justice, held a prelimary sitting, on Monday, and the Court was well filled, principally by counsel and Pressmen, long before the hour fixed for the commence- ment of the proceedings. Punctually at eleven o'clock Sir James Hantien and his colleagues entered the court.

Sir James Hannon said it was prepeseal to con- duct the inquiry as if this was issue between the de- fendants in the action of O'Donnell v. The Mlles and the persons against whom certain charges and allegations had been made. As the proceedings, said his lordship. were novel, he felt bound to state what he considered should be the scope and nature of the inquiry. As a court they derived their authority exclusively from an Act of Parliament, entitled the Special Commfssion Act, 1888, under the first section of which' they were bound to inquire and report upon the charges and allegations made against certain members of Parliament, and other persons in the course of the proceedings in the action entitled "O'Donnell v. Walter." The inquiry was there- fore restricted, both as to the persons and the charges and allegations. He knew from the summonses issued that the defendants In the action before referred to were before the Cour4 and some of the persons against whom the charges were made. The inquiry would be conducted as an issue between the parties, and, of course, they would reserve to themselves the power to call any persons whom they might think would be able to throw light on the issues involved, although neither side chose to call such witnesses. They would proceed with the inquiry in the manner he had indicated iudici- ally, and as far as the circumstances permit, according to the rules of procedure and evidence which prevail in other Courts of Justice. His Lordship concluded: We are here to-day to hear applications such as are gener- ally heard in Chambers. Who are before us? Sir Charles Russell: I appear, for the purposes of the present, with my friend Mr. A squith for all the members of the Irish Parliamentary Party-1 think 84 or 85 in number. . .

Sir James Hannen • That is a convenient form of stating it, but we should like a list of the names of those for whom you appear. Sir C. Russell I will supply that, but I may mention !hat at a later stage there may be some division of labour, and I may not appear for all these gentlemen. Mr. Graham: I appear with my learned friend, the Attorney-General, who is now in town, for the defend- ants in the action of O'Donnell_v. Walter and others.

A Solicit! said he appeared for Mr. Moser, late an in- spector of Scotland Yard. The President: Is Mr. Moser in any way implicated in these charges? The Solicitor: The inquiry may take a turn which may bring in his name. The Pregident: Then when it does we will hear your application Some discussion next took place as to the form of the inquiry, and the President said if the matter was left to he Commission to decide they were of opinion •it was for the defendants in the action of O'Donnell v. Walter to tender such evidence as they had in support of the charges. . .

Mr. Graham: Does your Lordship think that counsel should open the case before calling eyidon,e, or that merely witnesses shall be examined? Sir Charles Russell: I respectfully submit it would he desirable that counsel should open the case for the defendants, and those who appear for those charged should have an opportunity of putting your Lordships in full possession of their case before calling evidence. The President :We adopt that view. We are now pre- pared to hear applications. _Sir Charles Russell: We prefer five applications. One is for an inspection and photographs of certain incrimi- natory alleged forged letters; one for the dnicovery of documents; a third for particulars of the charges; the fourth for a Commission to examine witnesses in America; and the fifth for an order for the release of Mr John Dillon on such bail as the Court thinks right, Mr. Dillon being in Dundalk Prison undergoing a sentence for an offence under the Coercion or Crimes Act.

Mr. Graham: As I undersand only two letters are re- quired, I do not object to an inspection of them. Sir Charles Russell: My friend is mistaken. • One of !he main charges is the charge of direct knowledge, as- sociation with, and participation in crime by prominent members of the Irish Parliamentary party, and we want an inspection of all the letters read or referred to in the action O'Donnell v. Walter. There is one particular letter stated to be from Egan to Harris, in which it is said Mr. Parnell has no objection to an advance to the :und, and it is suggested that the fund means." the assassination fund." It is important we should have an inspection of this letter, the genuineness of which is denied. We want all the letters referred to in the trial. Mr. Graham: I do not know that I have them. The President; It you have not. you cannot product) hem.

• Mr. Graham : We will produce all the letters in our possession. It was next arranged that. any further apntication made after to-day, pending the next sitting, should be taken by Mr. Justice Hannan a.lttne.
The application for a photograph of documpnts vms consented to.

, Sir Charles Russell said his next applieation was for the discovery of documents. Inasmuch as his case was that the letters to be inquired into were forgeries, it was material to know if all such letters had been produced, or if there had merely been a disclosure of a selection from a larger number, which were, or had been, in the possession of Ike Times.

Mr. Graham said he had to opposethis application, an o he submitted his clients ought not to bo' ph.ced in the poeition of litigants in this matter. This particular form of the inquiry wee not .sought by them, arid the Legis- lature had thought fit to adopt certain allegations made in certain proceedings, to which his clients were the d 5. rendants, as the basis of the inquiry. Sir Charles Russell replied that for the perposes of the Act the parties to the inquiry were placed in a position analogous to that as if they were parties to a spit. If it were only within the compass of the court to Order die- novel-7 where there was a legal suit pending, the whole of the section as to the powers as to discovery and so forth would he entirely unnecessary. The President :We can compel the production of per. ticular documents; discovery ie a totally different. thing --the discovery cf other documents than those whicb you know anything about. Sir Charles Russell went on to contend that the power of their Lordships was in the early part of il second section, which said that the Commissioners should have. in addition to the special powers, all the powers, rights, and privileges vested in her Majesty's High Court, or any judge thereof, on the occa- eion of an action. It was in those lines that their lordships' jurisdiction came in the matter. If so, one of the clearest, duties of the Court yronld he that :here should be an order for an affidavit of d4s.covery With regard to the letters which The Times lied pub- lished, it was of the greatest consequence that they should know whether these documents were a selection e number of from a large other dee-temente which Intel:, have been 'foisted upon the prieieeeters, or whether those published were all they had. fie submitted his clienta were entitled to know. They were perfectly willing to assent to a similar application made against them, sule ject to qualifications which he thought the rules of the Court Set out. Mr. Asquith submitted their Lordships clearly had power to compel either his learned friend's clients or his Own to make a discovery of the documents. Mr. Graham replied, and their Lordships then retired to consider the point in private. After nearly half an hour's absence, the Commissioners returned, and Sir James Barmen inquired of Sir Charles Russell what qualification and restrictions he should claim in regard to Mr. Graham's application for the die. cowry of certain documents. An answer to that would assist, them in their determination as to the present application.

.. - Sir Charles Russell said his objection was that the demand on behalf of The Times was too wide It was scldressed to MT. Parnell and the 85 members who sun. ported him. It had been admitted that the charges vere really only against a limited number of those gentlemen, So surely it was absurd to call on 86 members to make affidavits as to the charges and allegations. There was a great deal of insinuation, but very little direct charging or naming of anyone, and he had to ask that they should have a list of the members charged, and next a statement of the charges and allegations to be advanced before the Com- mission. Sir Charles'then read several extracts from a published report of the action O'Donnell v. Walter, with a view of showing the vague nature of the charges, and lie asked to be told in downright plain, unmistakable lan- guage was it or was it not charged against the Irish mem- " hers, and if so, against whom, that they were guilty of com- plicity before or after the Phcenix Park murder? Was it charged that any of them had been in communication with Egan, or Sheridan, or Tynan, or Nathers after charges were made against them in respect of that crime; and was it charged against Mr. Parnell that he was privy to the murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish, or that•he was an accessory after the fact? All he wanted was the names of the persons charged, and the charges against them; and that he thought he was en- titled to have, if only to simplify the inquiry, Mr. Graham: I again respectfully protest against any attempt to place us in a false position. The President: Do you propose to substantiate any charges. Mr. Graham : I propose to give your Lordships all the information I can give. The President: But the Act of Parliament deals with charges and allegations. Do you propose to substantiate any charges and allegations? Mr. Graham i Ido not know, my lord. I propose to lay before you all the information we have, which we believe, coupled with other matters, will tend to sub- stantiate the charges and allegations which have been made.

The President: Which charges and alle&ations? Mr. Graham: I cannot tell which. We don't make charges and allegations against particular persons. We fay this organisation has been acting in a certain way, and the object of this Commission is to find out who are implicable. The President: Who ^are implicated in the things charged and alleged?" That is what, the Act of Puha- went mpg

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 22, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 22, 1888.
Mr. Gral,nro : this, I would respectfully submit, your lordships most find out. _ _ _

The President: Who did make these charge* and &legations that the Legislature has directed us to in- quire into? Did nobody make them? (A laugh.) Mr. Graham: They were made in the first place, take it, in the pleaa in the .action of O'Donnell o. Walters. Then they were made by the attorney in opening the ease for the defence. What these allega- tions are appear from the speech. Now, your lordship asks me to elaborate that, and make charges against individuals in the form of particulars now. The President: Did the Attorney-General make any charges against Individuals? Mr. Gram : He made the charges against the organ- isation. The President: Not against the individuals? Mr. Graham: The individuals were members of the organisation. The President: Will you specify which were the individuals? Mr. Graham : / do not know. The President: You are not asked to do it now, but at your leisure. Mr. Graham: I have no means of ascertaining. After luncheon, in giving the decision, Sir James Flannen said the Court was of opinion that it had the power to direct discovery of documents, and accordingly they directed that discovery be made by the defendants in the action of O'Donnell against Walter of such documents as might be in their possession or under their control relat- ing to the matters in issue. With regard to the matters in issue with regard to the particular charges, it was important that the court should know what charges and allegations Mr. Graham's clients proposed to give evidence in support of, and against what persons they proposed to give evidence in support of such charges. If Mr. Graham's clients could not do so the Court would, of course, have to do it itself, but he (the President) thought they would do so if they could. That Court were also of opinion that all parties were hound to discover all documents if ordered. Mr. Graham remarked that to make out such a list would require some little time. . _

- -.- Some conversation ensued as to when the Court should commence the actual hearing of the inquiry, and it was decided the date should be October 22nd next, the particulars as to the discovered documents being forthcoming a week earlier. viz.. October 15th. Sir Charles Russell then applied for a Commission v. issue to America to examine Mr. Patrick Egan, whose evidence, he said, was of vital importance, not only as to the forgery of the letters, but as to the mode by which they were made public. Mr. Graham admitted that Mr. E7an was concerned in the inquiry, but contended that did Mr. Egan attend before the Commission and make a full statement, Ile would receive a certificate staying any proceeding, against him. Sir Charles Russell pressed his application, and said it was absolutely necessary that evidence should be forth- coming, but he could not state the reasons publicly. ' The President said that the application was at least premature. Sir Charles Russell then applied that under the second clause of the sixth section of the Act, John Dillon 'nicht be released onon bail on the ground that 11^ was a de- fendant need.d to prepare his defence. Ai learned counsel, continuing, referred to the Act show, that such an application came within its meaning. He sub- mitted that, properly construed. the Act meant that a person -released should be at liberty not merely from day to day, but for a sufficient time to allow of preparing the defence. Mr. Dillon had for many years held a prominent position in public life, and should have opportunity of preparing his defence. Any conditions, such as refringing from political action, would, of course, be complied with. Mr Graham said he would take no part with regard to this application. There were two men convicted in connection with the Plicenix Park murders, and sen- tenced to penal servitude for life, and they would be called by The Times. • Sir Charles Russell : That would be the subject of an application under the Habeas Corpus Act. Mr. billon was one against whom serious charges were made, and in common justice he should have ample opportunity for preparing his defence. The President said the Court was of opinion that the. affidavit failed to convince them that Mr. Dillon could not communicate with his solicitor, and they were of opinion that the applization was premature, but the Court would make an order for the attendance of Mr. Dillon during the actual inquiry, with the condition that bp refrains from taking part in politics, the order would be that Mr. Dillon be released to attend the in- ouiry upon his own recognisances of £l,OOO, on October 18th, and until further notice.

Mr. Graham made an application for power to inspect the bankers' pass books and accounts relating to the League. The President: We think you are entitled to the order. The Court then adjourned until October 22nd.

div.head: WHITECHAPEL MURDER.
div.p: THE WHITECHAPEL MURDER.

The pensionet Stanley, who has been referred to as associating with the murdered woman, has given the police an account of his movements since he last saw the &ceased, which was on the Sunday preceding the murder. He has since been following his usual employ- ment without attempt at concealment. Stanley is said to be superior to the class frequenting lodging-houses in spitemeids, and has known Chapman some two years. The attention of the police is being directed to the elu- cidation of a very suspicious incident. After 10-30 p.m.. on Friday, 11 man passed through the Tower sub-way from the Surrey to the Middlesex Mde, and said to the caretaker, "flays you caught any of .the Whitechapei murderers yet?" He then produced a knife about a foot, long, with a curved blade, and remarked "this will to for tem." He was followed, hut ran away, and was lost sight of near Tooley-street. The man is described as about 50 years of age, Sit. 3in. high, complexion fair, with moustache and false whiskers, which he pulled off while running away; dressed in a new diagonal suit, light dust overcoat, and dark cloth double peak cap,
THE INQUEST. " The inquest on Mary Ann Nichols, who was fminci murdered in Buck's-row, Whitechapel, on August 31st, was resumed before Mr. Wynne Baxter, on Monday. . „ .

Dr. Ewin stated that upon re-examination of thfi body he did not find any part missing. . lifrs. Emma Green stated that she lived in Rucks-row She heard no noise during the night, although she was a light sleeper. Noisy people often passed through the street during the night, Thomas Eade, employed on the East London line, deposed that when in Cambridge Heath-road, on the' Bth josh, he saw a man of suspicious appearance on the opposite side of the road. He noticed a knife pertly concealed in his pocket. Witness called on some other men to assist in arresting him, hut they refused. Walter Purkis, living at Essex Wharf, stated that he and his wife slept in the front of a house overlooking Hock's-row. He retired about 11 30, was awake be- tween one and two, and did net wake again until called by the police. His wife had been awake for an hour previously, but neither of them heard any noise. Other unimportant witnesses having been examined, the police stated they had no other witness.—The in- quiry was adjourned until to-day.

div.head: AN_ IMPORTANT ARREST.
div.p: AN_ IMPORTANT ARREST.

An important charge was made at the Thames Police court, on Tuesday, which the police beleve may throw some light upon the tragedies in Whttechapel. Charles Ludwig, aged 40, a decently-dressed German, of No. 1. 'rhe Minories, was charged with being drunk and threatening to stab Alexander Finlay, of Leman-street, Whitechapel. The prosecutor said that at three o'clock yesterday morning he was standing at a coffee- stall in Whitechapel, when the accused went up drunk, and, in consequence, was refused refresh. meet. He then said to prosecutor, "What are you looking at?" and then pulled out a knife and tried to stab witness. The prisoner followed hint round the stall, and made several attempts to stab him. A constable came up, and he was given into custody.—Constable. 221 H said that prisoner was in a very excited condition. and witness had previously received information that the prisoner was wanted in the city for attempting to cot a woman's throat with a razor. On the way to the station, he dropped a long-bladed, open knife; and on him was found a razor and a long-bladed pair of scissors. Inspector Pimley, H Division, asked the magistrate to remand the prisoner, as they had not had sufficient time to make the necessary inquiries concerning him.—A City constable (John Jackson) stated that early yesterday he was on duty in the Minories, when he heard screams of - Murder " proceeding from a court, in which there were no lights. The court led to some railway arches, and was well known as a very dangerous locality. On going into the court he foynd the prisoner with a woman of bad character. The former appeared to be mder the influence of drink. Witness asked what he was doing there, when he replied, "Nothing." The woman, Who appeared to be in a very frightened and agitated condition, said, "Oh, policeman, do take me out of this!" The woman was so frightened that she could then make no further statement. He sent the man off, and walked with the woman to the end of his heat, when she said, "He frightened me very much when he pulled a big knife out." Witness said, "Why didn't you tell me that at the time.? " and she replied, "I was too much frightened." He then went and looked for the prisoner, but could not find him, and, therefore, warned several other constables of the occurrence. Witness had been out all the morning trying to find the woman, but without success. Ile should know her again. 'He believed the prisoner worked in the neighbourhood.—The magistrate there- upon remanded prisoner—The arrest has caused int&nse excitement in the neighbourhood. The prisonerlwo- fesses not to be able to speak English. Be has been in this country about three months, and accounts for his time for about three weeks; but nothing is known of his doings before that time.

„ It has been ascertained that the name of the man `.7harles Ludwig is Wetzel. He came to this country from Hamburg about 15 months ago, and is a hair- eresser. by trade. He bears an indifferent character, ming dascr4ied as cowardly and quarrelsome, and given to drink. The woman who complained. that Wetzel threatened to murder her has not yet been found, but there should be little difficulty in tracing her, as she has only one arm, . .

In reply to a communication from a committee in Mile-end-road as to the offer of a reward for the appre- hension of the Whitechapel murderer, .the Home Secre tary has written', throne his private secretary, statir that if he had considered the case a proper one for offering of a reward the Secretary of State would at once have offered one on behalf of the Government ; but the practice of offering rewards for the discovery of criminals was discontinued some years ago, be- cause experience showed that such offers tended to produce more harm _than good, and the Secretary of State was satisfied that there was nothing in the circum- stances of the recent case to justify a departure from this rule. -

The inquest on the body of Annie Chapman was con- tinued on Wednesday, when further evidence as to the mutilation of the body was given by the divisional sur- geon. Several witnesses were examined, including Stanley, known as the pensioner. The inquiry was ad- journed for a week, some of the jurymen urging strongly that the Government should offer a reward.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON THE IRISH QUESTION.—IMPORTANT STATEMENT. The articles which recently appeared in the Birminghm Daily Post under the title of "A Sketch of the Unionist Policy," and which were understood to reflect the views of Mr. Chamberlain, are being re - issued by the Radical Union in pamphlet form and accompanied by a preface from Mr. Chamberlain's own pen., Mr. Chamberlain writes :—The sketch 'of a Unionist policy for Ireland presented in the following pages is not, and does not pretend to be. a final and authoritative statement of the views of any section of the Monist party. It is an earnest attempt to exhibit for further discussion and consideration a practical solution of the great problems raised by Mr. Gladstone's hill, the pro- posals in which were condemned by the House of Com- mons and the country as unsafe, unworkable, and in- capable of affording a final or satisfactory settlement. Because a great leader at the end of his career has thrown up the task in despair, and having failed in successive attempts to cajole or compel the discon- tented party to submit has suddenly gone over to them, we, those of his followers whom he could not induce to keep him company, are now fighting on the side against all hie former declarations. It is our duty, and it may added it is our only hope of safety, to meet this un- paralleled desertion by a strenuous adherence to the old lines, and we shall fail if we do not show, not only that the policy hitherto identified with the enemies of one country and now suddenly adopted by so many of our old companions in arms ought still to be resisted and rejected, but also that the objects which its authors pro- fess to seek can be better and snore surely attained by methods in strict accordance with the old Liberal faith."

These " methods " Mr. Chamberlain describes at length. He is strongly in favour of the formation of public works, especially railways, by the State, and believes that this could be done remuneratively. But he attaches especial importance to the settlement of the agrarian difficulty. It is the duty of Statesmen to recognise the earth hunger of this agricultural people, and to endeavour to satisfy it by just and reasonable means. He does not believe in mere "tinkering with rents," as under Mr. Gladstone's Land Act, or in any in- definite extension of Lord Ashbourne's Act, whereby British credit might be further drawn upon. What is wanted is a scheme resting entirely on Irish credit and Irish resources. The attempt must be made to secure, by self interest, a public feeling in favour of the dis- charge of just obligations, and against the defaulter. Assuming,' that the social war which now exists in Ire- land were terminated by a reasonable settlement, there would, Mr. Chamberlain thinks, he strong reasons for desiring, on the one hand, to relieve the Imperial Parlia- ment of some of the constantly increasing burden of its local work, and, on the other hand, to open to Irishmen; in their own country, a larger field of • local ambition, together with greater liberty of action, and greater per- sonal responsibility.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

On Saturday inorning a number of boys, who were armed, fired six revolver, shots at Jeremiah Scannell, a butter merchant, who was on his way to Listowel Market The shooting occurred at Meen's Abbevfeale. Mr. Scannell fled with his horse, and escaped uninjured. It is stated that the cause of the incident was Mr. Scannell having a mowing machine.

Mr. Doyle, a young Dublin builder, travelled on Sun- day with a party of friends to St. Kevin's Bed, a delight- ful spot in county Wicklow. A Little child approached the verge of a precipice, and in hurriedly dragging it away Mt. Doyle overbalanced himself and fell over. De cried out that he was not hurt, but on his friends reach• ing him they found him dead, his neart having burst.

The Dublin coroner has adjourned an inquest on A boy of 13, named Thomas Dunne, who died very sud- denly on Friday morning. The medical evidence wee that the stomach was greatly congested, caused by a large dose of alcohol or some irritant poison. The mother of deceased stated that he had an inordinate love for chewing tobacco. The contents of the stomach will be analysed.

A great meeting was held in Phoenix Park, Dublin, on Sunday, to protest against the imprisonment of Thomas Mororiey; of Elerbertstown, and call for his release. He has been in prison for two years practically for declining to answer questions with regard to the money lodged under the Plan of Camoaign. Speeches were made from three platforms, and it is estimated that 25,000 people were present. The ellief speakers were Mr. T. D. Sulli- van, M.P., and Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P. The latter spoke in scathing terms of the coercion policy of the Govern- ment, and paid a high tribute to Mr. Gladstone's cease- less efforts in the Irish cause. THE IRISH REPUBLICAN BROTHERHOOD. Mr. John O'Leary has written a letter in which he gives an unqualified denial to the statement in the fore- cast of Mr. Davitt's evidence that the members of the 1.R.8. were bound by a solemn oath, the penalty for the violation of which was death. Mr. O'Leary says that up to the time of his Imprisonment there was no such penalty enforced or sought to be enforced by the leaders of the movement, nor was there, as fat as he knows, any such .penalty incurred by anyone. As to what happened after his conviction he cannot, of course, speak with any certainty, but he has not the smallest, reagm for believing that any such penalty was ever embodied in any oath, rule, or regulation of the society Mr O'Leary proceeds to express approval of Mr Davitt's recent speeches, and says lie is happy b• find himself for almost the first time in his life in nearly perfect accord with Mr. Davitt. It will, he adds, be ill for the Irish people if they minimise their claim for self- government or relak th-ir opposition to English rule through over•confidence either in a great statesman or a great party.
lOTIN .DILLON RELEASED.-CRITICAL _

div.head: STATE OF HIS HEALTH.
div.p: STATE OF HIS HEALTH.

By order of, the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland, Mr. John Dillon. M.P., was unconditionally released from Dundalk Prison, en Tuesday morning, owing to the state of his health. Mr. Diilon's term of imprisonment would not have expired till the end of the year. , . • .

Mr Dillon arrived in Dublin shortly after two .-i'clock in the afternoon, and was met by a large number of friends, who cheered him loudly. The hon. member looked much thinner and paler than when he " was committed. His release occa- sioned considerable surprise in Dublin. After acknow- ledging the congratulations of his friends, Mr. Dillon, accompanied by the Lord Mayor of Dublin, drove off to his residence. North Great George-street. Mr. William, Mr. T. D. Sullivan. and other members were at the station. The release of Mr. Dillon was a complete surprise to limself and his friends. 'Until the morninv he had nu ,lea he was to be set free. The first intimation in Dublin was received by Mr. Harrington,. secretary of the National League, only in time to collect the members of , Parliament in town to wet him on arriving from Dun- tialk. The order for Mr. Dillon's release is on. , conditional, and without cause being assigned Leadiug Nationalists say the intimation of the Commission that he would he let nut on the 22nd October, combined with his precarious state of health, precipi- tated the action of the atitherities in recommending his release to the Lord Lieutenant but his friends add that he would not accept his liberty, even from the Commis- sion, if trammelled by any conditions of personal bail or otherwise. The state of his health was giving cause for anxiety. Dr. Farrell, of the Prisons Board, visited Dundalk Prison to inquire particularly as to • his condition and treatment. Dr. Hercules McDonnell and the other prison officials were exceedingly kind and attentive. However, the confinement was telling on Mr. Dillon's constitution, and, latterly he was losing weight. Dr. Jos. Kenny, M.P., who, with the 'Lord Mayor of Dublin, Mr. Harrington. (secretary of the Nat:lona] League), and several other members of the Irish Parliamentary party, received Mr. I Dillot; on alighting from the train at Amiens-street Station, says that judging from his appearance, he is of opinion that imprisonment for a very short time , longer would have had very disastrous results for John Dillon, notwithstanding the great care bestowed on him by the medical and other officers of the prison, because as to his treatment he is satisfied that everything humanly possible was done to keep him in health. Mr. Dillon stayed some time at Dr. Kenny's residence, Rutland-square, and then went to his own home, 2, North Great George's-street, where he re- ceived some personal friends during the even- ing. Dr. Kenny has advised him to take rest and country Air till he recruits himself, and he will try and induce him to leave Dublin for the country. WI Tuesday night some of the trades bands turned out to give him an ovation, playing national airs opposite to his residence, and a large crowd cheered.

The health of Mr. John Bright continues to improve, and the right hon. gentleman looks upon his progress towards restoration as being so satisfactory at One Ash that he has for the present abandoned his intended visit to Llandudno.

The Marquis of Salisbury has consented to visit Scar- borough about the 28th December, for the purpose of opening a new constitutional club.

Late on Saturday night, the Protestant fife band en- tered Gifford, when a riot occurred, and a policeman was wounded in the eye, and several windows were broken. Two COLLIERS Kruam.—A fall of coal has occurred in the Ash pit of the Berry Bill Collieries, near kianley, by which two men, named George Evans and Geerge Leese, were killed, the unfortunate fellows being entirely buried beneath the debris. SI7PPOSED INFANTICIDE AT BRADPORD.—In a box which was found floating on the surface of the Corporation reservoir at Bradford, on Sunday. was found the body of a fully developed child. It is believed the child was living when thrown into the water.

THE WALTHAHSTOW POISONING CASR.—DISCHARGeOF SARRBR.—The grand jury at the Old Bailey. on Tutted iy afternoon, threw out the bill against William Bfirber. chemist's assistant, charged with poisoning Mary Annie French, at Walthamstow, some months ago. SHOCKING DRATIL—At Royton, near Oldham, on Satur- day, the body of Charles Brown, a hawker's son, was found half buried with soil in a ravine. The lad had been missing since August, and it is supposed that he fell asleep in the hollow and was suffocated by a fall of eartll.

GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO BIRMINORAIL—In reply to an invitation from the Mayor of Birmingham, Mr. Glad- stone has promised to attend a reception at the Council House on the 6th November, provided other arrange- ments connected with his visit to the National Liberal Federation meettng can be adjusted so as not to inter- fere.

At a meeting of Volunteers, held in Edinburgh, on Saturday, it was agreed that the new site for the National Rise Association meeting ought to be as near London as possible. Lord Wemyss said he held a very strong opinion that the meeting should be near London, and he preferred Aldershot to the site on Lord Want- age's land. Other speakers condemned Cannock Chase.

KICICFD TO DF,ATH BY AN OSTRICH.—A curious Acci- dent is reported from Marseilles. Thirty ostriches which had arrived from Algeria were being placed in the train for Paris, where they are to be exhibited in the Jardin d'Acclimitation, when a man endeavoured to pluck some feathers out of one of the "birds of the desert." He immediately received a kick from the ostrich, which killed him on the spot

HEROIC ENDURANCE OF ENGINE DRIVER AND STOKER. —On Saturday morning a serious accident befel a driver named Amos Thompson, and a stoker named Robert Hicks, who were driving an express train from Bradford to Leeds. The stoker opened the plate in front ot the fire, and the back-draught was so strong that the flames were driven out, and both men were severely burnt. They manfully stuck to their posts, but had on the arrival of the train to be carried to the Infirmary.

DESTRUCTIVE F/ RE : A LADY BURNED TO DRATTI. —At an early hour on Saturday a destructive tire broke Da on the premises of a firm of pastry cooks and confectioners in High-street, Portsmouth. ft, one house was completely gutted. A young lady H.— at, named Palmer, who was asleep in one of the ted uedrooms at the time the fire broke out, and was forgotten. was suffo- cated. A rescue party forced their way through the flooring of her room, but arrived too late to save her.

Two MEN DROWNED.—The steamer Indian Prince, from Newcastle. bound for the Mediterranean ran into Mr. Horton's yacht lona, on Saturday night, Mediterranean, two miles off the Start, in the Channel. The yacht by a quick move of the helm escaped being cut in two, yet was so much damaged that the crew thought she was foundering, and got out a boat. But in their haste they *:apsized it, and two men were drowned. Other two clinging to the boat's keel were rescued by a passing, steamer.

COLLIERS AND TTINIR WAGES.—The Council of the YDrkshire Miners' Association has issued a circular to all the colliery proprietors in the county, demanding on behalf of the men an advance of 10 per cent, in wages. This demand is based on the assumption "that the trade of Yorkshire is better to-day than it ever has been since the memory of man." The question will be considered by a Conference to be held at Manchester on the 25th Inst. The miners a South-West Lancashire are also making a demand for advanced wages. On Saturday, a fire oroke out in the hoot and shoe manufactory of Mr. Lewin, Brierley-street, Leicester, and was not extinguished till the whole okathe upper storeys had been burned out, and the whole of the stock in the lower apartments damaged. The roof fell in, and he house adjoining was also burned. The fire brigade had no sooner returned to their station than they were called to South Wigston to a flee at the Midland Rattan Works, which were destroyed. The loss is estimated' at CARDINAL MANNING AND THAI UNEMPLOYED.—AL a meeting of the London Workmen's County Council Com- mittee the following letter from Cardinal Manning /as read t•-•." It is not from want of will that I fail to give opinions on the vital question eontainea in your letter of the Bth inst. I may say with truth that they are always before me; but the experience of the last five years has made me almost hopeless. They who are chiefly responsible either do not know our State or win not act. But I shall be most happy to converge with you on these subjects." The object of the committee 'IS to advocate local self-government, reform and particu- iarly the provision of useful public works in the Metro- polis for the relief of the unemployed.

FATAL FIGHT BETWEEN SOLDIERS.—On Saturday nigiit, two privates of the Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry, named William Jones and James Barrett, stationed at Trigantle Fort, near Plymouth, had bedh drinking in the canteen, and it is stated that they were very drunk. They quarrelled, and at about hslf-past seven Jones challenged Barrett to fight. They went to the Axill Bat- tery, and, it is supposed, fought, for presently screams were heard, and the two men were found lying on the Hags below, a distance of 35 feet. Both men were re- moved to the hospital, where Barrett was found to be suffering from a fractured skull and severe internal hemorrage. He remained unconscious until about noon on Sunday, when he died. Jones is severely injured, but remains in hospital under treatment. On Monday a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned in the case of Private Barrett.

FIVE WHALERS WRECKED: RESCUE OF 109 LIVES.— Information received on Monday by the mail from San Francisco, and dated the 6th inst., reports theawrecks of no fewer than five whaling vessels, by which over 100 lives were placed in great jeopardy. the names of the vessels were the Young Phmnix, ship, the barques Fleet- ing and Mary and Susan, and the schooners Jane Gray and mo. They were all on the whaling grounds in the Behring Sea, on the 3rd ult., when a terrific storm arose. The above-named vessels were wrecked outright, and it is understood that others were damaged. The crews of the five wrecked vessels numbered 109 persons, and these were saved by the United States revenue cutter Bear, which was in the vicinity. The Bear brought nU the survivors to San Francisco, at which port they were landed on tile morning of the 6th inst. It was not stated in the despatch that any lives had been lost by the disaster to the whaling fleet. _ . - - -

CO-OPFRATIVE CONFERENCE AT BIIRT.—OR Saturday afternoon, nearly 200 delegates from the co-operative societies in the north-western section of the Co-operative Union assembled at the Co-operative Hall, Bury, for the purpose of discussing the question, "How to. promote tire growth of co-operative production, and the welfare of the societies established ?" Mr. T. Fallon, president of the Bury society, occupied the chair, and Mr. Joseph Greenwood, manager, Hehden Bridge, read a paper on the above-named subject. Ho pointed out that there were at present three forms of co-operative production actually at work which could claim the support of co- operators. First, we had Messrs. Thompson and- Sons, where the labourer was taken into partnership ; and the prol?ability was that this form of partnership of master manufacturers with employes would spread. Second, there was the Flebden Bridge form, where the workers and distributive societies were shareholders, allowing profits to labour and trade. Third, there were the societies on the plan of the Burnley Self-Help, which had the worker as the primary foundation, and which assigned to him all the risks and share of the profits. The last form was probably the best —Nearly two hours of discussion followed, the feeling of the meeting being ihat if the labourer wished to participate in more than his labour pay he should invest his capital in the con- cern, and then he would be entitled to something above his labour pay. The root of co-operative production was that the laboprer participated in both the profits and losses. WIGAN Itsvisiort COTTIVI%—STALLNOtDERS CAN VOTE,— On Monday, the revising barrister, Mr. Butler, gave his decision at Wigan as to the claims of several stallholders in the Wigan Tykrket Hall to be placed on the list of borough voters, tlyl claims having been brought by the Conservative parry. Be took the cases of shopholder and stallholder as types, ind said that it had been proved that all the holders had an exclusive use of a certain defined space, and the question was whether under the circumstances that amounted to a license or a demise. If it was a license, then they would have no vote; but if it was a demise and it was occupied by them, in his opinion they would have a vote. It seemed to him that the restrictions in the by-laws cf the market as to the hours of closing, &c., were only such restrictions as would be put in a lease if any tenant chose to take a shop under the circumstances. There were many agricultural leases in which there were all sorts of restrictions put on; so that although the person had the occupation he had not full use of it in the ordinary sense, while, though subject to those restrictions, he was the tenant and occupier. It seemed tcellim that all those claimants came under the- category of occupying tenants. If any of those persons were interfered with by strangers or by the Corporation, the lessors in the occupation of their holding, they could maintain an action for trespass, and the only plea the defendant could put in would be that of testing the right to the action. Be considered the claimants occupiers. The holder of a shop or stall was like a publican, who could not transact business after certain .hours, and, 'taking, all those things into con- sideration, those claimants were entitled to be registered as voters on Division No. 1. Each of the claimants had Adefinite and distinct space of land allotted to him, and was regarded as a tenant by the Corporation.—The votes Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength is Unequalled.,--4dvt.
T H F. PLEASURES OF A TRIOYCLING TOUR.-NO. 3. BY TOWNSMAN.

It is not every town that can boast of a genius. To my mind this is a fortunate circumstance, for were geniuses at all general ordinary mortals would be inclined, from a spirit of rivalry, to elevate the commonplace. There could be no WTI' for is, so strong becomes the feeling of revulsion from the sight of the constant parade of anything relating to the genius andof the universal worship of which he is the object. Particularly is this the case with Stratford-on-Avon. Not content to modest.y wear the undying fame conferred upon the town by the birth therein of England's greatest dramatist, every opportunity is taken to thrust before the visitor this well-known fact. The town is saturated with Shakesperianism. Turn where you will the legend "Shakespeare s" greets you, and with such per- sistency that if you avert your gaze to the sky you fully expect to see it written in the heavens, and are much surprised to find, it is not so. The magic word is inscribed upon houses, painted upon shops, suspended from hotels, carved upon schools, and even appears apon banks, though what the rollick- ing actor had to do with the latter it would be hard to say. Everything and everybody claims some connection with the poet, and his bust or photo' is in nearly every window, while shop-fronts are covered with Shakespearian views, and the towns- people do their utmost to keep the light of Stratford from under the bushel of neglect. 1`) this end they are doubtless incited by the thousands of worshippers who annually visit Shake- speare's shrine, but I think your readers will even- tually agree with me that the tricylists can scarcely be classed under this category. A rather Puritani- cal up-bringing has made them chary as to what they bow down to, and they certainly showed great indifference to the popular religion during their visit to Stratford. Some of this indifference may have arisen from the fact that entrance to every place of the slightest interest was barred by a monetary charge, and this barrier the treasurer of the party did not care to remove. One would have thought that local patriotism would at least have been sufficient to throw open to the public Shakespeare's birthplace, but it was and is not. This building, situ- ate. in a very quiet street in a very quiet town, had no- thing to distinguish it from its neighbours save the no- tice which announced the charge for admission. Exter- nally it was bright with the newness of fresh whitewash and varnish; but internally things were arranged as they are supposed to have been in Shakespeare's days Visitors are admitted by a tall, genial, elderly gentleman, who acts as money-gatherer and guide, at the summons of the bell. The principal features in the front room are the flagged floor, broken into apparentlycountless pieces, and the ancient ingle-nook *ere the drama- tist toasted his toes on wintry days. In the back room the chief furniture consisted of a low table, on which was placed a bulky tome, in which visitors subscribed their names. A remark as to the number of American names, elicited the fact that of lei,ooo visitors during the previous year, 4,000 were from across the Atlantic. The guide further informed us that , Barnum wished to cart the house over to America, to add to the already numerous attractions of the won- derful museum in New York. This, the old gentleman seemed to think,would have been an act of sacrilege, but one of our party said Barnum would only have been fol- lowing our example, for we English are the biggest thieves in the World. "It is only what we have been doing in Egypt, and we shall have the Egyptians waking up some day and fetching all their treasures back.' Having entered our names in the fast filling book, and been astonished by one of the ladies,who, in a moment of forgetftfiness, signed her maiden name, we ascended the stairs. Here we were met by a grey-haired fitly, appar- ently the wife of the gentleman below, who, before we had fairly entered, greetedus in a lofty style with: "Now, you're on classic ground, ladies. It was here that Shakes- peare\ uttered his first cry." All the room contained in the way of furniture was a small cabinet, but it also contained hundreds of autographs written on the walls and ceiling and scratched on the windows. Not,an inch of plaster could be seen that did not contain a name, and the many marks on the windows looked like cob- webs across the panes. Amongst the scratchings was the name of Sir Walter Scot, almost obiterated by sub- sequent inscriptions. Proceeding to another room, access to which was gained through a very. low door, in which one had to bend considerably, we were shown a portrait, in oil, of the immortal bard, Thepainting is in a state of great preservation, and as a protection against theft, it is kept in a strong safe. I The features are radiant with the glow of health, and the merry twinkle in the eyes gives to the portrait a r captivating expression. But our attention was soon, drawn from the contemplation of the portrait, to the more lively gestures of the guide, who gossiped :with great vivacity, and "who hath a story ready for your ear." She spoke with an air of disgust of the "fat and greasy citizens" who visited the place because "lis the fashion," and who horrified her by asking who in the world Shakespeare was, and what he did! More to her mind was the story of Mr. J. L. Toole. The great come- dian meeting a boy in the street, asked him what place it was.
"Stratford," proudly replied the boy. "Stratford, Stratford," said Mr. Toole, " I seem to have heard the name before. Whatever could it be about ?"

"Oh, sir, a great man was born here." "Indeed, and what might his name be?" "Shakespeare, sir." " Shakespeare ? And what did he do ?" " Oh, he was a writer, sir." "A writer, was he? And pray what did he write?" " In the Bible, sir." _ _ _

, Exeunt Mr. J. L. Toole, chuckling. At the bottom of the stairs was a room labelled "Museum," and as there was an extra charge to see this place, a discussion arose as to whether it was worth while doing so. " What do you think is in ?" said one. " Oh," replied another, "I guess Shakespeare's inkstand or perchance

the " poet's pen," that "gives to airy nothing, A local habitation and a name." "I propose that we take it as seen then," and the pro- position was duly agreed to. A move was made towards the dramatist's last resting place, and on the way some of the party felt a craving for fruit. A call was made at a fruit shop, the door of which was wide open, and a knock was given to summon the proprietor. Knock succeeded knock but no one responded, and then a bell was set in motion, but with a like result. Af- ter waiting for some time, we took a sample of the wares and departed for the next shop, where our wants were supplied. Traversing several quiet roads, we came to the church, which is approached by a shady avenue. On reaching the doors we found them closed against us, a notice in- timating that they would be opened on ringing the sell for the apparitor. The party, however, had no desire to disturb this functionary, and having seen photographs of the spot sufficient to engrave the scene on their memo- ries, they agreed to take this as seen also. One of the gentlemen, however, thought Shakespeare would not have been se mighty particular to set up that notice about his poor bones, had he had the least suspicion of the mercenary race that would succeed him, and of the care they would take to keep poor folks from his shrine.

Our youngest member, who had a hankering after a sail, thought the money would be better invested in a row on the river, and accordingly we made our way to the landing stage. We found the boats all aground, as the mill folks had drawn off the water to drive the mill! In a short time, however, the waters rose, and then we were soon floating with "the current that with gentle wiurmur glides" towards the Bristol Channel. We had not gone far, though, before we grounded in mid stream, having taken the wrong channel. As best we could-we re- traced our course, and entered the broader stream, which we first thought was blockaded by the boats of a num- ber of men engaged cutting osiers. The boats were drawn up and we sailed on, but the pleasure was not great. The stream was hardly wider than the boat's length, and the banks, covered with overhanging trees, whose branches stretched fax across the waters, hid everything from view. On our way we passed the pretty memorial theatre, which is quite a feature in the lands- cape, sailed under an old-fashioned stone bridge, and past a well-kept public bathing place, which filled one of the gentlemen with an ardent desire to plunge into the muddy waters. Then came the trees, which seemed to stretch for miles, and the solitUde of the river reaches was such that one might have been sailing in the back-woods of America.

Entering the town again we spent some time inspect- ing the Jubilee memorial presented to "Shakespeare's town" by an American gentleman. At first sight we thought it was not sufficiently massive at the base, and that it would have been greatly improved by the addi- tion of the flags under the paltry fountain in Bank Park. Viewed from another standpoint, however, we concluded that it was best without them, that the pretty and useful memorial was a decided ornament to the town, and that it was a far more sensible way of celebrating the Jubilee than indulging in fleeting fireworks. Making our way to the station—we came by train, this being our only railway journey—we observed we were not the only folks from Warrington, as a quantity of luggage lay on the platform addressed to that town. We kept a sharp look out for the owner, but were un- successful in tour search. As the train was about to start an old gin, who had just parted with her beau, got into our compartment, and we gave her a lively half hcrur with samples of our several and combined vocal abilities. This concluded our sight seeing in the dis- trict, and on reaching our lodging we prepared for our return journey home, which we accomplished safely, and to the surprise ef many friends who had prophesied our return by rail, Taken altogether we had a most enjoyable trip, for though it had its ups and' downs, the ' ups" decidedly predominated. We returned delighted with our excur- sion, and invigorated for the work of the coming year. L Already we have started local cyclists upon similar ex-
Peditions, and to anyone desiring a pleasant holiday, involving a complete changa, and combining enter- tainment and instruction, we can only say "Go and do. likewise."

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A meeting of the committee of this club was held 'at the Farmers' Stores. Bewsey-st., on Wednesday evening, under the chairmanship of Mr. George Percival, the president of the club. The first ques- tion discussed was that of the importation into England of adulterated American cheese.—The sub- ject was introduced by the,CHAnittszi, who aaid that cheese of various qualities was being intro- duced into England from abroad. There was, very likely, a fair sample of Canadian cheese, and some better qualities of the States cheese, that were pa.s- ' sable, but he had seen cheese offered for sale la Warrington market that was anything but good. Indeed, no one could approach it to within thirty yards and breathe freely. So long as cheese of that quality was offered for sale in the market it interfered with the general price of cheese. The market became half-filled with stuff that was not fit for human food. In order to stop this wholes'ale mixture of rubbish, made into cheese, that was offered for sale to the British public, they as tenant farmers must make a bold attempt to pre- vent its importation. Ile thought that 'under the dr cumstances the best plan would be to call the attention of the nuisance inspectors in the, district of the club to the matter' and ask them to keep a vigilant look out for such stuff that was exposed for sale, with a view to prosecutions before the magistrates.—Mr. Boxrom (Aston-on-Grange) then proposed a resolution to the effect that the attention of the Mayor and Nuisance Inspector of each Authority in the district of the club be called to the fraudulent use of mixtures, such as tallow, grease, cotton seed oil, and other fats, with the product of milk, ix the manufacture of American cheese, and its subsequent sale in this country' as pure cheese, with the object of prosecutions being instituted by them for the purpose of exposing and preventing this fraud. He also proposed that a copy of the resolution be sent to the Mayor and Nuisance Inspector of each Autho- rity in the district. In making this proposition, Mr. Buxton said that for a number of Years his attention had been called to the adulteration of foreign cheese. A gen- tleman who recently went through some cheese factories in America had told him that if the English people only knew how the American cheese was made, and saw the fat that was put in it, they vtould not on any account eat it. Free trade was right enough so long as a pure article was imported, but the importation of impure articles should be put a stop to.—Mr. BOARDMAN (Grap- penhall) seconded the resolution, which was unani- mously carried.—The SECRETARY (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) then referred to a defect in the Margarine Act, an Act which, he said, had done a great deal of good since its provisions had been enforced with some vigour in dif- ferent towns. The result was that the imports of mar- garine were decreasing, and there was an in- creased demand for fresh butter. In a case heard before the Wigan magistrates an Inspec- tor had seized some so-called kiel butter, which on analysis, proved to be adulterated with 20 per cent, of foreign fat. The grocer was summoned, and his plea was that he held a warranty from the shipper in Copen- hagen that freed him from liability. It was ultimhtely found that the penalties of the Margarine Act could not be enforced upon the grocer on account of his holding such warranty. The shipper, who resided out of juris- diction, could not be proceeded against. He suggested, with a view to having the act amended in this particular, a resolution should be adopted, calling the attention of the Government to this defect, and a.sking them to take.-

action to meet cases of the ki,nd he had quoted.—On the proposition of Mr. BUXTON, seconded by Mr. JOSEPH KNOWLES (Appleton), it was decided that such a resolu- tion be adcpted, and forwarded to the proper quarter.— This was all the business before the meeting.

Total LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT V. WARRINGTON.—PIayed on the Warrington ground on Saturday, for the benefit of the Warrington professimials, Tinsley and Fleetwood. The home team had the assistance of S. M. Crosfield, while Liverpool brought down a fairly strong team, though there were one or two short. The Warrington captain, having won the toss, decided to bat, and the home team Were represented by S. M. and J. Eros- field. F. Jones sent down the first over to the former, and from the second ball he scored a 3. Hornby opened the bowling from the pavilion end, and S. M. despatched his second ball for 3 ; but after scoring 12 he was given out lbw to Hornby. Lawton played good cricket. When H. B. Steel went on in the place of F. Jones he bowled Crosfield second ball. Tinsley next made his appearante, amidst much applause, but the second ball he received he skied to Woodhaad, in the long field, which that fielder safely held. Clarke now joined Lawton, who continued to play with freedom, but the former was twice missed. Evans then took the ball from Hornby, and with his first delivery he removed Lawton's bails, that player having shown by far the best cricket for his side. Clarke im- mediately succumbed to Evans, who was bowling finely, and after small contributions to the score, both Fodmore and Warburton fell victims to the same bowler. Fair- dough, after scoring 5, ran himself out • and afterFleet- ' wood had quickly scored 7 he was beaten by Evans. I Wallington brought up the rear (Jones haying resumed in place of Steel, but was smartly caught by Jolley ' without any addition to the score, Woodhead being not out 7. Liverpool commenced their innings with D. Q. Steel and C. L. Jones, to the deliveries of Fleetwood and Lawton. Runs were freely scored by the former, until Steel, taking advantage of a misfield by Clarke, called upon Jones to run, but Clarke smartly returned the ball to Warburton, who quickly whipped off the bails, and Jones was disposed of aftercontributing a single. Hornby came next, but could do nothing with the bowling of Fleetwood, being beaten time after time, and eventually was neatly stumped by Warburton. H. B. Steel, who filled the vacancy, hit out freely, andscered the majority of the runs until his brother was beaten by a good* ball from Lawton. Evans joined H B. Steel, and these two staved together, although when Tinsley and S. M. Cres- fiela went on the rum getting was somewhat checked. The pair played excellent cricket, especially Steel, who hit out brilliantly,and retired with 59th his credit, Evans being not out, 14. Scores r

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 22, 1885.

THE Rev. Dr. STUART MUIR, (of Edinburgh, has -been preaching in London on a text which has become prominent of late, namely, "Is marriage a failure ? " Judging from the brief report of his sermon which has appeared in the papers, it can- not be said that ho has added anything now to the controversy raised by Mrs. CAIRD'S article in the "Westminster Review for August. Nor does he sPpear to have dealt with the question in a way calculated to impress people who have begun to reason on the matter. "He contended," we are told, "that marriage was not e civil contract, but a Divine institution, and to affirm that it was a failure was equivalent to saying that God and Christianity were also failures. Our first parents Were lawfully and scripturally married. And yet there was no registrar in Eden. He did not ap- prove of marriage before a registrar; it should be entered into solemnly in the face of the Church, and being of God's appointment must be right, and no failure at all." If this view of the question is to hold good, it will, to begin with, have to be admitted that the law, at any rate, as to marriage is a failure; nay, more than that, it is immoral; for the State recognises marriage as "a civil contract" which is equally binding whether it be entered into before a registrar, or '4 solemnly in 4ho face of the Church." The Reverend Doctor is, as it seems to us, just a little too sweeping in his conclusion, for his argument implies—with a narrowness unfortu- nately too characteristic of the clergy—that there la neither true marriage nor true salvation to be found outside the pale of the church. And was it not imprudent of him to'make allusion to the Inarriage in the Garden of Eden, and the absence Of a registrar ? It is true that the remark is, as it was intended, somewhat hard on the registrar. Ilut it seems to us that it is equally hard on the Parson and the church; for, so far as we can learn, there is no mention of them in the accounts Which have come to hand of that marriage in the rden. If we were to go back to the primitive Ways of "our first parents,'4os suggested by Dr. ,MUIR, we are afraid the marriage question would soon be more unsettled even than it is at present; for in that case every youth who ventures, as Mu,- Ton has it To sport with Amaryllis in the shade, Or with th tangles of Necera's hair, 'night plead, in a certain contingency, that, not- Withstanding the absence of the parson, the church and the registrar, be was "lawfully and scriptur- ally married." It is a pity Doctors of Divinity are Sot better employed than in using arguments of this kind, for they do not tend to settle questions, and are the means of causing the reverend gentle- ken to be less revered. It is much more to the 11)nrpose to read the article by ELIZABETH RACHEL OEIArmAN, on "Marriage Rejection and Marriage -Iteform,"in the current issue of the "Westminster." is not intended as a reply to the paper in the Irevious issue by MTS. CAIRO, but, all the same, it is at issue with it on many points. The writer 4eals with marriage as an/institution which is sub- ject like other human institutions to the laws of evclution. She is altogether opposed to the theory of "Marriage rejection," which is being mooted in sorne quarters; and is, on the contrary, in agree- aleutt with Mr. HERBERT SPENCER, when he says 121 menogamy that "any changes to be antitipa- tefl " tin the connubial relation) "must be in the direction of completion and extension of it." he question is one upon which woman has an asPecialright to be heard. She has been treated through long centuries as the mere slave of man; and even now, with all our boasts about freedom "Icl equality, woman stands before the law in an Inferior position to man. The wife cannot fet a di circa for adultery as the hus- nand can she must be able to prove cruelty aa_ well as adultery. This is grossly unfair; it is monstrous injustice; and, although there is ;°body to defend it, it is still the law of the land. :ben again as to the custody of children, the .other is nOt recognised as having the same title 7_ the father. He is deemed by the law to be the

tura' guardian ; but the law is still so un- -I:l4.tural as to permit the father to appoint a guar- -2411 to act, in case of death, along with the mother. These issued do not, of course, do more than touch the fringe of the question—" Is mar- -jag° a failure ?" but they account for some of the dissatisfaction with the marriage tie which is elt bY women in what are called the higher e.asses. The lover classes—that is to say the reat mass of the people—do not seem to be taken account by the controversialists; and that tvhY the subject cannot be said to have, as yet, 11l ore than a passing interest. It will have to be ,41`111..53. ed on a lower plane before it can be brought t.....t4in the region of practical politics. It is too "`"444lltous a matter to be determined by a few
magazine articles—to say nothing of inconsequen- tial sermons by Doctors of Divinity.

THE Parnell Commission commenced its pro- ceedings, on Monday, in the Probate Court of the Royal Courts of Justice. Sir JAMES HANNEN presided, and was supported by Mr. Justice SMITH and Mr. Justice DAY, the other two Commission- ers. It is very gratifying to find, from the pre- liminary investigation, that the Parnellites are likely to have justice done to them. A Court of Law is an altogether different place to the House of Commons, where the majority, however much in the wrong,, may howl down the minority, how- ever much in the right. The Judges intimated that the inquiry would proceed as if an action were being tried, and what this meant was at once seen when the PRESIDENT referred to the proprietors of the " Times "as the defendants. The ATTORNEY- GENERAL, who has been retained on behalf of the "Times," did not think it necessary to appear in court on Monday. He left the issues raised to be argued by Mr. GRAHAM, who soon found himself in a difficulty. The first point to be dealt with was as to who was to begin with evidence; and when Mr. GRAHAM was asked by the PRESIDENT if he had anything to say, he had to answer that he had had no opportunity of consulting the ATTORNEY-GENERAL, or those who instructed him. Sir CHARLES RUSSELL, who represents the whole of the Parnellites in Parliament, pertinently remarked that he thought those who made the charges ought to begin by adducing evidence in their support. Sir JAMES HANNEN thought so too, and he there- fore said—" We are therefore of opinion that it lies with the defendants in the action of O'DoN- NELL V. WALTER to tender such evidence as they may think fit in support of the charges they have made." Mr. GRAHAM was quite taken abaci at this turn of the proceedings, and he will, no doubt, think it was a blunder, to begin with, not to have his chief at his elbow to take the lead, or advise him in the matter. Not that it would have made any difference as to the ruling. The Judges have made up their minds to proceed in a judicial manner; and what can be more reasonable, or more judicial, than to insist on those who make ' charges and allegations setting forth such evidence as they may have in proof of ,their accusations? This, to be sure, was not the way of the HOUSE) of Commons; it has not been the way of the I "Times" and of the Tories generally. Proof of their foul charges is about the last thing they seem to have had in their minds. But they would have a Commission of Inquiry, and it looks as if they were about to be caught in their own net. The next issue raised was as to the inspection of the originals of all letters read by the counsel for the " Times "in the action brought by Mr. I O'DoNmEn.L. As to this Mr. GRAHAM sought to I limit the inspection to the two which have already been published in fee-simile, but the PRESIDENT said an order would be made for the inspection of all documents produced at the late trial. A long i argument then ensued as to what is technically I termed "the discovery of documents" bearing on the charges made. Judging from the ferocious way in which the proprietors of the "Times" have 1 flourished the tomahawk, it was natural to sup- 1 Pose that nothing would ,suit them better than i the opportunity of disclosing the documents in their possession, which go to prove, or which they affect to believe go to prove, that the Parnellites 1 have been guilty of conspiracy to murder. But i when it is suggested that they should be called 1 upon to take this course, it is soon seen that they will do anything but that, if they can in any way , shuffle out. But they are not, however, permitted to lie low, as they have done, and fire irregular I shots. They are compelled to come forward and 4 fight in the open. There is to be a discovery of I documents, and, as this applies to both parties, it i obviously fair to both parties. Further, the Commission, unlike Parliament, has decided that particulars must be given of the charges and alleg- ations, and the names of the persons charged are to be specified. It was really pitiful to see how Mr. GRAHAM tried to shirk this just demand am the part of Sir CHARLES RussuLt ;f but the counsel or the " Times " was pulled up suddenly when the PRESIDENT asked—" Who made the charges and allegations that the Legislature has directed us to inquire into? Did nobody make them ?" Other minor points were considered, the result in each case showing that the " Times " (as well as the Parnellites) is being brought to book as to the charges that are made in " Parnellistn and Crime." There is, it is now apparent, to be a fair trial in I open court, and that is all that reasonable men , require.
TOUCH AND Go. The football season has set in. It is a case of—to alter Mark Twain's rhyme— Punith, brothers, punch; punch with care; Punch in the presence of the " spectatare."

"Light bread" is usually in demand as a good thing; but a Runcorn tradesman was fined on Monday for selling a four pound loaf which was found to be five and a half ounces light. This was altogether too light.

-- The objector has been objected to; Mr. John Hampson, the Conservative agent for the borough of Warrington, has been struck off the list for Great Sankey. "'Tie sport to have the engineer hoist with his own peter."

St. Helena and Runcorn join hands by the marriage of Miss Agnes MeKeelinie and,Mr. A. R. Norman. "Happy is the bride whom the sun shines on." And again— All who joy would win, Must share it—Happiness was born a twia.

It is reported that the Pope has addressed a strong remonstrance to the English Government on their present policy towards Ireland. There is nothing like being " mighty impartial." This, as following on the Reseript to the Clergy, would tend to make things even.

Speculators have made another "corner in cotton, but to avoid the crush—and to give a squeeze in return—the cotton spinners of Lanca- shire al9 arranging for a run of short time. It is to be hoped they will be sliccessful ; " corner- men" aught to be punished.

It is suggested that the Americans, who are discussing what flower should be adopted as the National emblem, should fix on the new blue rose. But, as the Yankee is spry and showy, we would venture to suggest that the most appropriate would be the dandy-lion."

Next week there will appear in our columns a low, and interesting letter on San Francisco Schools, written by a daughter of Mr. H. Whit- ham. It is a lively epistle, and we can commend it to every schoolboy and schoolgirl as something they will enjoy reading.

The members of the Warrington Farmers' Club are doing the right thing in directing the atten- tion of the authorities to the sale of cheese in the market which is absolutely unfit for human food. It does not matter whether it is manufactured at home or abroad, if it is really not fit to eat it ought to he destroyed.
Think of Mr. Chamberlain defending coercion as he did on Wednesday I The voice is the

' voice of Joseph, but the words' are the words of Balfour. The member for West Birming- ham has "advanced" a great many steps back- ward since he said—" I hate coercion ; I hate the name—l hate the thing."

Keep a sharp look out. Mr. P. C. Campbell announces that probably within a month" he will be in a position to sail, with his new flying machine, "from one city to another." How nice I But why not from one town, or from one tree, to another? Well, it will be something for city men to see our dainty Peter fly—that is when he does fly.

We have pleasure in directing the attention of our readers to a lengthy article by" Home Rule," which will be found on another page. It is writ- ten by a townsman of position who has read much and thought much upon the Irish question; and he expresses himself with so much moderation that his views cannot but commend themselves to all sections of Liberals.

Overheard at Wigan: Bill: Thee! Tha knows nowt; tha doesn't know th' name o'th' Queen F—Dick : It's,—let me see; aw've forgetten just neaw.—Bill Tha never knew; but aw con tell thi ; it's Brunswick.—Dick: Is it (hecky) as like F Aw know wod it is, but aw've forgetten. Aw wer towd bi a chap in Scofield Lone.—Bill: Thee Tha knows nowt. (Left sitting.)

It is a gratifying feature in connection with the few smallpox cases there have been in Warrington that they have not proved a centre of infection. The Medical Officer of Health is down on a case "like a thousand o' bricks" as soon as he hears of it; and he soon hears of it from the fact that War- rington is ahead of most towns in having in operation the compulsory system of notification of infectious disease.

The Rector of Warrington has done a sensible thing in giving, in the course of a sermon, his im- pressions of a recent visit to Germany. Practical moratising of this kind cannot fail to interest, and prove of benefit. If clergymen would take the trouble to "get home," in this and in other ways, to the minds of their hearers there would be less of the beggarly array of empty pews which so often prevails in churches and chapels.

The Tichborne cltiimant is still alive, and was reciting his woes to a Runcorn audience on Satur- day night. He 'threatens another trial, and alleges that " a lady friend of his had kindly promised to defray the whole of the expense—£loo,ooo if re- quired." It would be better for the lady, the claimant, and the public if they would divide one thousand pounds only, and leave the law courts alone. Life is too short for another Tichborne trial.

John Mandeville was imprisoned unto death; but Mr. Balfour does not wish to have the stain of another tragedy, and so he has ordered the release of John Dillon. He is conquered by his fears, and not by his feelings; and the release therefore does him no credit. As he would not have set free a felon because he happened to be ill, what becomes of his bold assertion that he made no difference with prisoners? It is just so much humbug; it is Balfour's bosh.

A curious argument used by opponents of Free Education is based on the fact that the lowest per centage of attendance is to be found where the fee is only a penny. From this it is intended that the inference shall be drawn that, if there were no foe the attendance would be lower still. But how absurd! "Penny Schools" are invariably established in poor neighbourhoods, and the ques- tion to ask is—Would there not, in all piobability, be a better attendance in these particular schools if no fee was required?

By-the-by is it not stupid of the managers of these t‘ Penny Schools" not to raise the fee, if that, as is implied, means that it would result in increasing the attendance? Reasoning of this kind is on a par with that of the minister who ar- gued that it was a proof of God's goodness, and of des4n in creation, that He had caused the large rivers to run by the large towns,

Mr. Caine, MY., still preaches temperance, but he is the despair of legislators. Speaking at the conference at Hull, the other day, he said "he did not believe there was a single town in the United Kingdom that would adopt local option if it was passed to-morrow." Other temperance advocates believe that the very reverse of ,this statement is the truth. But what does he mean by local op- tion ? He must not confound it with total pro- hibition, which is a totally different thing. IVIr. gaine is lost to the faith in more ways than one:

The annual report of the Inspector General in Bankruptcy reveals an unsatisfactory state of things. The loss to creditors in England and Wales through bankruptcy proceftadings for the year 1887 is estimated at £7,114,905, against £5,919,802 in' the previous year, showing an in- crease of £1,105,103. Can it 1:e that insolvent traders are ceasing to be afraid of M. Chamber- lain's Bankruptcy Act ? If that be the case' it will require to be made more stringent. It is be- yond belief that trade was worse in 1887 than in 1886. There is something wrong somewhere.

:THBFT BY A WIDNES LAD AT WARRINGTON.-At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thurs- ' day, before Major Litton and Alderman Webster, a lad, named Wm. Glaesey, aged 13, who comes from Widnes, was charged with stealing from the yard of John Piinston, greengrocer, Allen-st., Warring- ton, six tacks and a coat.—P.C. Bell stated that he beard of someone stealing in Allen-st., and on pro- ceeding there he foand the prisoner with the stolen articles in his possession. He also admitted to witness having stolen from the yard before.—Pri- goner was ordered to feceive twelve strokes witit the birch. _

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. - The monthly meeting of this committee was held at the Town Hall. on Wedtesday evening. There were present the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., Messrs. J. Simpson, F. S. Norman, P. A. Lake, T. Riley. and J. D. Jones (librarian.)—The Librarian having read the notice of appointment of the committee by the Board of Commissioners, Mr. Simpson moved that Mr. Handley be re-appointed chairman for the en- suing year.—Mr F. A. Lake seconded the proposition, which was carried unanitnously.—On the motion of Mr. F. S. Norman, seconded by Mr. Riley, the Rev. A. M. Wood was re-appointed vice-chairman, and took the chair for the meeting.—The Librarian pre- sented the I%ixth annual retort, which stmed that the library had been open for the issue of books 141 days, and the number of issues was 21,758, being an increase of 1067 over the previous year. Of th eseissues 17,167 were prose fiction. The average daily issue was 154. The number of borrowers' ticke•A issued 'during the year was 805, an increase of 79 over last year. During the year 58G volumes had been added to the library, 483 by purchase, and 103 by gift. The total number of volumes on the shelves was 4.590. A list of books recommended to be purchased at a cost of about .£3O, by the Book Selection Com- mittee, was adopted.
