div.head: EXAMINER, SAM TWA SEPTEMBER 22, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAM TWA SEPTEMBER 22, 1888.
LOCAL NEWS.

FOOT RACE AT WIDNES.—A youths' race came off on , Saturday afternoon on the Millfield ground between James Thompson and William Peters ior a gold watch, value £lO. Peters started favourite, but Thompson at once assumed the lead, which he kept all the way, and won in an easy fashion by eight yards. Fred Wright fired the pistol, and W. Jones was the referee. A good number of spectators were present. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—A young man named William Ward, of 132, Mersey-road,,was seriously injured at Ilutchinson's \chemical works, on Saturday. He was employed at a caustic drain, when he slipped and fell into it, both legs being immersed in the hot liquid as high as the knees. The limbs were seriously scalded. He is an inmate of the Accitent Hospital, and under the care of Dr Hutchinson is progressing favourably. POISONED BY PARAFFIN OIL AT WIDNES.—On Monday Dr. Hutchinson was summoned to the house 27, John-st , to attend tho soh (aged two years) of Wm. Jenkins It appeared that the infant, .whilst alone in the kitchen, had seized a bottle of paraffin oil, and had drank a portion of I the contents. Alarming symptoms of poisoning quickly I developed, but Dr. Hutchinson having administered an emetic, followed by an antidote, the child rallied, and is now recovered. , UNSAFE WITHOUT UNIFORM. George Jones, of on settled residence, was brought up at Widnes Court on 'Monday, charged with having been drunk and refusing to quit the Ram's Head Inn—P.C. Cummings said the prisoner was making a great disturbance in the bar, and the landlord refused to serve him.. He (the constable) was in plain clothes, and as he thought, it was not safe to meddle with him he went home and put on his uni- form. On returning he saw the prisoner strike a man, and he took him into custody. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was fined 7s 6d andocosts, or in default, 7 days' hard labour. FLAT IN FLAMES AT RUNCORN.—The coasting flat Llan- fair, belonging to Messrs. Haynes and Co., of Liverpool, and trading between Llandulas and West Bank Dock, Widnes, was destroyed by fire on Thursday night. In coming up the river on Wednesday night the flat groun- ded on a sand bank off No Man's Land, and at high tide at noon on Thursday the flat sprung a leak, and the water getting to the cargo of limestone, combustion was set up, and the flat was set on fire. The crew succeeded in carrying away the sails and a portion of the stores before the flames enveloped the vessel. Hundreds if persons visited the river-side at night to View the scene. The loss is estimated at about £5OO. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL, WIDNES.—The an- nual services in aid of this school were held in Milton Congregational Church on Sunday. The pulpit was oc- cupied both morning and evening by the Rev. W. Kar- foot, M.A., L.C.D. of Leigh. who delivered two admir- able discourses. The choir and scholars renderedspecially- selected anthems and hymns. In the afternoon the scholars rendered the service of song entitled The de- sire of all nations," in a manner that suggested careful training on the part of Mrs. Gibson, who conducted. The narrative was read by Mrs. Robinson, of Hope House, Famworth, and Mr. Eustace Carey presided over the proceedings. Satisfactory congregations assembled, and the collections realized upwards of £l4. DRIVEN TO STBAL AT WIDNES.—Mary Stewart., a mar- ried woman, of 49, Victoria-st., was charged with steal- ing a tablecloth and a quantity of other linen. worth ss, the property of Mary Ann lilkington, of Manchester Be,erhouse, Wellington-st. The articles were missed on IThursday, and it was proved that on the day previous the prisoner had pledged them for is 6d at Mr. Neil's pawnshop in A nne-st. The prisoner said she took the goods in order that she might get locked up. Her hus- band was not a bad man, but he put her out frequently. P.S. Strickland said he had seen the woman in the street and she had complained of her husband's violence, but she was in drink at the time. Her husband was a hard- working man. The Bench sentenced the woman tb a month's hard labour. She said she wished she had to go for six months. UNWEIGHED BREAD AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Stringer. of Heath-road. was charged with selling bread otherwise than by weight. He pleaded guilty. On the 12th instant P.C. Breeze . sent a boy named Buckley into the defendant's shop to purchase a 21b. loaf. The defendant supplied the bread, . but did not weigh it, and the constable afterwards ascer- tained that the loaf was It ounces light. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed.—Edward Johnson, of Bridge-st., was summoned for a similar offence. P.C. Breeze saw a woman named Saxon purchase a 411). loaf, and noticed that the shopinan did not weigh it. When the loaf was weighed it was found to be five ounces and a half light. As the defendant had been previously convicted he was tined lfis and costs.—James Byrne, of Church-st., for selling a 21b. loaf an ounce light, was fined ss. and costs. HOUSEBREAKING BY BOYS AT WIDNES.—On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, John O'Brien (16), John Deve- reaux (16), and John McDermott (13) were charged with having broken into a shop in Victoria-st. belonging to John Kershaw, plumber and contractor, of Halton-view, and stolen several pairs of boots The shop was properly secured on Saturday night by Mr. Kershaw, who found on Monday morning that a window at the back had been forced open and six pairs of boots stolen. On the samq morning P.C. Holbrook saw a young boy named Williaiff Kavanagh wearing a pair of the missing boots, and from what he stated the prisoners were apprehended. Mc- Dexmott, in reply to the charge, said he had taken the boots from the yard gate, and O'Brien and Devereaux admitted having stolen shoes, and given a pair to Kay- anagh.—McDermott was discharged with a caution, and the other prisoners, who had a record against them, were committed to the quarter sessions for trial.

TERAPASSING ON THU RAILWAY AT BOLD.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Geskell, jun., five colliers named Darnel Jones, 12, Bishop-st. ; Robert Jones, 230, Park-road; Wm. Jena, 12, Bishop-st. •' John Hughes, 80, Chaucer- lane and Owen Roberts, 27, Bishop's-court, all of Parr, were charged with trespassing on the London and North- Western Railway, at Bold, on the 24th August. Mr. 1 Preston. jun., appeared for the company, and stated that it was the custom of the Collins Green colliers to walk on i the line to and from their • work; and in order to do so I they either broke down or climbed over the fences. During the time these men were on the line 19 trains— passengers and goods—passed between Collies Green and St. Helens Junction. He asked the Bench to inflict such penalties as would put a stop to this dangerous practice. , The defendants pleaded guilty, and were each fined lOs and costs, 12s. A RETURNED CONVICT AT RUNCORN'. —Before Major Hazlehurst, atßuncorn Petty Sessions on Monday. Jas. Smith, an elderly man, was charged that he being the bailee of £2 belonging to Henry Urmson, did appropriate the same to his own use.—lt appeareft that Urmson is the keeper of the Manchester House beerhouse, Bridge- at, and is owner of the flat Douglas, of which John Roden is the captain. On the 13th inst. the flat was in the Weaver canal at King's Works, Clifton, and the prisoner was employed on board. Urmson gave the prisoner £2, to be handed over to the captain to pay canal dues and towage, but the prisoner, instead of doing so, went and spent the money in drinking at Frodsham. When appre- hended by P.C. Dale he had only 7d in his possession. The prisoner, who denied stealing the money, but admit- ted having spent it, was committed to take hisitrial at Knutsford Quarter Sessions. He has previously served two terms of seven years' penal servitude, and there are several records of nine months against him. MISPLACED SYMPATHY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, a neatly dressed young woman, named Matilda Barnish, who gave her address as Chesterfield, was charged with hav- ing stolen a tin bonnet box, a shawl, and other articles, together with 20s in money, belonging to Robert Yearsly, of Moor-lane, Ditton. It appeared that on Friday, the 7th inst., Mrs. Yearsley engaged the prisoner as a domestic servant " out of charity. On Monday meriting, the 10th inst., Mrs. Yearsley called the prisoner at half-past five. An hour later Mrs. Yearsley arose and found that the prisoner had decamped, taking with her the articles mentioned. On the same day P.C. Hudson apprehended the prisoner in a pawnshop- in Church-st.' at Warrington.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, said she was 19 years of age.—Superintendent Johnstone in- formed the Bench that the prisoner had been oncl pre- viously convicted of felony at Derby, and she was now "wanted" at Rochdale, Stockport, and Egremont. —The prisoner was sentenced to one month's hard labour.

Itewsen FOR BRAVERY.—The Royal Humane Society's testimonial, engrossed on Vellum, has been awarded to Gilbert Booth, a boy of thirteen, for saving a little boy of three, who fell into the Bridgewater Canal at Run- corn, on July 30th, Booth wading in up to his chin. WIDNES Scuoot. BOARD.—Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, on Thursday, prosecuted a ' number of persons for not sending their children regu- larly to school. The cases were proved by Attendance Officers Joynson, Rowe, and Grant, and the usual fine of 5s was imposed upon each defendant. • SUDDEN DRAM; AT WlDNES.—Michael Dodd, 48 years of age, of 9, North-st., Widnes, died very suddenly on Wednesday morning. For some time Dodd had been in delicate health, and on getting up at half-past five on Wednesday morning he complained of being very ill. He, however, went to the works of Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co. to follow his employment, but on arriving there he fell in the yard. Dr. Richards was sent for, but he expired before that gentleman's arrival. The Coroner deemed an ihquest unnecessary. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT Dirrox.—On Wednesday even- ing, as a boy narhed Thomas Royle was riding a hors- past the Ball Inn, Ditton, some lads came up behind ane Struck the horse several times, which caused it to stard off at a rapid pace along the lane, with the result that the rider was precipitated to the ground with considert able violence, dislocating his elbow, and fracturing his arm above the wrist. The boy was at once driven in a trap to the surgery of Dr. Hutchinson, i and that gentle- man has since attended him. Boyle s favourably re- covering from the shock sustained. _ _

MR. BRUNNER AND TRE .RUNCORN FORESTERS.—At thel invitation of the members of Court Runcorn (No. 429) of I the ancient order of Foresters, Mr. J. T. Brunner; M.P., and Dr. McLennan attended at the Court-room, Fores- ters' Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday afternoon, for the pur- pose of being initiated as honorary members of the Court. Prior to the ceremony* about 100 of the inemb.,rs sit down to a knife and fork tea, which was catered for by Mr. Lydiatt. The ladies presiding at the tables were Miss Riley, Mrs. Lydiatt,Mrs. Rushton, and Miss Rushton. After tea the initiation of the inembor for the-Northwich division of Cheshite and of Dr. McLennan took place, and was performed by Brother T. Riley, CAI., who was Supported by Bros. W. Hankin4on, P.C.R., W. Rushton, P.O R.. and T. Lydiatt, S.C.R. Afterwards Mr. Brunner gave a brief congratulatory address. MUSICAL FESTIVAL Al'AT' IDNES.—With the object of obtaining funds for the purchase of a new harmonium for Hutchinson-st. Primitive Methodist Chapel, a floral musical service was held in that edifice on Wednesday evening. The chapel was elaborately and beautifully decorated with flowers and plants, chiefly from the gar- den of Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss. M.P., and appropriate mottoes adorned the walls. There was a capital attend- ance of members and friends, and Mr. H. Wade-De-aeon occupied the chair. The music consisted of anthems, hymns, and solos given by a well-trained choir of sixty voices, interspersed by appropriate readings given by Mr. Eustace Carey. An- orchestral band added to the pleasure of those present. Mr. G. T. Barker presided at the organ, and Mr. F. Whitby was at the piano. Solos and duets were.. given by Mrs. Lock, Mrs. J. H. Cooper, Miss Alice Betney, Miss Owen, Miss Paulston. The performance was repeated on Thursday evening. THE MINERS: WAGES QUESTIOS. —On Saturday morning the'tniners of South-West Ltncashire dis- trict, sent in to their employers notices asking for an advance of ten per cent. The demand is made on the ground that the state of trade generally has improved, and particularly that an increase has been made in the price of coal. The notice affects about 40,000 miners, and if the demand be acceded to, the increase will come into effect on the let of October. • . .

PLADOING HIS LIES CHRTIFICA.TR.—A singular case was heard at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, when Michael Garrity,•of New Bridge-st., Salford, was summoned at the instance of Chief Constable Wood for pawning his military identity paper. Mr. Wood stated that he was instructed to prosecute by the military autnorities.' The defen- dant was a first-class Army Roserve man, and pledged his life certificate as a security for a debt, which was contrary to the conditions of military service. Mr. Clarke, pawnbroker. of Westfield-st., gave evidence, after which the defendant, who did net appear, was fined 5s and. costs. Tits 110 AX ON LOCAL TRADBSILAN.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday. George Wilcox, an elderly man, was charged with having failed to report him- self whilst under police surveillance.—Superinten- dent Johnson stated that the maecame to the town on the 16th August, and he daily reported himself. A few days afterwards he departed Without noti- fying his change of residence. This was the man who had hoaxed a number of tradesmen isi Widnes, Warrington, and Manchester. He had sent a Wid- nes undertaker to Ditton to measure a corpse when Ithere was none to be found, and a bricklayer and a mineral water manufacturer were also victimised by receiving extensive orders of a fictitious charac- ter.—The prisoner, who said his head had been in such satate lately that he did not know what he was doing, was sent to gaol for a month. - THB HOUR IRON TitADE.—The English iron mar- ket maintains a steadily upward tendency, and an activity which Des seldom been surpassed. At the same time, the trade done is of a thoroughly sound character, and the demand genuine. very little speculative business being attempted. Although the Glasgow warrant market has fluctuated greatly during the week, this has not interfered with the trade done by Scotch makers, who have advanced their quotations, the enhancement ranging from 64. to 2s 6d k ton, according to brand. Cleveland iron- masters are also holding out for more money, and the price of No. 3 Middlesbrough is firm at 35s 3d prompt, or 3d a ton more, In Lancashire, pig-Iron is Is a ton dearer. Bessemer iron, in the north-west, has been put up from 3d to 6d per ton. The manu- factured iron market is very active.—lrert. A LUNATIC CHOKED AT RATNirna:=John Dale, an inmate of Rainhill Asylum, died on Saturday from choking, owing to a piece of crust of bread lodging in the throat during one of the meals. The deceased, who was 48 years of age, was admitted to the asylum in March last. An inquest on the body ,was held before the county coroner. Mr. S. Brig- house, at the Asylum, Rainbill, on Tuesday. Dr. Joseph Wiglesworth. one of the medical officers of the institution, said the deceased formerly, resided at Bootle, and his age was forty-eight years. He was far advanced in general paralysis, and had not many months to live. The witness was called to deceased on Saturday evening last, and three crusts of bread were found at the back of the throat. which witness at once removed. An attempt to resuscitate the deceased was made, but without avail, and death ensued in a few minutes. The cause of death was suffocation. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at Widnes Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. R. Bradshaw presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe. Major Wareing, Messrs. H. Wade Deacon, J. B. 'raison, C. E. Barlow, F. Heyes, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

DISTRICT EDUCATION. The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing the month of August (five weeks) there were 214 applications for payment of school fees, Which were re- commended to be paid in 194 cases. There were 84 persons summoned before the magistrates for contra- vention of the Education Act, and 87 were convicted.

div.head: SATISFACTORY CENSUS.
div.p: A SATISFACTORY CENSUS.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing the holidays the attendance officers were employed in taking a census of the children of the district, and the results were submitted in tabular form. Mr. Deacon made an explanatory statement. The school ascomo- dation had increased at Simms Cross school, from 1,392 to 1,512, and at West Bank from 1,116 to 1,290. The total number of school places last year was 6,696, at pre- sent they numbered 6.992, an increase of about 300. The lumber of children between 3 and 13 was 7,645, against. 7,300 odd last year, an increase of about 330. According to the method of deductions recognised by the Educa- tion Department, the number of school-going children was 5,570, but the deductions in Widnes were not so large as in other portions of the kingdom. The number of houses had increased by about 100, and the number , of empty houses had dimisbed by 14. There were 5,229 I houses in the town, of which 5,055 were inhabited, 174 empty, and 18 in course of erection. The total number of children taken by the officers was 78.98. The number of children between 13 and 14 years was 253, and there were 1,660 children between 3 and 5 years. thus showing that the number of children between 5 and 13 which might he on the rolls was 5,880. The total number of 'children who ought to be on the rolls was 6,412, and the number on the rolls was 6,296. There were, therefore, 116 children who ought to be on the rolls, but were not against 172 last year. There were children who were almost invariably just over five years, so that the re- sult of the census was satisfactory and showed that the work of the committee, and of the officers, had been well done during the past year. They would never have tbe number down to nothing, and if they kept it to 100 or 150 the Committee would be satisfied. The number of children under private instruction was 105, and the Committee regarded with gratification that the number of children so taught had been steadily decreasing for years. The proportion of school going children to total population in Widnes (estimated at 30,000) was 1 to s•3B.—The Chairman remarked that the census was highly satisfactory, and he proposed that the thanks of the Board be tendered to the Committee for their labours.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: MA ILRIAGE OF THE REV. G. H. ST. PATRICK GARRETT.
div.p: MA ILRIAGE OF THE REV. G. H. ST. PATRICK GARRETT.

The marriage of the recently-appointed minister to the Widnes parish, the Rev. George Henry St. Patrick Garrett. B.D , will be learned with no little interest. The affair has been entirely of a private character. The ceremony was performed on Wed- nesday, the 12th inst., at Christ Church, Leeson Park, Dublin (where the Vicar was the late citrate), by his father, the Rev. George Garrett, M.A., as- sisted by the Rev. Canon Neligan, D.D. (who Was rector when Mr. Garrett was in Dublin), and the Rev. C. W. Fleury, M.A., brother-in-law of the bride, who is 3ti-s Helen W. Greer, of 15, Raglan-road, Dublin, the youngest daughter of the late Mr. Robert W. Greer, of Ballyconan, county Louth. The Rev. Charles Dowse, 8.A., curate of ?erne, bounty Wexford, officiated as best man, and the bride, who was attired in her, travelling dress, was given away by her brother, Mr. Edward Greer, solicitor, Dublin. The happy pair proceeded soon after the nuptial knot had been tied, which ceremony was gone through early in the morning, by the nine o'clock train from Dublin, for Connemara and Achil Island, around which district they are making a tour, and are expected to return about the 3rd of October, to take up their abode at the Vicarage, Widnes. The Rev. John Connell, curate, is at pre- sent staying at the Vicarage during Mr. Garrett's absence, and on his superior's return will move to 25, Deacoo-road.

div.head: BANKRUPTCY OF A RUNCORN FISH
div.p: BANKRUPTCY OF A RUNCORN FISH
DEALER.

At the Warringtoa County Court, yesterday morn- ink, Peter Sinnot, a master mariner and fish dealer, who recently carried on business in Warrington, trnderwent a public examination in bankruptcy by the Official Receiver, Mr. C. J. Dibb. In his state- ment to the Official Receiver the debtor set forth that in 1882 he commenced business as a ship's chandler and grocer, at Runcorn, with a capital of £2,200. Previously he had been for about 20 years a master mariner. He remained in the ship chandlery and grocery business for about four years, when he gave it up in favour of his son and brother-in-law. In or about 1883 he invested some money in ships, and became managing owner of them. He continued to act in that capacity until about two years ago. About three or four years ago he com- menced to trade as a fish merchant and poulterer at Runcorn ; and carried on the business until about two months ago, when he left Runcorn and went to New Ferry, where his wife opened a shop. He was not now able to do any business, and had not been for nearly twelve months past in consequence of an accident he had at the Runcorn Station. When he commenced business in 1832 lie was worth about £2,200. He had shortly be- fore obtained £2,500 from the Midland Railway • Com- pany, as damages for an accident, which, after paying expenses, left about £2,000 clear. He had besides about £2OO cash at the bank. He further stated that he first I became aware of his insolvency, when a verdict was given against him at the last Liverpool Spring Assizes, in the action which lie had brought against the London and North-Western Railway Company, to recover damages in respect of an accident he had sustained at the Runcorn Station about 12 months previously. The deficiency was put down at £5OO 7s Bd, and the as- sets, with the exception of about £27 book debts, were nil. In June last he was possessed of two dwelling- houses and shops, and six cottages in Regent and Cross- sts., Runcorn. They were mortgaged for £1,200, and were sold by the mortgagees on the 21st of June last, when they only realised £1,250, scarcely sufficient to pay principal, interest, and costs. He had to mortgage the property,in consequence of severe losses sustainedin ship- ping. Ile attributed his failure to the accident at Run- corn, and the costs that he had become liable for in con- nection with the action that he lost when he sought to recover damages for the accident. In answer to the Official Receiver, he denied having parted with his estate with the object of preventing the Railway Company get- ting their costs. The examination was adjourned for the production of further accounts.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. A. R. NORMAN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. A. R. NORMAN.

The neighbourhood of the Presbyterian Church, Hardshaw-st., St. Helens, was on Tuesday morning in a flutter of pleasant excitement. The occasion was the marriage at Mists Agnes MeKeehnie. the eldest daughter of the Mayor (Alderman D. Mc- Ilechnia), to Mr. Alfred Robert Norman, formerly of Parr's Bank, St, Helens but now of Parr's Bank, Cook-st., Liverpool, and of Higher Runcorn, second son of the late Mr. Thomas Norman, of Runcorn. The proceedings were of a very simple character, and were quite in keeping with the unostentatious disposi- tion of His Worship and his family. Miss McKechnie had been a good while one of the lady.teachcr3 in the I Sunday School, and if she did not take a prominent part she took an interesting part in everything that went on there. She had endeared herself greatly to the teachers, who made her a handsome presentation on the approach of the happy event, as also did the scholars in herelam. In the church itself the usual preparation had been made. The choir vaeated its usual position to give place to the bridal party, and occupied seats on the right of the pulpit. Crimson baize had been placed on the steps and into the entrance of the church. The church was crowded long before the hour for the service to begin, and even the stairs and vestibule were crowded with the fair sex. The day was delightfully warm and bright, and no doubt many would regard that fact as an omen of future happiness. The bridal party and the groomsmen arrived in the church early, and punctually at eleven o'clock the bride entered leaning on her father, and followed 15v her bridpsmaids, the choir at the same time rising and singing Sir Henry Baker's beautiful wed- ding hymn, "How welcome was the call, And sweet the festal lay." The bride wore a simple cream cloth travelling dress, with electric blue hat, and blue feathers with white rib- bons. Site also carried in her hand a magnificent bou- quet of flowers, while on the table before the bridal party was a beautiful collection of flowers The brides- maids were Miss Kate McKechnie and Miss Norman. I They each wore copper-coloured cloth dresses and plush hats to match, and carried bouquets. The family and guests present, in addition to those already mentioned, were Mrs. McKechnie and family, Mr. and Mrs. Fred

Norman, Mr. C. Norman, Mr. and Mrs. Daniel McKech- nie, Mr. and Mrs. Brown (Kilmarnock), and Mrs. J. Brown. At the conclusion of the hymn already men- tioned, the Rev. J. Brown, the pastor of the church, offered prayer. In conformity with the Presbyterian form of marriage. the Mayor, in reply to the pastor, for- mally gave his daughter away. The very brief marriage ceremony was then gone through. At the conclusion of the benediction, the choir (which was under the conduc- torship of Mr. (leo. Benson, in the absence of Mr. Nicoll) sang the hymn, . .

• "Oh Fatker, all created, Whose wisdom, love, and power, First bound two lives together, In Eden's primal hoar." The bride and bridegroom, after having been heartily congratulated by the pastor and the Mayor, then ad- journed to the vestry, where the register was signed. On emerging from the vestry the organist (Mr. Brown) struck up the" Wedding march," and when the happy pair reached the doer they were greeted with the usual showers of rice. The party at once returned to Olive Mount, where luncheon was provided, and Mr. and Mrs. Norman at once left for London and the Isle of Wight, where the honeymoon will be spent. On their return they will take up their residence at Runcorn. The pre- sents numbered over 100, including one from the teachers, of the Sunday school and the bride's scholars, and were of a valuable character.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " Anna."
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " Anna."

I That Carlyle said "Man is nothing without clothes," and Constable Cummings, of Widnes, ap- pears to think that a policeman is of very little use without his uniform. While wearing his ordinary attire this officer saw a man conducting himself vio- lently in a public-house, but he deemed it unsafe to reason with him until he was arrayed in all the majesty of blue cloth and bright buttons. He therefore went home and changed his clothes. Re- turning, he boldly wrested the quarrelsome ineb- riate, whose passions quickly cooled down in the solitude of a police cell. That the census taken by the Widnes School Board shows that the important work of getting children to school is admirably performed. Out of 7,645 children there are only 116 not on the rolls of any school who ought to be thus recorded—a fact that speaks volumes for the labours of Mr. Deacon, and his fellow-workers on the Committee. That Mr. Librarian Joses has drawn attention to a cause a much annoyance to frequenters of the Runcorn Reading Room—the practice some people make of converting into a conversation room, a place intended for quiet study. The worst offenders ' are usually persons a little higher in the social scale than the ordinary visitor, and ought to know better. , A few notices "No conversation allowed" may ' bring them to .1 sense of their short-comings, and I have a beneficial effect upon their conduct. ' That Mr. Brunner had a gratifying reception from his numerous Runcorn constituents on Thurs- day evening. . .

That they listened with great interest to a lucid exposition of Local Government as it would be under the new Act, and what it ought to be in order that justice might be done to the wants of the people. That our member was in good form and treated the somewhat dry, though to him familiar, subject in a manner that conveyed much valuable informa- tion to the audience.
That Mr. Brunner is to visit other portions of the constituency to give an account of his steward- ship.
THE POPULATION OF WARRINGTON.

On the 12th of May last a census was taken of the population of Warrington, with a view of ascer- taining whether the borough would be entitled to claim to-be a town county under the new Local Government Bill. The result of the census is that the population of Warrington is found to be 47,325. On Thursday evening the Clerk of the Peace for the county of Lancaster issued, under the direction of a committee of county justices, a scheme for the for mation of electoral divisions in the county for the new county council. The committee will meet at the County Offices in Preston, on Tuesday, the 16th of October, to further consider the scheme and agree upon the report to the Court of Annual Ses- sion. The scheme assigns three representatives on the Council to the borough of Warrington, and two to that portion of the Union of Warrington which is outsicie the area of the borough.

div.head: "EAST LYNNE" AT THE PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: "EAST LYNNE" AT THE PUBLIC HALL.

Warrington has this week been visited by Mr. Pitt Ilardacre's specially organised company in the well-known and ever-popular drama "East Lynne. Although this play has been so many times performed in Warrington, it is one of those dramas whose popularity never seems to wane; and throtrzliout the week the attendance at the l'ublic Hall has been sufficient to show its sterling worth. One of the greatest attractions in the'Per- fortnances has been the acting of Miss Margaret Soulby, who takes the dual character of Lady Isa- bel Carlyle and Madame Vine, and who makes her first appearance in Warrington. Miss Soulby has been highly spoken of by the London Press, and her performance during the present week fully justifies her reputation. Of the other characters the most popular were Mr. Maurice Hoffman as Francis Levi- son, Mr. Henry Lee as Justice Hare, and Mr. C. Franklyn as Bullock, the policeman. Mrs. Clarke gave a good impersonation of Cornelia CarlyleXhe eccentric sister of the hero of the drama, while Miss Ferris ,took the part of Barbara Hare very creditably. The other principal characters were sustained by Mr. Gordon Phillips as Lord Mount- severn, Mr. Fred Merer as Archibald Carlyle, Mr. Leonard Yorke as Richard Hare, and Mr. Kelly Robinson as Lawyer Dill. Taken altogether, the present is as good a representation of "East Lynne' as we have seen in Warrington.

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION IN WARRINGTON.

The committee recently appointed by the War- rington Association for the Promotion of Technical' Instruction to ascertain and report the extent to which Technical Instruction is lready given in Warrington have drawn up the following state- ment :

ELEMENTARY Scitoms.—Returns have been obtained: from 18 schools attended by 3,050 boys and 2,468 girls, over six years of age. The boys are distributed amongst the different standards thus :-1, 530; 2, 808; 3. 587: 4, 598; 5, 449; 8, 198; 7, 74; Ex 7, 8-3,050. We point out in passing that the powers conferred by tne Govern- ment Bill for Technical Instruction, introduced during the late session, could only have been exercised on behalf of the 74 boys in Standard 7, With regard to the extent to which Technical Instruction is already being riven in the elementary schools, we find that of the 3,050 boys, 1,385, or 45 per cent., receive instruction in drawing, whilst 345, or 11 percent., receive instrir,tion in elemen- tary mathematics, and that no other scientific or techni- cabinstruction is provided. Of the 2,488 girls, 220, or 9 per cent., are being taught drawing, and 50 algebra, whilst 189, or 7 per cent., receive technical instruction,. either in domestic economy or in cookery, in addition to the instruction in needlework which is given to the whole number.

SECONDARY SCHOOLS.—The total number of boys in the Grammar School is 120, of whom 70 are receiving in- struction in mathematics, 60 in science., viz., phvsiog- raphy ; 90 in French, 50 in German, and the whole school in drawing. . . . . . . .

EVENINC7 CLASSE9.—In the School of Art about 30 stu-- dents receive instruction in science, viz., in mechanical drawing, and 220 in the art department, which includes classes in designing (20 students), modelling in clay (20), glass etching, house decoration, Sze. At the Museum, classes for German (with 28 students), and for French (with 14 students) are being carried on, and so far as we are aware this is the only instruction of any kind which is being given in public evening classes outsidetheSchool of Art.
A meeting of the Association is announced to be hold at the Museum, next Monday evening, when the Rev. M. Stevenson will read a paper on "Recreative :evening classes."

WYCLIFFE (WARRINGTON) V. SALFORD TEMyEGANCE.— 'This match was playedat Warrington,onSaturday,when, after an hour's play, victory rested with the visiting team by 1 goal and 4 minors to 1 try and Sminors. The home team wore bands of crape as a token of respect for the late Mr. C. 0. Barker, who was a member of the Wycliffe team. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH v. HALTON JOCEETS.—This match was played on the ground of the Church in fine weather, and after a good but one-sided game victory rested with the Church, who scored 1 goal, 4 tries, and 4 minors, to nil. Woodward (2). Dunba'vand (2), and Jones scored the .tries, and, Watson kicked a goal. Church team: Full back, Dunbavand ; three-quarters backs, Peacock, Hosker, and Clarke ; half backs, WiNiam- son and Jones; forwards, Woodward, Watson, Walker, Ward, Coxhill (captain), Coward, Tonks, Kniveton, and Derbyshire. WIDNES IN-WORKS FOOTBALL COACPETITION.—This competition, organised by the Widnes Club with the in- tention of fostering local talent, was completed on Mon- ' dag eventng, before a large number of spectators. Ori- ginally there were 11 clubs in the competition, but the lnal lay between a team from Widnes Alkali Works and a team from the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon. At the finish victory rested with the Alkali team by one goal and two minors (10 points) to one try (4 points.) The play was not of a very high-class character, the ex- , .cited state of the players in their eagerne,ss to win milita- ting against a good exhibition. Deacon's team exhibited the greater smartness with the ball, and had a fair snare of the game, but the forwards were much too light for the opposing nine, and consequently the backs did not get many opportunities. Brennan es- pecially distinguished himself at back. The try was , scored by Burgess, after a splendid dribble by Johnson and Woolstencroft, but Brennan unfortunately failed to improve upon a very easy place. It was only in the last minute that the Alkali succeeded in scoring the winning point. Hughes obtained a try from a maul, and Farrell ( Curley"), who had worked like a Trojan through- -out, kicked a magnificent goal from a most difficult place. The members of the winning team will each be presented with a gold mddal, abd the runners-up will each have a silver medal with a gold centre Teams: —Alkali (No 1) : Bark, D Burton; three-quarters, J. Donoghue. J Hartles, and E. Gordon; half backs, E. Farrell and W. Beasley; forwards, T. Hughes, J. Gandy, R. Dolan, R. Rbberts, T. Gregory, T. Whelan, J. Currie, W. Moorcroft, and W. Wright. Messrs. Kiddie and Laws were the umpires, and Mr. T. Warren, of Warring- ton, was the referee. RUNCOF.N v. SALFORD (2ND Taams.)—Played„at Run- corn, on Saturday. Salford kicked off, and CawleV re- turned into touch. Mallinson setting hold put in a grand kick, which Booth. responded to, and Hailwood and Abrams following Well up dribbled the ball on to the visitors' 25, the ball going into touch. From the line-out S. Abrams getting hold passed to Woods, who took his drop at goal, but just missed, a touchdown resulting. Flay was fast and exciting, the ball travelling from end to end of the field. The home 'team eventually got in close quarters to the visitors' line, where a scrimmage was formed, and oh the ball coming out Woods secured and dropped the ball over the bar. Half-time was soon afterwards called, the score standing—Runcorn, 1 goal and 3aitinors, to Salford 1 minor. Bowyer re-started from centre, and play was equally fast and exciting, both sides showing good football.. The home forwards worked splendidly, and after several close scrimmages on the visitors' line, Gatley was successful in grounding over the line close to touch. Woods, however, failed at the place. Shortly after the drop-out Burton, Cheetham, Mallinson, and Edge experienced had lines, but could not get past the home backs. No side was called, soon after, and the home team won a grand game by 1 goal 1 try and 4 minors to Salford 2 minors. Teams :—Runcorn: S. Booth, back: E. Lunt, T. Woods, and W. EL Cawley, three-quarter backs; W. Evans and S. Abrams, half backs; J. Galley (captain), J. J. Bowyer, W. Shaw, W. itigby, H. Barker, T. Abrams, J. Ford, E. Andrew's, and R. flailwood. forwards. Salford: E. J: Parker, back: W. Burton, B. Cheetham, and J. Mallinson, three-quar- ter backs; L. Boothman and J. W. Edge, balf backs; R. Bullock, J. F. Bullock, T. Price, A. Handforth, J. Morris, G. Tongue, W. Longworth, T. King, and G. Eccles, for- wards. WIDNES v. JACK BRTGGS' LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE "Tetx.—This match was played on Saturday, on the Lower Tiouse-la.ne ground, for the benefit of Briggs, the Widnes professional. The game was witnessed by more than 2,000 spectators, and the weather was very favour- able, until near the close of the contest. The visitors had no chance whatever with the Widnesians, with tH'e result that the game ended considerably in favour of the latter—three goals, four tries, and five minors, to nil. The home team won the toss, and played with the wind, and Jack Briggs kicked off at half-past five. The ball was quickly returned, followed by a scrimmage in the centre of the ground. Then Plumpton made a splendid run, and gained a try, but failed at goal. Kiddie made a few slight dribbles, and eventually securedanothertrv, which Plumpton failed to improve. Another try was gained by Plumpton, but Farrell failed to improve the point. Joe Briggs made several desperate attempts to score for his side, and in one he relieved from near the posts, but was subsequently caught by Kiddie, Parkin- son after a commendable run placed the ball over the visitor's line, gaining another try. Farrell kicked, and landed a goal. In the second half Plumpton kicked off, • and after some little time a try was added to the rest of the score by Wilkinson in a very easy manner. Pimp- ton landed a fine goal. After some very good passing by the homesters, the ball dropped in Bingham's hands, who kicked in touch. Plumpton relieved, and made a splen- did run half the length of the field, and with compara- tively no obstruction secured a try. E. Farrell kicked and placed a neat goal. After a minor had been added, Farrell put in a plausible run, and grounded another try, but failed to improve in the kick. The game caused no little amount of excitement: Some of the visitors played very well, but they appeared to have little or no chance with their opponents. When the whistle blew for the last time the game stood as above stated. Plumpton, Farrell, Parkinson, Smith, Kiddie, Woods, and -Barber were the pick of the Widnesians, and Joe Briggs played ' well for the strangers. The teams were : back, Owen; three-quarters, Plumpton (captain), Parkinson, and S. Bingham; half-backs, Farrell and Wilkinson; forwards, Smith, Kiddie, Woods, Pennington, Barber, Wright, Williams, Gordon, and Fairley. Briggs' team Jack Briggs, back; Joe Briggs (Bramley), Morris (Widnes), and Shepherd (Birch), three-quarters; A. Sut- ton (Manchester), and Lloyd (Chorlton), half backs; J. Tune (Broughton Rangers), H. Heywood (Broughton), A. Jackson (8.R.), Johnson (Widnes), Bainbridge (Man- chester), Thornley, Whitehead (Chorlton), Hunt (Man- chester), and another, forwards. Mr. W. Ireland was the referee. RUNCORN V. SALFORD: A WIN FOR RUNCORN.—SaIford .on Saturday was the 'scene of a tough struggle for supremacy between two of the principal clubs in the neighbouring shires. The interest exhibited by the sup- porters of each team was very keen. A large number - accompanied the team from Runcorn, while a large as- somblage greeted the team at Salford. Punctually to the time advertised for the " kick off" the following teams appeared :—Salford: W Mainwaring„ t back; It eooke, J Priestley, and W Burton, threequarter backs; H Clegg and Smith, half backs; T Roberts, Tsmith, Shaw, G Jackson, F Bradshaw, H Handforth, E Austin, T Gorman, and Flaslam. forwards. Runcorn: J Brazen- , dale, back; T H Davies, J H Crompton, and W A Riley, threequartet backs • II Hughes and J Hollingworth, half backs; W Hirdies, George Wainwright, W H Broady, W Faulkner, J Gayter, R Dolan, P Riley, W Stubbs, and Handcock, forwards. After the usual preliminaries, Shaw kicked off from centre. W Hughes replied, send-

lug the ball into touch at centre. Brazendale was soon called upon, to which he responded by some huge kick- ing. The ball getting towards the Runcorn quarter, Cook tried at goal, Brazendale touching down. Some tall kicking by Priestly and Brazendale elicited admira- tion. Forward play ensued, to which the play was chiefly confined during the game, the backs having com- paratively few chances. A strong determined effort by the " paak " forced Salford to act on the defensive and to touch down. To the drop out Brazendale sent the ball bounding back again towards the home quarter, Faulkner, Gayter, and W Hughes dribbling on near the line, Hollingworth pounding on Priestley before he could relieve. Cook tried for an opening on the left, finishing a run by a drop kick to the Runcorn back, who returned the compliment with interest to within the Salford half, Gayter and Hancock leading on with a dribble to the line, Cook saving in time to prevent a certain try. Not, however, to be baffled, another effort by Gayter was crowned with success, a good try being scored, though Brazendale failed to add to its value. From this point Runcorn still continued to have the best of the play, but the worst Of luck. The score at the charge of end stood —Runcorn, a try, five minors, to Salford a minor point. After the usual interval, W Hughes kicked off. Burton rather mulled the return. The forwards getting up a scrimmage was formed near the lino. Gorman and Shaw tried to get way, but Wainwright quickly assumed the aggressive, and ran strongly to the line. Salford eased the pressure, Priestley., relieving, kicking well, from which W Hughes claimed a mark, Brazendale trying for goal. Following, Crompton and Hughes both had a shy at the goal, but without success. A long kick by Faul- kner was smartly followed up by Davies, who scored, but, strange to say, an appeal to the referee was made, who disallowed the try, though the point was almost in- disputable. The forwards still had the most of the work, the backs being left with very little to do, except Brazendale, who played a champion game all through. The forwards had quite enough of a hard game, which ended in a win for Runcorn by a try and nine minors to two minors. WAREINGTON "A" TEAM v. TYLDESLIEST 2ND —The War- rington" A" team journeyed to Tyldesley, on Satur- day, to play their opening fixture with the Tyldesley 2nd team. The weather was fine' and a good number of spectators witnessed the match. Bibby played wing three-quarter in place of Sanson, and in the absence of Jolley, BDSCOW took the position of full back, and did his work creditably. In the first half Warrington had all the best of the game, the forwards working well to- gether, and the passing of the backs being a treat to witness, eliciting praise from the spectators. The second half was not so interesting, the Warrington players ap- parently getting rather indifferent, and not praying so well together, although Tyldesley in this half played a good defensive game. The visitors' captain (C. Adam- son) won the toss, and elected to play uphill. Simmons kicked off for Tyldesley at 3-30 p.m., Roscoe., returning to Molyneux, who obtained a free kick, 13oscow again returning, this time into touch. From the line-out the ball was passed to Fearnley, whose kick Evans .charged down and dribbled to centre. Lawless carried play into the home half, where J. Bate passed to Daniels, who was collared by Briscrow ; but from the scrimmage which ensued Lawless secured possession, and after a capital run gronnded the ball over the line, J. Bate landing a goal from the place. Hindley restarted,Evans returning nicely to centre. Good passing between .T- Bate, Evans, and Bibby took place, the latter player getting in a good kick, which was followed up. the for- wards dribbling to the, line, Lawless succeeded in ob- taining his second try, Bate this time failing to improve the point. Simmons dropped out, J. Bate returning to Brobin, who sent the oval into touch in the Tyldesley half. Lawless next passed nicely to .T. Bate, who threw- the ball to Daniels. and this player, going off at full speed, knocked aside all opposition, and planted the ball over the line. Boscow was allowed the kick at goal,. but failed. Thenext item of note was a combined dribble of the Warrington forwards, but Fearnley stopped their progress, and sent the ball into touch. Eyes, F. Bate. and Holmes broke away from a scrim. mage. forcingthe home full-back to touch down.. Imme- diately after this drop-out, Lawless got hold from a pack near centre, and ran and passed to Daniels, who again scored after a dashing run, Holmes failing at goal. From: the drop-out play rested in mid-field, but the passing and running of the Warringion backs soon again forced the home team on the defensive Adamson, Molyneaux, and Lloyd were next conspicuoes ; then Lawless threw the ball across the scrimmage to J. Bate, who passed nicely to Evans, the latter player, after threading his way beautifully past the home backs, gaining a try be- tween the posts. J. Bate kicked another goal. Half time was now called, the scoring etanding—Warrington 2 goals, 3 tries, and I minor point, Tyldesley nothing. The second half was of a tame description, and calls for no special comment, the visitors not caring to increase the score, and the match finally ended in a victory for the Warringtonians by 2 goals, 3 tries, and I minor, to Tyldesley nil. Teams Warrington—Full back, Bos- cow ; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Evans, and Bibby half backs, J. Bate and Lawless • forwards, Adamson; (captain), Molyneaux, Eyes, F. hate, Holmes„ Lloyd, Beard, Acton, and Neald. Tyldesley—Full back,Rigby ; three-quarter backs, Molyneanx, Fearnley. and Briscow ; half backs. Simmons (captain) and Hilton; forwards, Hindley, Brobin, Toddat Smith, Hilton, Bowker, Aldred, Shaw, and Wilson.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. TYLDESLEY.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. TYLDESLEY.

...... Warrington opened their season on Saturday afternoon in a match against Tyldesley, the holders of the West Lan^,ashire Challenge trophy. The unflagging interest which the public feels in the robust winter game as very clearly shown by the crowds of spectators who flocked on to the Wilderspool ground, the crowd num- bering, we should think, between 3,000 and 4,000. The local team turned out as we indicated last week, with the ~exception of Buxton and Frank Turner, who were pre- vented, by different causes, from attending. The place at full back of the former, was taken by Sanson, and that of the latter, at forward, by Cragan. The visitors also came in full strength, under the the captaincy of Shaw.

Isherwood set the ball in motion, but for the first few minutes play was in Warrington ground. However, Sanson came to the rescue of his side, and, aided by the good dribbling powers of the Warrington forwards, placed the Tyldesley men on their defence. After Barnes had got in a good kick to Fearnley, Berry negotiated a neat pass to the same player, but the transfer was quickly spoiled by the safe tackling of Littlewood. Povey was next conspicuous, and after Hardman had been the means of transferring play to the Warrington 25, Barnes passed grandly to Jolley, who ran and punted with excellent judgment, eliciting great cheering. Neat passing was again indulged by Barnes, Speakman, and Jolley, but the first minor was brought about by a long kick of Samson's. Barnes, immediately after the drop- out, almost lowered the Tyldesley goal by a smart drop, the ball aoing wide by the merest shade. Minor points were not to be the order of the day, for soon after re- starting Isherwood had indeed hard lines in not scoring a major point, and although Antrobus tried hard to get rl away his efforts were frustrated by the unfair play of the Tyldesley wing forwards. A movement started by Barnes at centre, was follotved up by Fair Turner, who dribbled with splendid precision, and being joined by his com- rades, the opposing backs were completely beaten, and the ball was taken over, Ashton completing the try All eyes were now fixed on Barnes, who took the place, and loud cheers announced his success. Shaw restarted from centre, and Handles seemed bent on scoring, until his career was checked by Kenyon. Massey and Sanson were both doing good work at this juncture of the game, but the effort of the latter was somewhat marred by a mistake from which Woodward was enabled to score, no goal resulting. Half-time was called with the scare— Warrington, 1 goal 2 minors to 1 try. The second half was eagerly contested, the Tyldesley men having slightly the best of the game until a grand passing movement by the Warrington forwards resulted in the oval being taken three parts the length of the field, the ball going into touch. Soon after Fair Turner came through the pack in gallant style, anl although E Dillon got over the try was disallowed. Barnes, Massey, and indeed all the team strove hard to add to their score, but the fates were against them, and eventually victory rested with the home team, after seventy minutes' play, by 1 goal 2 minors, to 1 try 4 minors. Taken all round the game was pretty even. Tyldesley are strong forward, but their over-eager wing play in scrimmaging has a tendency to mar good football. The Warrington forwards were also in eood form, while the three-quarters showed all their old dash Sanson did well at full-back with the exception of the slip which let the visitors score their try. The following were the teams :—Warrington---Sanson, back; Jolley, Barnes, and Massey, three-quarter backs; Antrobus and Speakman, half-backs; W Dillon (captain) Fair Turner, Craghan, Littlewood, Randle, Ashton, Isherwood, Povey, and E Dillon, forwards. Tyldesley— Smith, back; J Feamley, Shaw, and Kenyon, three- quarter backs; Berry and Hardman, half-backs; Sut- cliffe, Woodward, Leach, Grundy, P Fearley, Hampson, Battetsby, Flowers, and A Smith, forwards. Referee, Mr. Trevor Smith, Manchester.

div.head: NOTES BY TETF, WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY TETF, WAY.

So far as the patronage of spectators was concerned the opening match of the Warrington Football Club was a decided success. For more than a quarter of an hour before the time fixed for the beginning of the game, there was a steady flow of humanity along Wilderspool Causeway, and some time before the game began the large arena was surrounded by a cordon of on-lookers, which was pretty compact at most points. From this it may be fairly augured that the Warrington club is, financially speaking, in for another successful season. The play of Saturday: was also fully up to the stan- dard of a first match, and the lowering of the colours of the West Lancashire cup-holders—who had already played two or three games—was, to say the least, a pro- mising beginning. Individually the players all round seemed to be in good font, but collectively, there was some lack of combination. Prompt and systematic pas- sing was not so much practised as is desirable, espcially by the half-backs, though it is only fair to say that really good half-back play was spoiled by the wing tac- tics of the visiting team. As it .was the play of the play of the home team contrasted, favourably- in most respects with that of their opponents, and a little culti- vation of intelligent passing will long before the end
of the season bring it up to a very high stAxsdard in- deed.

Football players who follow the Rugby game will be interested in a number of new !tiles and alterations of rules which will come on for diftussion after the aromal meeting of the Rugby Union on October 4th. Further recommendations for the guidahee of umpires and re- ferees will also be moved. It is proposed to dml -severely with what are known as" wing players, and foul and rough play generally. Surrey and the Australians met on Thursday at Ken- nington Oval for the third time this season. The Aus- tralians were batting all day, and made 259 in their first innings.

The cry of the lad and thy signt was so .haarttrending that it was a few moments before anyone ran to,his aesistance. The mass of flesh was replaced and tiedl by a handker- chief, while the same locomotive took litn, to Thelwall Hospital in the anus fat the man who bound, up the terri- ble Injury. It has been found necessary no, amputate the left leg. The amputation wag successfull4y-performed Thelwall Hospital on Tuesday.—Another tncldent, by which a man got his leg broken, took place at wee= TWlnly in Statham on Wednesday last. Ho was conveyed to libe Thelwall Hospit. where the injury was attended to by the resident surges ELOPING WITH A NAVVY.

Some excitement has been caused in the neiglibour, lofod of Cadishead and Partington, by the news being spread that a navvy, who wke recently employed- oirthe Ship C'onal works, had eloped-in' company with .the wife , of a laieourer, who works at the paper mills at Parting- ton. The navvy had, it appeared, taken up lodgings with the-labourer, and had by degrees succeeded in gain ing the affections of the mistress of the house. The neighbaars at first began toentertain suspicions when' they notified that the navvy made. a practice on Satur- day everings of going with his landlady to "do the mar- keting" liar the following week. It was also noticed that the cettple bad a habit of dropping in at the village public-hocees and partaking of fkiendly glasses. The husband othe woman, hearing of these doings, charged his wife with being unfaithfal, andsdbmestie trouble fol- lowed. The navvy lodger received notice to quit, and complied, hat in a few weeks time he- and the erring I wife were o`iiserved together in a neglibouring village. On another cecasion they were ascertained to have been ,drinking together at Irlam, and in consequence of these matters coming to light, the husband cf the woman del dared his intention of obtaining a separatforr, She, how- ever, promisedito mend her ways, and was forgiven, but a day or two afterwards she disappeared, leaving four young children, behind her, and taking some spare cash and a quantity of wearing apparel witlrher. At the • satne time time-the former lodger was found' to be miss- ing. THE LiVE'RSION OF THE MERSEY. The valley of 'thelryrell presents one continuous scene of activity, and matte and steam Issue frorrelecomotive engiaes on every hand. At Cadishead the vatting of the canai has been extended as far as Latchford!on the Che- shire side, and a track bridge crosses the It-well near Rixten. A portien; of the engine sheds at ' Steer Rock; Cadishead, have been removed to PartingtOn; and the pay otices converted into houses for the navvies. On this section there-are seven' locomotives at work. At Partington where there are four locomotivesthere are three track bridges across the river, and a large-cutting is beinwmade to divert the Mersey into the Itwelt at a point oposite Irlam-knovrn as Sandywar,p. A ballast has been constructed from Irlam station on the Cheshire Lines into Flixton, where-, opposite Irlam Boat; ariumbei of workmen's huts have been erected. Both at' Parting- to n and Flixton—there-being five locomotive engines' at, the latter place—enginesheds, hospitals, and offaes have been erected. At Stickihs Island a portion of thelrwell has been filed up, and where the locks will be-situate the depth of the canal has been reached. At the-Aque- duct at Barton, piles are being driven into the river, and also under the southern arches of the bridges whiehspan the Irwell, so as to forma track railway to connect the ballast lines which lia east and west of the meadows at Barton. Bridges are being- constructed across the -river at various points, so that through means of commrtnibae. tion by rail cat be-stabliahed between Salford Docks-and those at Eastham. The whole face of the country iSicei. ing changed betweern these places and whilst vast erm- bankments are being raised on both sides of the river- orchards of fruit trees arefest disappearing.

THE COMPANY AND. THE PURIFICATION OF THE' IRWELL. Representatives-frinn. the Salford, Bolton, and, 'Reich- dale Corporations, the Bbwdon, Famworth, Heaton Mersey, and Levenskulme•Local Boards, and the Al- trincham and Barton-upon-Irwell Rural Sanitary Anthe- ritieS met, the Chairman and Deputy Chairman off- the Manchester Ship Cairal Company on Tuesday to consider the reports received from the various local autheritiesl and also to considerwhat further steps might be taken. to give effect to the resolutions yassed at the con- ference of local authorities-which vrasheld in Manchester - in January last. Lord Egerton reported that 6M the• local authorities were'renresented at the conference- out of the 75 invited to attend'.. From the reports his- lord- ship had since received he found that 13 of the autho• - rities in the basin efthe firsey and Irwell, above- the • junction of those rivers, have sewage works in operation, six have works in. course of construction, 12 have made arrangements for the, consti eution of works, 16 have the question of the disposal oftheir sewage under considera- tion, and in some cases have already purchased land. whilst nine of the authorities are known to have not yet taken action, and with-regard to 19 no information has- as vet been obtained! Mr. Alderman Walmsley-(Salfeilrd) made an interesting statement with respect to theactiori taken by Salford against other authorities during the present year, which, we understand, will shortly-be pub- lished. Besides othantusiness, it was decided that the Committee should communicate with those authorities which have not hitherto dealt with their sewage-and the pollution of the streams in their districts, urgirig them either to construct works themselves or take atidantago of other undertakicge their vicinity which might, be• adailable. It was coesidered that the authorities repre- sented on the CornnUitee would rendervaluabreassistance, by having the streams in their immediate neigiAbOu placed under inspection.

div.head: MANCHESTE It SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTE It SHIP CANAL.
EASTHAM, &c.

The bank near the ferry at Las i tham s being rapidly filled in, as is also the bank on the south side of the canal, where it cross the foreshore near Boston Wood. The cutting of rock at Ellesmere Port proceeds satis- factorily, and the second lift is now being worked here. The great basin which is to form the site of the locks at the Eastham terminus has now assumed the acipear- ance of a great ravine, 200 yards in width. Shun the works were commenced, it is computed that cubic yards of earth have been removed on this section:' In order to get rid of this tremendous amount of materiall it has been found necessary to form what is practically , new land in the vicinity. "The Ilollows".at Easthani, ' near the shore, have been felled up over an area coverg many acres. A largo quantity of green-heart timberpii kind of lairrh—the most durable timber known for stan- ding tho action of the water—has just arrived on the ground, ready for the building of the lock-gates, which' will be the largest in the worki, excepting, perhaps, the. gates constructed for the new docks at Hull. The lock- gates will be 80 feet wide in the clear. Three locks I are to be constructed abreast of each other: the smal- lest will be 150Seet by 30 feet,. the next 350 feet by 501 feet by 30 feet, and the largest 600 feet by 80 feet. The I canal, on its way to Ellesmere Port, will cross Pool Bay: and here the line of railway crossing the bay is nearly completed. Working from both ends of the bay the line is withinlooyardaof joining. When c-ornpleted , the railway embankment will ferns the base far the outer wall of the canal in that part of the cutting. The summer strength of the forces employed, which W 2,3 about 1,800, has now been rafiuced to the winter level,, an average of 1,000 to 1,200. There are nine steam navvies constantly engaged excavating the canal, on this section.

INCE. The Vicar of Ince, Mr. Rawson, occasionally holds services in the Ship Canal Mission-room, as well as the resident missionary for the section, Mr. Pickles. A house for Mr. Pickles is being built near to the mission. room.

div.head: FRODSHAM MARSH.
div.p: FRODSHAM MARSH.

Here there are one German and twc•American navvies at work. Several of the huts for the navvies are tenan- ted, and the remainder will soon be tenanted. NVALTON AND STOCKTON HEATH : DISCOVERY OF ROMAN POTTERY. _ _

Great headway is being made with the work in the neighbourhood of StocktonHeath,Waltort, Acton Grange, and Moore. The recent spell of fine weather has been of great benefit to the work on all parts-of the canal, but nowhere, perhaps, has it been more appreciated than on these sections. where the rain that has collected in the cutting has been a great hindrance• to. work. Progress during the past week has been even. more rapid than usual, the German excavator especially making great headway. The railway embankment extends with sur- prising rapidity, the tipping arrangemonts being ex, trowel', ingenious. At Acton a Grange the new navvies' huts, the mission room, and missionary's. house will shortly be completed, and the opening, services are ex- pected to be held'very soon. The steam " diggers "on Morley Common are making great headway, and the railway which has been laid along the towing path of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal is incontinualuse. Through George's Bank,ea piece of rising land on the Warrington side of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, between Tom Paine's and Twenty Step Bridges,. a. steana navvy has been steadily cutting its way, and, has now almost reached the canal at the latter bridge: Am interesting discovery has been made at this spot During the pro- greas of the excavations traces have been met with of an old Roman road that is known to have misted in the neighbourhood, and several fragments of pottery of the Roman period have been found. Mr- Madeley, librarian at the Warrington Library,. on. Wednesday visited the works and examined the pottery, which he found to be similar to specimens that are already preserved in the Museum. Large q,uantities of broken pottery of the Roman period ,were found at the same spot about twenty years -ago. In addition to the fragments of pottery that the Ship Canal erwavations have brought to light, there has also been found a broken "quern," or hand-mill, of the Roman period. The " quern " is of an interesting pattern,, and aS.a relic it is of some value. There is nothing remarkable about the fragments of pottery. The relics -are in.the posses- sion of the agent of the contractor. .

div.head: THELWALL..
div.p: THELWALL..

To anyone who wishes to See what steam. navvies can do when kept steadily at work a visit to Morris Brook may be recommended. Here, on the scene of the future Latchford locks, there are three ef . these mechanical workers in constant operation during working hours with the result that a channel which is.already wide and deep is rapidly made wider and deeper. Locomotives are also busily engaged in drawing away trains of wag- gons filled with "spoil" and in , bringing back the empty waggons. In connectionwitheach stemanavvy two or three men and horses are regularly employed in.drawing waggons singly along lines of -rails to within. reach of the movable crane of the navvy where:, they are quickly filled and drawn away by the same means to be formed into trains for tho locomotidlts to remove to. the spoil ibanks. The cutting is now within a, few yards of that part of Thelwall-lane lying between Cedar Lawn and Morris Brook, and there are not wanting signs that this lane—which, as we have mentioned before, is to be demolished to make way for the docks—will soon be trenched upon. The road which is to be substituted is being very rapidily put into useable condition, at all eventa for that part of its length between Morris Brook farm buildings and Cross-lane. A solid foundation of hard material of various description has-been laid down and over this is being placed a thick coating of good macadam. A well made cinder footpath runs along one side of the road, the channels are kerbe.d, and connected by means of grids with an apparently well-laid sewer. In some parts the road has already been rolled, and it is quite evident from what may be seen, that so 1 far as its qualities as a highway are concerned, it will be a decided improvemeat on the prssent means of com- munication between Warrington and, Thelwall. The length of canal between Morris Brook and the Mersey at Thelwall is now comparatively, quiet, though another row of navvies' huts has been completed. and inhabited. Across the river, however, at Thelwall, the work of ex- cavating the new channel, into which tho river is to be d4verted, goes on unremittingly, and the. spoil heap to the south of the cutting is now.- a very great height and width.

PARTINGTON AND LRLAM. A steam navvy ha .s lasen inserted in. the 'cutting at Partiugton, and another is being built. This is the site of the proposed coal basin, wherein: ships may coal, re- ceiving their coal from the railway waggons direct into the hold of the vessel. It is in close proximity both to the Warrington and Manchester- and Warrington and Stockport lines, and will be a most suitable depot for the Derbyshire and South-West- Lancashire coal fields. In the cutting at Irlam, two more steam navvies are be- ing added to the two already:at wotk. An engine-shed and fitting-shop is being added tsuthe buildings here.

div.head: BARTON. SziL
div.p: BARTON. SziL

The French navvy has completed the cutting on Sticken's Island, and has been removed to the Salford end of the section. This cutting is virtually completed, being cut the required depth, and the sides and odd parts of the cutting are being finished by an American navvy and by hand labour. The construction of a rail- way route under the arches at Barton Bridge has been Ixtun, to connect the cuttings on either side. A good quality of stone is still being obtained at the Eccles cut- ting, which is being used for building the boundary wall of Trafford Park. 'Near this' quarry a new cutting has been started, and a steam navvy inserted ,which is work- ing its way towards Barton. At Mode Wheel a cutting is being made to strike across the fields toward Trafford- road, on the south side of the river, where there are now three steam navvies at work. In No. 1 Dock the north wall has its foundation- laid—with the exception of a few yards—the whole length, and for three-fourths of the length the wall is three feet above the foundation: for about a couple of hundred yards it is six feet high. A large quantity of granite copings are already on the ground for the tops of the walls. In Docks Nos. 2 and 3 a steam navvy is a,t work in each, clearing the way for the walls.

div.head: POMONA BUILDINGS.
div.p: THE POMONA BUILDINGS.

In consequence. of the contractor for the works being ready to enter into possession of the land at Pomona, it has been found expedient to put the various buildings 'up for sale. Owing to the short time that was allowed to tha buyers to clear away the property, the prices ' realised were in most cases very low. THEFT BY A LODGER. At Lymm Petty Sessions on Friday, a young man. named Edward Fay was charged -with having stolen a jacket, a vest, a shirt, and other articles of clothing, of the value of ZI 4,5, at Thelwall. Mrs. Hill, wifeof William Hill, who lives at Thetwall. said she kept lodgers who were employed on the canal. Defendant came to her house and asked far lodgings, fepresentin,g that he was employed in the shed on the aerial works, and she accordingly took him in. After 'edging with her for less than a week he carried off the articles in question, some of which belonged to her other,ledgers.— Prisoner acknowledged the charge, and said that he stole the articles through "souse queer temptation coming over him," but he was sorry for doing such a, thing.— The Chairman (Mr. T. P. Norris) commented severely upon the action of Fay in carrying off the property of his fellow lodgers, and sant that he would be sent to Knuts- I ford gaol for two months' hard labour.

YENBANK, Arrorrs.—Five years ago this last August `f.:pt with a serious accident in a collision between a ling bridge an a vessel on which I was working. I 4 so badly hurt that I had to go to the Leeds Infirmary undergo an operation, which gave me temporary m- il. t• I went to my usual work, but soon found that I tt;attl not received the relief I had expected. I suffered itttellse pain across the loins and back, and thought time that I would surely die. I applied to the 'rZYsicians, but could get no medicines that would give tj the slightest relief. I also found that my urine con- rianled bloody matter, and this in itself showed me that case was a desperate one. I lost flesh so rapidly • o.almost become a skeleton, and was unable to do Slightest work : in fact, I was completely prostra- Ike and distracted in mind, not being able to get any , P except by getting up into a chair. I read ,an ac- of Warner's SAFE Cure n the Wakefield Express, • also received a pamphlet from Mr. Wilkinson, che- at Normanton. I resolved to give the medicine a Ll,l, and began by taking one bottle, which I used by ng three doses a day. It began to dispel the bloff- lgw which before was so great as to prevent my getting a stooping position to lace my boots. James Walker, who, like myself, is a vessel man, I t his daughter has been greatly benefited by its use. t;lave recommended it to a young man who suffered th 13,11,1 Pains in the back and loins, and' he has told me i :.• after taking two bottles of Warner's Sian Cure he greatly benefited from its use. THE MAGISTRI.TEE AND IRREGULAR ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOLS.—William Phillips, an old roan, was charged with not having complied with an order of the justices that his grandson, of which he was the guardian, should attend Lymm Parochial School regularly. Mr. Cutter, clerk to the Altrincham Board of Guardians, attended to prosecute, and said that he did so because the Guar- dians had reason to think the cases were not thoreughly and properly put before the Bench. In the present case every endeavour had been made to get the child to school, and defendant had been before the committee no fewer than eleven times, and he had been summoned before the magistrates several times, but no fine had been imposed.--Mr. Lister said it was not a question for the Bench what the Xducation, Committees had done. ,The Bench must deal with every case as it came before them on its own merits.—Mr. Cutter said the Bench had had that man before them six times.—The Chairman said that as far as his experience went he could assure , Mr. Cutter that cases of that kind had had every atten- tion on the part of the Bench, who had taken no end of trouble over those cases.—Mr. Cutter said the Guardians were rather under the impression that the cases had not been fully put before them.—The IChairman thought Mr. Moore had always put the cases very well.—Mr. Lister said he certainly took exception Ito a paragraph relating to those cases in a circular issued by the Guardians.—Mr. Cutter could only regret the circumstance if it had given offence.—The Chairman said no offence had been given.—Mr. Moore, the school attendance officer, then gave evidence, from which it ap- peared that the lad in question had during the period covered by the order been at school 17 times, and absent 12 times. A fine of Is, including costs, was imposed on Philips.—Peter Forster and Joseph Brazendale were charged with similar offences, the former case being ad- journed, and a fine of 2s 6cl being imposed in the other. ALLEGED FURIOUS DRIVING.—JOIIII Hatton, butcher, Lymm, was charged with having driven a horse and trap at a furious rate on the 6th of September. The case was dismissed. DRUNK IN A PUISLIC-HOUSE. Nellie M. Steel was charged with having unlawfully sold beer to a drunken person atothe Railway Hotel on the 17th met, and Jphn Flynn was charged with having been drunk on the said premises. In each case a fine of 5s and costs was im- posed, the license of the public-house not to be en- dorsed. A Doe CASH.—Frederick Lockyer was charged with having kept a dog without a license at Lymm, but the case was dismissed. CIALK AGAINST A WORKMAN.—Thomas Jennings, tan- ner, claimed 20s from Jeremiah Barr on account of the latter leaving his work without giving a week's notice. As it appeared that there had been no arrangement as to giving the week's notice, and no intimation to that effect had been posted in the works, the claim wale not al- lowed.

ASSAULTS.--John Shaw, who did not appear, for hav- ing assaulted Ann Collins on the 25th August, was fined 5s and costs.—Mr. We!ford, solicitor, applied on behalf of Martha Brown for a judicial separation from her hus- band, William Brown. It was given in evidence that defendant had been in the habit for some time of abusing his wife, and on one occasion .had kicked her very se- verely on the legs and body. The order for judicial se- paration was granted, and defendant was fkned 108 and costs, or in default, 14 days' imprisonment. THE BROOKLANDS POACHING AFFRAY.—Edward Connor, a young man, was charged with having been one of the poachers who so seriously assaulted three Altrincham police officers, at Brooklands, on the 4th November last. Evidence was given by Mary Jane Scott, wife of one of the gang of poachers, who has already been sent to gaol on account of the affair, to the effect that on the night before the assault Connor left her house in Little Bridgewater-st., Manchester, in company with her hus- band. Ilex husband was out all night, and Connor and he came in together next morning.—P.C. Proudlove, a constable who was made insensible, gave evidence as to the affray, but did not identify Connor as one of the men.—Superintendent Leighton then asked for a remand for a week, and mentioned that two of the men—Scott and Ga,vter—who had already been sent to gaol, had made statements which implicated Connor.—The remand was granted.
