DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—David Cane, John Allamby, and John Collins were each fined lOs and costs for being drunk and disorderly. Dominic O'Hara Owen Williams, and Ellen Barker were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk. Frank Allanby was brought np on a charge of fighting with his brother, but he was discharged. SWINS *Fv.vait.—George Thomson, of Canal-st., was charged with having removed a pig into a swine fever infected area without having a license. He was fined is and costs, 8s 6d - A SIGNALMAN WANTED.—Woolton Gray, of Neston, was summoned for using a traction engine on the highway at Sutton Weaver, without having a signalman in front, on the 3rd September. The engine was convoying stone to ' the waterworks Norton.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. SATURDAY,—Before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon. . _

_ SLEAPING 017 T —William Walla,oe (14), 24, Water-st, James Glynn ,(14), 23, Sank7-st, and Peter Connolley (13), 23, Sankey-st, were charged with sleeping in Hut- chinson's chemical works, and. were discharged with a caution.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, and Mr. H. junr. DRUNKENNESS.—WiIIiam Smith, of Albert-road, pleaded to having been drunk, and he was fined 7s 6d and costs. —For being drunk and ,lisorderly, Martin Weir, of 6, Neyon-st, was fined 5s and costs.

_ BECRACH or THE l'EACll.—A,yeung woman named Mary Jane Riley, of 22, Water-st, pleaded guilty to baying created a breach of the peace in Sankey-st, on Saturday night, and she was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, herself in £lO, and two sureties of £5 each.

SLBEPING IN CHEMICAL WORKS.—William Dwyer, an old ' offender, of no settled residence, was sentenced to two month' imprisonment, with hard labour, forsleep- ing in Messrs. Hutchinson's works, on Sunday morning. —Greorge Starkey and Martin Gallagher, of no settled in a cabin at Widnes goal for seven days for sleeping residence were sent to Dock.
WIDNES PETTY SF-SSIONS. THIIRSDAT.—Before Mr. P. 11. Gossage and Mr. H. Gaskeri "junior.

_ DRINK AGAIN.—John Rutter, no residence ; Martin Keenaghan, Warrington-road .; James Campbell, Major Cross-st. ; William Mort, Midwood-at.; were each fined for being drunk and disorderly.' Bna....cnos OP THE PEACE.--Tohanna Kirwin, of Peel- st., and Michael Price, of Grove-st., were each bound over to be of good behaviour for two months, in the usual sureties, for creating breaches of the peace.—Mary Daley, of Grove-st., was summoned to answer a similar charge and she was dismissed. DOGS AT LARGB.—For allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled, Charles McLean, ,of 4, Milton-road, was fined 23 6d and costs.—William Gerrard, of Mill Brow, was fined 5s and costs for a similar offence. ASSAULT ON THE Pmacr. George Kenwright, a rough-looking fellow from Sankey, was charged with having been drunk, and also assaulted P.C. Field. About nine o'clock on Tuesday night Constables Field and Worsfield were called into a refreshment house in Church- st., and found the prisoner in a very drunken state lying across the table. The officers ejected the prisoner, who then became very disorderly, and he was taken into cus- tody. On the way to the police station the prisoner kicked Field on the legs and struck him on the face.— The prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was ordered to pay 15s and costs, or go to gaol for 21 days with hard labour.

FELONISS.—Martin Griffin, of no settled residence, pleaded guilty to having, on Monday last, stolen a spade belonging to Messrs. John C,owburn and Co., contrac- tor, who are constructing a sewer in Victoria-road. He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour —Frederick Monks, of Edge-lane, Liverpool, was charged with steal- ing a coat belonging to John O'Neil, of Old Swan, Liver- pool. O'Neil is employed in the construction of a building in Hutchinson-at., and on Monday morning he left his coat in the building. At noon it had disappeared, and it was ascertained that the prisoner had received 4s 6d for it from Mr. Syred, pawnbroker. The prisouer, who said he did not know what he was doing when he took the coat, was fined 208, or, in default, fourteen days' hard labour.

• " TOWNSMAN " ON A TRICYCLING TOUR. Sir,-1 have been much amused by "Townsman's" account of his tricycling tour, and much more by his re- ply to some common-sense observations and advice ad- dressed to him through your columns by "A Cyclist." As one who had, I believe, the bliss of seeing "Townsman and Co." en route, I should like to say :that, to my idea, the picture of the "Tourists," drawn by "A Cyclist" is tolerably correct. I was going along Sankey-st, when I heard a rattle as of old iron behind me, accompanied by a " titter" along the footpath. I turned round and saw 1 what I have since discovered was "the tourists." For a *description, I should refer to " Cyclist's " last letter. I 1 canna improve it. I might mention, however, that if the machines had been chosen with rather more regard to "fit" and less to antiquity, the turn-out of the party would have looked better. As it was, to quote " Towns- man " the progress of the party "to many towns-folk was as diverting as a circus procession." The party however, from both accounts given by "Townsman," appear to have enjoyed themselves, and that is everything in any holiday; so that while not quite agreeing with the lady tourist that " Cyclist " has been " knocked flat," I, myself, despite appearances, thoroughly believe the trip was thoroughly enjoyed by its participators.—l am, sir, yours Stc.,
READER.

THE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION AND THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. Sir,—As the municipal elections are drawingvery near, one is anxious to know whether the Ratepayers' Associa- tion Committee are still in the flesh, and whether they are on their guard as to who the retiring Councillors are, and how far they have voted in furtherance of the rate- payers' interests. It is a question worthy to be answered, because if the committee can show, at their coming general meeting, that they have been able to keep their own financially, and are determined to further try and ease the burden of the ratepayers, the annual Subscriptions coming due should be forthcoming twenty- fold: There is a mighty question—if I may so term it— , beforethe people of Warrington in the matter of Long- fbrd and the two intercepting depots; and if due care is not taken it will cost the heavy-burdened ratepayers a pretty item. It is a question either the association or someone \else will have to take up. lam not here going to say one word in defence of Mr. Dinwiddie's conduct, or of Mr. Alderman Burgess's extraordinary harsh pro- ceedings; but after this Burgess v Dinwiddie business Is at an end. I may have a word or two to say. I am glad that the present Mayor has, to some extent, shown a good example in dispensing with so many " At Homes, &c ," during his Mayoralty, and if the "happy family" business could only be broken up, and Coun- cillors left to be-free agents, the ratepayers' interests would immensely gain. I am also glad, Mr. Editor, that our borough surveyor is still with us, because as he and Mr. ALlerman Burgess claim the credit of having put down the" best sanitary scheme in the world," but which no other town to my knowledge has adopted, not- withstanding the number of exhibits which leave been made at our expense. I think it would be too bad to leave their adopted child in the lurch. In a word, I would like to see both these gentlemen remain in office sufficiently long to see come to pass what I have before predicted—a total failure of what the plant was first in- tended to do.—Yours truly, WILLIAM DIGGLE.

THEFT VERSUS CRUELTY. Sir,—l should like to draw the attention of the public, and especially of those enlightened mortals who, on oc- casion. occupy the magistrates' bench, to the sentences in the two following cases, which I take from your last week's columns. (1), "A labourer was charged with having stolen a basket, of the value of 6d, from a house. It appeared that the prisoner lodged at the house in ques- tion, and the basket being missed ;it was suspected that he had taken it, and it was found in a shed where he kept his tools. Prisoner, who denied having stolen the Article, said the prosecutrix had lent it to him to carry ;his tools in. The Bench, ordered the prisoner to go to gaol for a month, with hard labour."—(2), "Two men Ihvere summoned by the Society for the Prevention of Cimelty to Animals, for Nl-treating a donkey, by working

it in an unfit state.—lnspector Aplin, R.S.P.C.A., said that the defendants came from Chester to Warrington with a donkey. The animal was in a wretched state, lame, poor, and half-starved. Upon its body it had thir- teen wounds, some of which were large ones, from which blood and matter dropped at every step it took. The legs, where it had been beaten, were quite raw. All the wounds had been caused by ill-usage, and he had never seen an animal in a worse state.—ln defence it was stated that the men had only driven it from Chester to Warrington.—The Bench decided to fine the men 5s and costs, and lOs and costs respectively." I have erased the names and dates, but in other respects nothing in the cases has been left out. I should like to know whether those are the penalties considered by English law to fully meet the cases. If so, the sooner the law is amended the better. For my own part I think that "Mr. Perkins's" theory about the leniency of a well-fed jury- man, must apply to the occupants of the Warrington magistrates bench. In the early part of this year, l— and I believe others also—hoped that honorary officials of this kind might be done away with, and a Stipendiary magistrate might create a change in the extraordinary sentences inflicted under the present system. My dream is upset, but surely something can be done, even with the present " justices " if they are wakened from their sweet content by the voice of Public Opinion.—l am, sir, yours' &c., FAIR PLAY. Warrington, September 12th, 1883.

div.head: BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: THE BREWSTER SESSIONS.

Sir,—Monday next being the date fixed for the ad- journed Warrington Brewster Sessions, hundreds of the more thoughtful kind of our people are anxiously await- ing the final decision of the full bench of our honourable magistracy on that day, respecting the two new licenses recommended on the 3rd inst. by the Licensing Commit- tee, the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alderman Harrison, Alderman Holmes, Major Litton, and Councillor Fran- comb. I was in the Police Court on the day referred to, and I I submit the only reason of any weight laid before the I court by the brewers and their allies was "the wants of the people " in the respective neighhourhoods, viz., Bew- , spy and Battersby-lane. Wants of the people! mind you. Now, sir, I should think the Licensing Committee would not for one moment wish to do anything which would cast a suspicious hue upon them ; that they were culpable of recommending the granting of new licenses for the wants of publicans and brewers, and against the wants of the people. But— The stern behests of duty, The doom-books open throw." And he who runs may read. Our Licensing Committee turned a deaf ear to the wants of the people," and granted the request of the foxy publicans, greedy brewers, and their allies. A number of respectable peo- ple from Bewsey and Battersby-lane told the Bench that no more drinking places were needed in their midst ; and many more ratepayers were in the court anxiously waiting to protest against the monopoly of publicans and brewers. But they did not get called on to speak. Neither did the Licensing Committee, when appealed to, give any of the reverend gentlemen out of the large num- ber who were present an opportunity to speak on behalf of the ratepaying portion of their respective flocks, whose opinions on the drink shops, all must admit, are much better understood by the clergy, who daily go among and talk to their flocks on these matters, than can possibly be understood by the present Licensing Corn-

div.head: inittee.
div.p: inittee.

On the 25th and 28th of August, last year, as requested by the Warrington Temperance Federation, I took a petition from house to house in Battersby-lane and neighbourhood, with the result that, out of the hun- dreds of people then residing there, nearly the whole of them eagerly signed the petition against the granting of any new licenses for the sale of strong drink in their midst. I believe only about 20 of them declined to sign the petition. The voice of the people against the drink- ing dens applied for by the brewers was the voice of God, crying—" Take up the stumbling block out of the way of my pcople." This is the want- of the people, sir, in our town, where drunkenness is so lamentably on the increase. But I should say that the petition referred to, as well as one signed by nearly all the rev, gentlemen of the town, was ruled out of court last Brewster Sessions. Yet, thanks be unto the magistrates who then formed the Licensing Committee, and granted the wants of the people by rejecting the wants of the brewers and their friends. And somehow lam led to hope that our worthy and honourable magistrates on Monday next, will firmly and nobli follow the lines of former years, safely atten- ding to the wants of the people, who have declared against additional snares being pl aced in the way of their feet, the feet of their sons, and of their daughters— yea, in the way of their souls, by the deadly business of Igreedy brewers, which St. Augustine declares to be— " The mother of all mischief, the root of crimes, the spring of vices, the whirlwind of the brain, the over- throw of the sense, the tempest of the tongue, the ruin of the body, the wreck of chastity, a loss of time, a vol- untary rage, a shardeful weakness, the shame of life, the stain of honesty, and the plague and corruption of the soul." .
God help our magistracy to save the people from the brewers' plagueli—Yours, &c.,
R. STOREY.
Warrington, Sept. 19th, 1888.

div.head: TTIF. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: TTIF. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
(Continued from page 6.)
WESTON.

Considerable progress is being made on this section. The cutting on Frodsham Marsh is rapidly being ex- tended by means of the French and German navvies, which daily excavate an immense amount of material. The carpenters are busily engaged in completing the vil- lage of huts, and those structures that are erected are I already occupied. A considerable number of men are ' also employed in preparing for fixing the first lock that is to connect the Weaver with the Mersey. 'On Thursday a young man who was working near the water tanks on Frodsham Marsh was struck by a passing locomotive, and he was much bruised abcut the body. lie was con- veyed to a hut, and the contractor was called in and at- tended to the injured man. RUNCORN.

Work on this section still continues very quiet. The ' docks at Old Quay, however, present an appearance of great activity. Huge beams are daily arriving by water, and are being stacked in immense piles on the quay side. There is also stored a considerable number of blocks of granite, weighing from five to eight tons each, and this week a schooner arrived with another cargo of the stones. A locomotive crane, weighing 32 tons, and capable of lifting ten tons, is employed in this work, and performs it with great satisfaction to Mr. Rhead, the store agent. The makers are the Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Dallam Forge, of Warrington. For the amuse- ment and instruction of the employes of the contractor a social club and other institutions are to be formed dur- ing the winter, Mr. Watson. the missionary, being a moving spirit in the matter. This gentleman is also accomplishing good work at the chapel in Irwell- lane. . _ _

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

At Wednesday's meeting of the Barton Rural Authority the Inspector reported that Mr. Rogers, of Cadishead, had erected four wooden dwelling-houses at Cadishead, one of which was inhabited, without obtaining the necessary certificates for a supply of water to the same. They were erected to meet the wants of the navvies during the 1 construction of the Ship'Canal. Thehouses had been run 1 up in a great hurry, and, in some respects,were also desti- tute of proper sanitary arrangements. The Surveyor , would, however, deal with the owner on this head. It was agreed that the Inspector should wait upon the owner and report to the next meeting. 1 NIGHT WORK. .

_ Thc men employed on the section between Barton and Stickins Island have received notice of the dis- continuance of night work. The other evening, dur- ing the fog, two ballast engines came into collision on Stickins Island. A track railway is now being constructed underneath the southern arches of the Aqueduct and Bar ton Bridge.

--- DRUNZENNESS.—On Tuesday, at the Lymm Police Court, a Ship Canal navvy was committed to gaol for seven days' with hard labour, for being drunk in the village on the previous day. FEVER : CLOSING OF ScHooLs.—Oughtrington schools were closed on Monday, in consequence of an outbreak of scarlet fever in the head-master's house. It is ex- pected that the schools will not be opened for some weeks. LIBERAL CLUB.—At a meeting of the members of this I club, arrangements for meetings to be held in the dis- trict during the winter months, were considered. It was resolved to endeavour to secure the services of the Right 119 n. U. H. FowAer (the member for Wolverhampton), or tlfe prght Hon. Sir George Trevelyan (member for Bridgeton, Glasgow). NARROW ESCAPE FROM Drumm, On Monday af- ternoon a lad, aged three years, son of Mr. Henry Mos- ton, who lives at Yeald-brow, Statham, accidentally fell into the Bridgewater Canal An alarm was given, and a woman named Mrs Jump ran with a long clothes prop by which means she was able to keep the child above water until more efficient assistance came. When the boy was taken out it was thought that he was lifeless, but by dint of restoratives and moving of the arms and body, life was restored. The child is now in a fair way of recovery. CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCROOLS.—OR Sunday, the anniversary"services were held in connection with these schools, special sermons being preached morning and' evening by the Rev. F. Carter, of Northwich. In the afternoon a special service for children was held in the church, many-of the scholars from the Sunday schools in the neighbourhood attending. The hymns, which had been prepared for the occasion, were:sung with much taste ty_tne children, and the Rev. F. Carter do- livered a vernteresting and instructive address. Large congregations assembled at each service, the day being beautifully fine. The collections, which were in aid of the school funds, realised about £l5. LYMM TOWER OF REFUGE LODGE OF GOOD TEid- PLaas.—On Tuesday the usual weekly meeting of this Lodge was held in the Congregational Schools, under the presidency nf Brother Thomas, W.C.T. It had been an- nounced as a "half-pound so members of the

lodge provided parcels of good things, which were set out at the conclusion of the routine business. A some- what unexpected influx of guests occurred. The Bone- hill Branch Lodge from Warrington having arranged a surprise visit to Lymm, they with other visitors num- bered about thirty, and after assisting to dispose of the eatables and coffee they gave an excellent programme of songs and recitations, and the meeting separated after a hearty vote of thanks to the visitors, the hope being ex- pressed that they would pay a surprise visit another time.

LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN. SPEECH BY MR. BRUNNER, M.P. Under the auspices of the Northavich Division Liberal Associatioa, a public meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday evening; and a large audience assembled to hear Mr. J T. Brunner, the member for the Division, speak on" The work of the past session." In the absence of Mr. J. R. Frith, who was away from home owing to family affliction, the Rev. J. D. Thomas occupied the chair. On the platform were Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., Mr. T. E Ellis, M.P., Messrs. T. Handley, B. Kniveton, W. Littler, R. Forester, T. Clegg, W. Faulkner, and W. Handley (the secretary). The Chairman said he had no doubt that all of them had watched Mr. Brunner's career in Parliament with a great deal of interest. They had watched him not as a cat watched a bird, ready to spring upon it whenever there was an opportunity, but they had watched him as a mother watched her little child beginning to walk. (Ap- plause.) They accorded to him that evening a very hearty welcome, and hoped that he would long live to represent that division of Cheshire in Parliament. (Ap- plause.) Mr. B. Kniveton then made a brief speech on the Irish question. They had had, he said, two years out of the 20 years of resolute Government that Lord Salisbury promised that they should have,to settle the Irish ques- tion. He asked their friends the Unionists and the Con- servatives—Had it succeeded? A prominent Conserva- tive admitted to him the other day that the Conservative policy had not succeeded, and that the Irish question was not being settled. (Applause.) People were begin- ning to see what the Irish question meant in all its bear- ings, and he had no hesitation in saying that when the next appeal to the constituencies was made Mr. Glad- stone's policy—(applause)—which was a statutory Par- liament at Dublin, for the management of purely Irish affairs, would be heartily endorsed. (Applause.) In Northwich, at all events, they were right on the Irish question, and they must keep themselves ready for the fray, and take care that the more than splendid victory they achieved last year was repeated, and improved. (Applause). Mr. Brunner, veho received a most cordial welcome, thanked the chairman for having: spoken of him in such terms, but he rather fancied that he was beginning to be one of the old politicians and not one of the young ones; and that if he were not yet able to walk, why God help him he never should be, (Laughter.) It seemed to him that this motion of a member going to give an account of his stewardship was, to use an American phrase, "about played out ;" for he found wherever he went in the con- stituency, and to whoever he talked,that he bad been, as his friend Mr. Thomas said, very closely watched in- deed, and that he could not really tell them anything new about what he did in Parliament, for they knew au about it, just as he did. Perhaps he might say a few words about what the Tories had done and what they had not done, which was a much larger subject, because whenever they had a Tory measure in the House of Com- mons they found that it omitted to do very much more than what it did. (Hear, hear.) He was very much afraid that the result of the Local Government Bill would, in the minds of a good many- of them, and especially those whose minds were situated deep down in their pockets, would be by no means an improvement. He was per- fectly satisfied that,much as we had grumbled at having to pay county rates without having any control what- ever over the expenditure, they would find before ' many months were over that the county rate was going to be a great •deal heavier than it had been. He meant to speak at some considerable length upon this County Government Bill, and he warned them before hand that it was a dry subject. They were not in the throes of an election contest—the sooner the better though--(ap- plause)—for he was ready for the fight if they were. (Applause.) They were therefore bound to consider matters which were unexciting. They had had an ideal Local Government Bill shadowed forth by many reformew in years gone by. And what was it they had hoped for? In the first instance the greatest amount of self-government, not only for the county but for the township and for the village. It had been the wish of those who were real Liberals to give such machinery of self-eovernmento would have interested in the welfare of themselves and of their fellows as large a number of men as possible. They would consider by and bye how this Act, which had been passed, met the first condition. There ought to have been Local Government not only for the coun- ties but for the towns, the townships, and the villages, each of them having the clearest possible defined areas, and each having the clearest possible defined duties. They ought to have granted to the county councils every- thing which concerned the county, and not as it was now that the magistrates had the management to a small degree in their own hands, and that the management was to a very large degree in the hands of the Home Secretary. We ought to have had a county to manage the county affairs, a town council to manage all town affairs, a township to manage township affairs, and a village to manage all the affairs of interest to the village. There ought to have been given to these bodies effective control of all that closely touched the life and progress of the people. We ought to have made this en- tirely simple by giving areas as fairly defined as possible, and ought to have made the local taxation fair by divi- ding the rates between the owner and occupier. (Ap- plause). He lived at Widnes from 1881 to 1872, and during that time he saw the population nearly doubled. He saw land which, when he went there, was worth, perhaps, £.BO an acre, rise in value to £2,000 an acre. All that time he was paying rates as+S.n occupier and not as an owner; he was paying rates which included not only the cost' of annual maintenance, but also the payment of interest and repayment of capital for waterworks and gasworks; for sewers and for roads. He claimed that he paid for those improve- ments; it was he, amongst others, who raised the value of that land from £6B to £2,000. (Applause.) But what said the law? It said that the tenknt who'came to-day and went to-morrow should pay all 'rates, and all the profits that are made out of the payments of the tenants should go into the pocket of the landlord. Here they had a condition of the law that compelled the tenant—the man who worked—to pay all the rates, in- cluding the repayment of capital for the improvement of the town, and the richest man, who could afford to do without income, waiting until the land grimed and , growed through the labour of these fellows, they not paying taxes at all. (Applause.) The Local Govern- ment Bill as it came into the House of Commons gave the County Councils a number of powers under different Acts of Parliament which hitherto had rested in three departments of Government—the department of the Home Secretary, the department of the Board of trade, and that other department called the Local Government Board. The Right Hon. Mr. Chaplin, bet- ter known as the owner of Hermit—(laughter)—pro- posed that these powers should be struck out of the bill, and the Government gladly consented, with the result that upon the County Council will only devolve the ad- ministrative business of the Quarter Sessions. Now that business consisted largely of the management of police stations, the repair, and occasionally, the building of county bridges, the ordering of dogs to be muzzled— (laughter)—and the occasional grant of a pension to a police constable. (Rendived laueehttr.) There was very little more. Theugh these large powers of the three London departments were struck out of the bill, they might depend upon it that one after another large and important powers would be granted to the council in years to come; and it very much depended upon how these county councils managed their business as to what powers the Government will put into their hands. He expected that hereafter there would reside in the county councils powers to manage the education of the chil- dren of the 'county. (Hear, hear.) This Local Government Act increased from about three millions a year, to about five millions a year, the grant from the consolidated fund -- from the taxes—th the relief and benefit of local rates. For many years this had been a favourite project of the Tory party, for the reason that it is property that paid rates, and it was work that paid taxes; and if they took from the fund created by industry, and gave towards the rates raised in the main from property, they gave from the workers for the benefit of the idlers. It was taking money out of the pockets of the working people in order to give it to property owners. He considered that the Government had done very wrong indeed in this matter, and if the Liberals ever caine back into power he trusted that they would reverse that policy. (Applause.) The system of collecting rates was still in as great confusion as ever. There were just as many rates and taxes, and there were as many rate collectors as there were. The areas were just in the same mess as before. Mr. Brunner illustrated this statement, and went on to say that one of the most important defects of the Cloven- merit Bill was that it did not touch the administration of the Poor Law. In all his experience as a political wor- ker he had never met one workingman who wanted a county council, but he had met many who wanted an imptovement in the administration of the poor law. He had met a great many who said that our management of the poor law was a disgrace to the country,and'who con- sidered that it was a very great wrong when they took decent people who had paid their way all their lives, and when old age had come they found they were unable to maintain themselves—it was a foul wrong to thrust those in the workhouse to herd with the dirty scum that had come along the road the day before. (Applause.) He had found a great many workingmen who had com- plained that it was necessary to pay £25 a year before they could qualify to be a guardian, of the poor. (Hear, hear.) But there was no-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 22, 1888. '
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 22, 1888. '

thing about this in the Tory Local Government Bill. The Bill left the control of the police in as unsatisfactory con- dition as they had found it. The Coundl as yet had very little to do with what closely concerned the people ; it had very little to do with land, with education, with charities, and it had very little to do with the licensing question. (Hear, hear.) He was satisfied of this, that it did notmatter whether they liked beer or not, it did not matter whether they liked Scotch or Irish—(laughter)— this everyone of them knew at the bottom of his heart, that it was their business to say whether they would have a public-house next door or not, aid it was notthe business of the magistrates. (Applause.) In dealing with the IS amendments he proposed to the Bill in the House of Commons, many of which he carried; Mr.Bruo- ner said he proposed to reject those clauses one and all which the Government had put is , to creater for the publicans an enormous amoutrt 1 of compensation if their licenses were ta.kea away from them ; and a great deal of good had been done by compelling the Government to drop these compensa- tion clauses. The publicans were finding out for the sakes of their own pockets that there were too many 1 public-houses, and if Parliament had passed those com- pensation clauses, they would have been very glad in- deed to have given up many of them at the expense of I i the people. Parliament had put an end for ever to all idea of paying publicans such enormous grants at the cost of the people. (Applause.). They were present that night as citizens, but he thougsht they might take it that there were more Liberals than Tories in that room. It would be difficult indeed to fill' a room its Runcorn with- out having more Liberals than Tbries he it. (Laughter and applause.) Their duty towards the' County Council as Liberals was to send a man who, would preserve to the public all their public rights and all public pro- perty. Wherever there was a common he wanted the candidate to promise that none of it should be stolen by Lords of the' Manor. (Applause.): He wanted , that no one should be allowed to advance' his hedge on to the road ; that all those strips of road side green should be preserved inst as they' are-;; that no man should be allowed to shut up a footpatiracross a pleas- ' eat field—(applause)—and compel men; always to trudge on the dusty high road. He wanted the people to get representatives who would give the public-control of the charities. There were a great many in Cheshire. They had an income of MOUT or £l4*AM:se:year ;-and almost everyone of them in the hands of the parson. So far as his reading went, take the whole country through, the result was that it was very hard to get a loaf of bread from a- charity unless the applicant went to churcfh (Applause.), It seemed to him (Mr. Brunner) that when a charity was hundreds of years old it was right that it should belong to- everybody and not to the parson (Hear, hear, and applause.) He should like to have the local authorities empowered to take land at fair pribes for schools, forworkmen's dwel- lings, and for labourers alletments. If they could get a man to swallow all these pledges send him. to the County C,ouneil If they got ar good' many men of that sort in the county of Cheshire it would whip- creation—there would not be another like, it in the country.. (Laughter and, applause.) Alluding to the Irish: question, Mr. 'Brunner said that, Mr. Chamberlain had just pub- lished his 23rd plan for the management of affairs in Ireland. (Laughter.) Mt. Gladstone proposed that there should be one Parliament in Ireland ;: Mr. Cliam- berlain thought , so. well' of Parliaments that he wanted four. Mr. Chamberlain on the previous evenirw said that all those whowere fighting against the law itt Ire- land were rightly punished ; that the Irish tenantswere in a more favourable position than any tenants-in the world, and that, therefore, if tenants would not pay their rents the evictions that were now- going on could not be described as unjust. Could Mr. Cham- berlain point to . any country in the world where the tenants, from one end of the country to the other, had built their houses and had then .paid rent on them? He (Mr. Brunner) was perfectly satisfied that in no other country in the world' would be found such a hideous ex- hibition of injustice as was found in Ireland to-day. (Applause.) To talk about honesty and the beauty of obeying the law, and the dishonesty of refusing to sell the last stick in order to pay rent for the house which had been built by their own hands, was to his mind hol- low hypocrisy. (Applause.) Having, thanked the audience for their kind reception, Mr. Brunner resumed his seat, amid loud cheers. Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., then delivered an address, in which he described in a in manner several personal incidents that occurred m the House-of Commons during the past session. Mr. T. Handley proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Brunner for the attentiorahe had paid to his parliamen- tary duties. He said that Mr. Brunner, after he was elected, went up to London, and voted in every division during the remainder of the session. This year he had been quite as active, and they had had a. sample of the business-like way-in which he had enforced his amend- ments upon the attention of the Government by the very able resume of the Bill they had had that night. (Art. plause.) Upon the Irish question,. they knew that gr. Brunner and Mr. Ellis had done noly. They wenV to Ireland last year to inquire into the subject thoroughly, and they gave Mr. Arthur _Balfour the opportunity of running them in if he thought proper. (Applause.) Mr. T. Clegg seconded the motion in a huraourous speech, and it was carried with enthusiasm. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meet- ing.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

WORKINGMEN'S MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.,--A fruit banquet was held on Saturday for the purpose of opening the coming session in connectiOn with the above society. A nice variety of fruit was provided, which was greatly apprecia- ted by those present. The following officers were elected for the ensuing session—President, Mr. .7. Dawber ; vice-president, Mr. D. Price; secretary, Mr. H. Halford. After a very pleasant evening the meeting was closed by singing the doxology. ILLNESS OF THE REV. WILLIAM BROOM:M-0n saturelay morning, the Rev. William Brookes, k Wesleyan minister well-known and highly respected in the Warririgton circuit, was taken seriously ill, and has been confined to his house ever since. He is suffering from inflammation of the 'bowels, and at first grave consequences were feared. The danger was, however, averted. Reference was made to his illness at Bewsey-road Chapel on Sunday. From an inquiry made last evening we learn that the rev, gentleman is nuich better. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CHIE.D.—On Thursday MI. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry at the General Wolfe Inn, War- rington, touching the death of a child named Edith Clarke, aged four years, the daughter of Robert Clarke, a sawyer, of 78, Church-st. It appeared from the evidence that the child, along witn others, was playing with a gate. which leads from General- st. into Litherland's Croft, near the child's home. Deceased was behind the gate, when the other chil- dren. not knowing she was there, pushed it, and the child's head was crushed between the gate and the wane. A woman named Molyneux, seeing 'from a distance that something was wrong, came and picked up the child, and carried it to a chemist. On it being seen, however, that the case was a very bad one, the injured girl was moved to the Infirmary. On reaching that institution she was examined by the house-surgeon, and found to be dead.—After hearing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." Nook IN THE Manxim—At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and other magi- strates. John Baguley, Mill-st., and James Back- house, Orford-st., were summoned for "crying cer- tain articles fot sale in the market, contrary to the bye-laws," on the Bth inst. Market-Inspector Place said that he had cautioned the deMidants, and Baguley especially, several times, but they would not desist. Baguley was engaged at a fruit stall, and Backhouse at a meat stall. Baguley said he wished to know why the inspector allowed the auctioneers in the market to shout, and stopped Warrington salesmen from doing so.—Alderman Davies: There is a difference between " bawling and" shouting." though you may not think so.— The Mayor said the magistrates did not approve of any kind of shouting in the market, and he thought that one should be put down as well as another. The defendants, if they would promise not to repeat the offence, would be discharged that, time. They made the required promises. THE BOWLING -MAIN AT THE CONSERVATIVE Cf.tre.—On Saturday the annual main of bowls pro- moted by the members of this club was brought to a conclusion. Afterwards about a hundred of the members assembled in the first-class billiard-room, where prizes were distributed to the successful com- petitors. In presenting them Mr. John Tinsley said that some of the games bad been of a most exciting i character, and some good play had been witnessed., The following prizes were then handed over to the 'winners :---lst, timepiece, value £5, Thomas Ogden;' 2nd, timepiece, value £4, Thomas Atherton; 3rd, travelling bag, value £1 6s, Edward Finch; 4th, glass flower stand, value £1 2s 6d, F. Berry; sth, cruet-stand, value £l, William Watson; 6th. knives and forks, value 15s 6d, Wm. Millington; 7th, cop- per kettle, value 12s 6d, Thomas Horrobin ; Bth, tea- pot, value lle 6d, Walter Holden; 9th, umbrella, I value lOs 6d, Wm. Dooley; 10th, carvers, value fis„ John Thornton. In proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, secretary, and members of the Bowl; ing Green Committee, Councillor Wright said that the whole of the arranglements had been most satis- factorily carried out, and coupled with the name of the manager of the club (Mr. Stanley Higham), who had also worked hard to forward the success of he main. After the motion had been curie& Mr. John Roberts, chairman of the Bowling Greco Committee, and Mr. T. Mason (hon. sec.) spoke In reply. A Tote of thanks to Mr. Tinsley for distributing the prizes brought the proCeedings to szolcukeion.
Si. PAUL'S HARVEST FESTIVAL is announced to be held next Wednesday, when the Venerable Arch- deacon Lefroy will lbe the preacher. BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN CI4APEL.—An aclireAse-

_ meat in another column states that to-morrow (Sunday)*a harvest thanksgiving festival will be held eit this chapel. On the following Tuesday She Rev. Peter Mackenzie will preach in the afternoon., and in the evening he 'will give a lecture entitled, " Queen Esther." Saarons ASSAULT ON L VirONTAX.—At the Bor- ough Police Court, on Tuesday, a young man named James Clare was brought up, on a warrant charged with having assaulted Jane Tickler on the 15th inst. Complainant stated that prisoner came to her house, and' because she wouleUnot cat/ her daughter to him he kicked and struck her. It win the second , time he had` aasaulted her, and she was very much af raid of !ft.—Defendant, whose head was bound called the complainant's daughter; who said that 4:in the occaaion in question she saw her mother with a poker; and Clare's head bleeding.—Clare said that complainant struck him with the•poicer.— The Blanch, considering the assault proved; sena prisoner to,goal for two months, with havi'labour. SBOP ROBBERY By A NAVVY:—At the' Borough Pblice Court, on Monday, before- the. Mayor and other magistrates, James Williams, a• Ship, Canal labourer, was charged with stealing from the shop of Messrs. Scales and Son, Bridge-et, aipair of men@ boats; value /3.—Mr. Hunt, the chief c metable, stated that the prisoner, who came from Worcester- shire; and was employed on the Ship Canal, at Theltrall, was observed by an engine.driver, named JohirMitchell, employed at the " Surlight" Soap Works', on Saturday night, at about nine o'clock, loitering about the shop of Messrs. Sales and Son, Bridge-st. After- looking round to see if anyone saw him, prisoner was seen by Mitchell to snatch the beets from a. nail at the door mid make off with them. Mitchell followed Min and gave infor- mation to P.C. Bruen, who apprehended the pai- soner with the boots in his possession.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months with hard labiamr, and Mitchell was complimented by the• Mayor for his conduct in the affair. FAILURE OF A.N EARLESTOWN TRADES:KAN.—At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday morn- ing, Thomas Waring, plumber and painter, of 7 Stanley-st., Earlestown, came up for his first public examination. In answer to the Official Receiver (Mr. C. J. Dibb) the debtor said that a receiving order had been madeugainst him on his own peti•-• tion. Ile had resort to the Bankruptcy Cciurt in consequence •of one of the creditors having com— menced an action against hini. He commenced, business in 1885, prior to which time he was a. journeyman. The liabilities were .£313 7s Bd, and:, assets were disclosed'to the value of £l3O, after de- ducting a small sunuclue to preferential creditors. He attributed his failure to loss on a purchase of property, and-to bad debts. If he had not bought some property on which he sustained a loss he should have been solvent. The Official Receiver expressed himself satisfied with the examination, which was adjaurned for a week for the debtor to, sign the shorthand writer's transcript. A FAMILY Ph:I7I),AT EIIRTONWOOD.—At the War-- rington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Fairclough, a Burtonwood farmer, and has wife, Jane Fairclough, appeared in answer to a summons charging them with having assaulted another Burtortwood farmer named Samuel KU- shall. The statement of the complainant, who is cousin and brother-in-law to Thomas Fairclough, was to the effect that last evening week he went to the house of the Faircloughs, where his wife was, to ask if she was-coming home. When he asked' for his wife, he alleged, Mrs. Fairclough Called him a "scamp" and a" wastrel," and pushed him into the yard. Her husband, the male defendant, then knocked him down, got on the top of him, and gave him a " good laying on." Finally complainant was left bleeding on the ground, according to his own statement, a towel having been brought him with which to staunch the blood. For the defence the male defendant said that Kilsh all gave his wife a blow that knoeked her down, and he then com- mitted the assault, and Mrs. Fairclough said that the squabble originated because Kilshall had not been kind to his-wife. The magistrates told the parties that thejrahould endeavour to avoid 'such family squabbles. They discharged Mrs. Fair- clough, and fined Thomas Fairclough 5s and costs. VEGETABLE STEALING AT ORFORD.—On Wednes- day, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, two men named John Mather and John Warburton, were charged with having stolen thirteen celery roots and a quantity of potatoes, value 4s, from land at Orford, the property of John Fisher, a farmer. From the evidence of Police-sergeant Barns, it appeared that last Sunday morning, shortly after four o'clock, hie saw the twoprisoners going along Win wick-road, .n the direction of Winwick In about half an hour's

time he again! saw the prisoners, and Warburton was then carrying thirteen sticks of celery and the potatoes produced. Questioned as to how tney.be- came possessed orthe articles, prisoners replied that they had got them from a man named Tim. Finerty, of CroW-Ihnew Newton. The sergeant,. who had heard a'dogat Fisher's farm barking, took.the pri- soners there. Mr. Fisher was knocked up, andit was then discovered that thirteen sticks of oelery, had been pulled up, as well 118 a quantity of Beta-- , toes. On the advice of Mr. Browne, who appeared. for the prisoners, they decided to plead guilty: Mrc Browne then referred to the previous good charac- ter of Mather, 'and said that last Saturday night the men got drunk, and were suffering from the effects of drink when they committed the theft.. The magistrates limed Mather 208 and costs,, and sent Warburton to prison for a month. Birnewouns.—During Sunday night, ,or -early on the follovrim morning,- the.residence Of Mr: George, Howard, broker, 5, Hall-st., was broken into. and.a. robbery committed. Entrance was effected' by breaking a window. It is supposed that the thief, or 'thieves, must have gone upstairs, passed, through a bedroom in which two young women were sleep- ing, and entered the front room, occupied. by. Mr. and Mrs Hoivard. Some clothing was rifled; and a lady's gold watch, some loose silver, andankey were. taken. A sum of Bs, which was lying on the. mantlepiece, remained untouched. Another bed- room was afterwards entered, and a silver watch taken. Nothing was disturbed in the shop down- stairs. The robbery was not discovered, until the family arose on Monday morning: Mrs Howard had been upwith her infant twice duringthe night, but heard no noise. Her daughter was awakened by a smashing sound, but thinking it was caused by the cat breaking something, she paid, no heed to it.—On Sunday motning the premises of Messrs. A. Crofts and Brothers, outfitters, 346, Knutsford-road were broken into, and a quantity of clothing. was abstracted. At half-past twelve o'clock on Satur- day night the shop was securely fastened., but upon going downstairs at a quarter to sirs on Sunday morning Mr. Arthur Crofts noticed that a laigepane of glass, forming ariertion of the shop window, was broken, and discovered that several articles of cloth- ing had been stolen,, the value of the miesing goods being estimated at .£5. About a a.m. on Sunday, Mr. Luke Ellison,. the postmaster ot'Latch ford, who resides close by,. heard a crash as ofbreaking of glass, which caused him to' get up and; examine his pre- mises, but he found everything safe. Both cases • are being investigated by the police. ALLEGND TNNWNWS IN EillaiMMT OP,'GANZ:— At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesdayi Williena Ratcliffe and Williaet Bibby, young men, who live in Warrington, were brought up on a charge of having,on the 4th inst, been found on the highway in possession of a poaching net and pegs, under circumstances that led) to. the suspicion that they had been unlawfully in pursuit of game. The only evideno3 adduced for the prosoeution was that of Constable Parker (max stationed at Winwick, who said that soon after four o'clock on the morn- ing of the day in' question he saw the two defen- dants, in company with, two other men, who had been summoned, but did not appear, in Mill-lane„. Winwick. He searched l defendant Ratcliffe, ant found in his possession the-net produced. It was- wet, and was in his coat pocket. It appeared, the, constable said, to have been recently used. Rat- cliffe, 'who at the time gave the name of Rollinson, asserted that he had got the net at St. Helens. De- fendant William Bibby, whogave the name of Joe. Rollins, was carrying some net pegs that had also been recently used. The trousers of the defendants were wet up to the.knees,, and they, as well as the others who did not appear; gave wrong names and addresses. When 'accosted by the officer, they were ) coming from 'be-direction a land preserved by Mr. R. Stone, of Newton. They had no game about them, and denied having been poaching. When:be- fore thern. magistrates both defendants strongly de- nied havingbeen from home at the time in question. and Ratcliffe brought two witnesses who swore positiVely that he went to bed at ten o'clock on the night of the 3rd instant, and was seen in bed a, about Ave o'clock on the morning of the 4th inst.. and did not leave the house until after six o'clock , on the same morning. The magistrates adjourned the case for a fortnight, allowing the defendants )1 their liberty on their entering into recogulueens to I appear at the expiration of that period.

Herbert James Leadbeater was remanded at Dewsbury on Friday charged with stealing a mail bag. It is authovitatively announced that Canon Jayne, the vicar of Leecles.will be consecrated Etishop of Chester at York Minster on. November 13th.

The Royal yacht Osborne left Portsmouth on Friday for Ostend, where she embarked the Princess of Wales-1 and her daughters for Port Victoria. A dense fog prevailed at Belfast and on the coasts of 'Down and Antrim on Friday forenoon. Two steamers bound for Belfast grounded ra the Lough. Cottisiox ON TIM CLYDE.—The Sligosteamer Ivy col- lided with the riversteamer Sultana, on the Clyde on Fiiday. The Sultana has a large hole in her starboard bow, and the bulkhead is filled with water. The passen- gers were landed at lour o'cloch. The Sultana was after- wards docked.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT'EMAR LEICE3TER.-011 Friday morn- ing two coal trains collided at Rearsby Station, on the Midland Railway. Considerable damage was done to the rolling stock, but with the exception of a slight hurt to one of the stokers, nemersonal imiuries were reported The cause of the accident is not yst knewn. The mails were delayed. THE,: NEW Wimetenote:.—Another site has been offered to the,National Rifle Association for the annual shooting meeting. It consists of two , farms aggregating about seven hundred acres, and is situated four miles from Windser Castle. It is sakrto , afford many natural ad- vantages, and to have been, favourably spoken of by Lord Wintage and other competent judges. THE MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF A YOUNG-LADY.— The body of Miss Lyall, daughter of Mr. Watson. Lyall, proprietor of the " Sportsman's Guide," vrhomysteriously disappeared some days age at North Berwick, was found on Friday in the water near Leithes Rocks thcre. Miss Lyall was quite young, and well-known in the West End of London for beauty and grace.: The young lady, it is said, was engaged to a son of the late Mr. Tom Taylor, the dramatist. SHORT TIME IN THE COTTON TRADE.—Two-thirds-of the Spinning trade using American cotton having agreed to adopt short time, it was decided, at a meeting; of the Executive-Committee of the United Cotton Spinners' As- sociation, held in Manchester, on Friday afternoon, that the resolution take effect. By this means it is,theped the operations of speculative rings, which have dope serious mischief to the manufacturing interest,, will be thwarted. The employed are co-operating with the em- ployers. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A MAGISTRATE.*A shocking ac- cident was on Friday reported from. Aberystwith, where Mr. Richard James, borough magistrate and member of the Town Council, was killed whilst superintending some repairs at his residence, Broncastell. It appears that workmen were repairing the roof of the house,- and Mr. James, ascending the roof, fell through the ceiling to the paved floor beneath, death resulting shortly afterwards. -Mr. James was a large employer of labour, and was a candidate for the forthcoming Mayoral. election. Tire WHITECHAPEL TRAGEDIES : A NEW THEORY.—A 'London correspondent telegraphs that in connection with the Whitechapel murders the police, since the evidence given at the adjourned inquest on the woman Chapman, have gone on quite a new track. ,Thee now think it probable that the murder was committed by a ,prazy medical student. The anatomical knowledge dis- played in the mutilation of the • body has, of 'course, suggested this idea. Another fact which tends to strengthen the belief is that certain organs of the body were taken away by the assassin. The detectives are 'now making inquiries at the different hospital's with a "view to ascertain if any of the medical students have recently shown signs of mental aberration or have been at all eccentric in their behaviour. ' THE CANONIIIIRY MURDER.—Henry Glenn, apprehen- , ;Ind on Wednesday, on suspicion of being concerned in the murder of an old lady named Wright. at Canonbury, lin May last, was, on Friday, brought up at Clerkenwell ;Mice Court, and formally charged. Prisoner refused his address, but gave his occupation as a fitter of hot water apparatus. He is 24 years of age, and' o.f 'very re- spectable appearance. Detective-Sergeant Mahoney proved having apprehended prisoner on Wednesday night near King's Cross Station. When charged with, the of- fence he replied he would say nothing then. He admit- ted that the carpet bag sworn to by 'former fellOw work- men, and left behind by one of the murderers was for- merly his property, but said he some time back sold it to a man he did not know. A witness nameclffbnes gave it as his opinion that the prisoner was the man whom, on the date of the murder, he saw coming from the direction of Canonbury Terrace with a bag, but who then escaped. He could not swear to the prisoner, how- ever,- though he had picked him out- from . others. Pri- soner was•remanded.

THE YELLOW FEVER EPIDEMIC. A New York correspondent says that the yellow fever epidernic-appears to be spreading westwards. The announ- cement made on Thursday of its appearance in Alabama has beew followed by intelligence that the disease has broken out in the Mississippi, where five • cases are re- ported from Jackson, the State capital.
THE STANLEY EXPEDITION : ANOTHER CALAMI-
TOUS DEATH.

FRIISSELS, FRIDAY.—An official despatch received here by the officials of the Congo State announces that Mr. JameFon, who assumed command of the Stanley relief expedition after the death of Major Barttelot,.died of fever on the,l7th August, at Bangalas Station. It is believed here that any attempt to relieve Stanley by means of a fresh)expedition is now hopeless.
